item.title: Human Hunger
item.description:
Just after Christmas – on the 28th – I was in Kisumu, walking out of a pharmacy, when I ran into someone who said hello with unsettling enthusiasm. Right there at Acacia Mall. He wasn’t familiar to me. By how perky he was, I assumed he wanted to sell me something or ask me to donate something. Like my kidney.

I tried to walk around him, but Jesus had just been born not long ago, and it felt humane to stop and indulge him. Also, it was in how he confronted me – with a handshake. Very gung-ho. Confident. Certain I would take it.

It’s lazy to say I had no choice but to shake his outstretched hand. I did have a choice. We all have choices. Still, I shook his hand, even though I would have preferred a fist bump. You don’t know what people touch. If you knew half the things someone touched before they shook your hand, you’d get amoeba just from the thought.

We stood there, human traffic flowing all around us, and did the whole small-talk thing. The how-is-it. The how-have-you-beens. I didn’t want to be rude and ask him who the hell he was, or how exactly we knew each other. I figured if he spoke long enough, the penny would drop.

Then he mentioned a Steve.

“How is he doing?” he asked.

Which made me assume I was closer to Steve than he was. Because why else would he ask me? I’m not Steve’s keeper. I know a few Steves. Everybody knows a Steve. I’m not close to the Steves I know – at least not close enough for someone to ask me how they’re doing. The only Steve I was ever close to was way back in college. Many moons ago.

Seeing as I was already waist-deep in this deception, I heard myself say that Steve was doing great.

“Oh yeah?”

“Yeah. Have you not spoken to him lately?” I inquired.

“I haven’t seen or spoken to him since he came back from Dubai in, what, 2023?” he said.

Now I was sure I didn’t know this Steve. Because I don’t know any Steve in Dubai. At this point, I should have politely excused myself and run off. But guess what I did – and I’m not proud of it – I figured I’d take this conversation to the very top of the hill.

“Steve came back and got married almost right away -” I said recklessly.

“What do you mean?” He blinked fast. People who blink fast scare me. “What happened to Cynthia?”

Who the hell is..

“Oh, Cynthia… Cynthia left Steve.”

“What?”

Yeah, what?

“Yeah. When he came back, he got gangrene on his foot.”

“Gangrene?”

“Some sort of foot disease. Turns your foot black. Ugly thing.”

“Oh, I’m sorry…”

Sorry? I didn’t know why the hell he was apologising to me. I didn’t know who Steve was. Hell, I didn’t even know who this man was. He had thick hair – spongy, trimmed obsessively on the sides. The kind of hair you want to pat, for reasons you can’t immediately explain. Anyway, now we had a Steve with gangrene. The big question was, where do we go from here? What do we do with him and his rotten foot? We forge ahead, that’s what, albeit limping.

“Yeah, so it got worse by the day,” I mumbled, avoiding his eyes. “Eventually, they had to cut off his toe. The right toe, I think.”

He gasped a little too dramatically, as if it were his toe that had just been cut off. His eyes widened, searching for mine, which were still avoiding his. I think he was an empath, this fellow. He was on the chubby side of the scale. Most chubby fellows are very empathetic. I imagine. Like chubby babes, who, on top of being empaths, also have great laughs and can sing.

“That’s really bad!” he cried.

Oh, you think? It can get worse.

“So what happened was that when he lost his toe, he started losing his balance,” I continued. “Did you know that when you lose a toe or an ear, you sort of lose your balance?”

He was still shaking his head in disbelief at Steve’s rotten fortune, which was encouraging.

“Yeah, so anyway, his balance just went. He’d walk and stumble. Or fall. Like he was constantly drunk. We really take things like toes and ears for granted. And after they cut his toe, it was a struggle for a bit. I think it might have depressed him. I don’t know for sure, but I imagine. Imagine losing your toe. The next thing I heard was that Eunice just left.”

“Cynthia…”

Shit!

“Yeah, Cynthia. I don’t know why Eunice is in my head,” I chuckled. “But I’m not sure if she left because of the toe thing, or if Steve was a real pain in the ass and she was going to leave anyway and when he lost the toe she thought, ah, now is as good a time as any. He completely lost balance after that. Literally and figuratively.”

He caught himself from chuckling, but not in time. I grinned, as if to tell him it was okay to laugh at one man’s misfortune.

“And the kids?”

Kids? Steve has kids?

“No, their toes are fine,” I said.

He laughed.

“No, she left with the kids,I think – except the oldest one. That one was very close to Steve. Looks a bit like him too, wouldn’t you say?”

“I saw him when he was very little.”

Oh a him. Thought it was a girl. Fine.

“Oh, he grew into Steve, that one. Anyway, Steve went through it, man. I once ran into him at a petrol station.” I didn’t want to mention which petrol station, because I wasn’t sure which city Steve even lived in. “He had grown this disturbing stubble. You could tell from that stubble that he was going through a storm. You know how those student leaders – kina Orengo- looked in the 70s and 80s?”

“Yeah.”

“Yeah.”

“Was this after he had lost his foot?”

“He didn’t lose his foot – he lost his toe,” I corrected him, realising this was madness, what I was doing, but unable to stop. I was committed. “And yes, it was after. He was wobbly. Using a cane. I saw him at an ATM, holding the hand of a little boy he said was his nephew.”

I think I knew what the problem was. I had driven for six hours alone to Kisumu. Left before dawn, when it was still very dark, listening to a lot of Johnny Gill. In all that time, I hadn’t spoken to another human being. By the time I got to Kisumu, I was in a space – with a surplus of words that needed using. I felt an overwhelming need to connect with another human being. Verbally. I had what I prefer to call human hunger.

I also realised I needed to stop this delirium of fiction I was in. But I figured it was his fault. He had stopped me. I was minding my own business – picking up drugs from a pharmacy, then heading out to join my sister. I hadn’t asked for this interaction. He could have let me get on with my day. But he wanted to talk. This is what you get for stopping strangers. You get a cock-and-bull story.

“I wonder what happened to Cynthia?” He stared at the floor, certainly not looking for Cynthia there. “She was such a great wife.”

Yeah. Because you were married to her.

I wanted to kick him in the shin for making that naive statement.

People should stop commenting on what kind of wife or husband other people’s spouses were just because they interacted with them as friends and found them pleasant. Someone can be a great friend. A fantastic, compassionate colleague. And still be a truly dreadful spouse. The only person qualified to comment on what kind of wife Cynthia was… was Steve.

“In any case, Cynthia is married to some guy now,” I said. “I might have seen something like that on Facebook. A guy with a sloping forehead.”

He chuckled – not with humour, but incredulity.

“Are you serious?”

Yeah. Like a missing toe.

I shrugged.

We were officially gossiping now. The moment someone asks, are you serious? – it’s gossip. “You know how it is nowadays as a man,” I said conspiratorily. “You lose a toe and off she goes, running into another man’s arms – with all his toes.”

He laughed. “Man, I shouldn’t laugh.”

“No, you should,” I said. “Why wouldn’t you? It’s funny. I bet if you met Steve now and he told you this story, you’d laugh about it too. Not back then, of course. Then it was raw and painful.”

“It’s so strange. I used to run into his social media feed, ” he said.  “They looked so happy in Dubai.”

“Social media is window dressing,” I said, glumly.

I needed to run now, otherwise this man was going to discover I was a phony. He was still stunned by how Steve’s life had turned. Or maybe by how I had turned it. People love tragic stories. We warm ourselves against them. Maybe they make our own small tragedies feel manageable. I felt a flicker of guilt for ruining Steve’s life, so I figured I’d throw him a bone.

“But the silver lining,” I said, “was that he got a good job.”

“Oh yeah?”

“Yeah. I heard he’s doing really well. When God takes your toe and your wife, sometimes He gives you a good job,” I said. “Like Job in the Bible. Job really had it in the neck. But look at him now.”

I said this as if Job lives in Old Muthaiga and you can occasionally bump into him at the club having a Pilsner.

“Where does he work now?”

Who, Job?

“I’m not sure.” I really needed to go now. I’d had had my fun. I had taken Steve’s toe, taken away his wife, but given him a job. A great job. I felt I’d been more than generous. You can’t get another toe, yes – but you can always get another job and wife, right? I didn’t feel bad. Besides, I’m sure Steve has done some shit in this lifetime that needed punishing.

“I hope you’ve been well,” I told him, signalling my desire to sod off.

“Oh yeah, yeah. Not bad actually. I got transferred to Eldoret. I’m now running our office there.”

“Oh, that’s good. That’s good,” I said distractedly. “That’s going well, I suppose. You look like you’re making some money.” I pointed playfully at his belly.

“Bwana, this has to go in the New Year,” he said, then pulling out his phone, “I don’t think I still have your number.”

I quickly said I had changed my numbers. So I gave him one off the top of my head – something like 0720 876 365. And because I knew he’d want to call immediately so I could get his, which would blow my cover, I added, “Text me yours – my other phone is in the car.”

Which is something you hear a lot in Kisumu. Only there, they say my other iPhone.

“Good to see you, boss,” he said, extending that hand again for a handshake.

“A real pleasure,” I said. And I ran out of there.

I don’t know who the hell that fellow was. Or who Steve is. But I wish them well. I hope the year pans out well. I hope he never loses a toe. His balance. Or his wife.

This brief interaction isn’t the most interesting thing that happened to me in December – but it’s certainly one of them. What happened to you over these holidays?

Welcome back here.

Shall we do this tango all over again?

item.title: Love Is A Barricade
item.description:
In 2020, a gentleman called Abdirahman emailed me out of the blue and said, “You saved my life when I was working in Mogadishu.” I didn’t know what the hell was going on with him, but he said the blog made him “survive” that phase of his life and that he owed me a whisky from the commissary.

(“Is that not haram?” I gasped righteously on email.)

He was back home from Mogadishu and heading to Kendu Bay for work, then onwards to Homa Bay, Kisii and Migori. He’d never been to that part of the country. Just a Somali boy who had never gone past Uthiru. Would I care to give him insights on that side of the country?

Insights? Like what – eat the head of the fish first? Pee in the shrub, if you must?

I emailed him back and told him, “We all speak English better in that part of the country. So address everybody in English.”

We emailed back and forth for a few weeks (he wrote witty emails) and finally exchanged numbers and met up. We’ve remained friends since.

When we met, he was in a phase where he was struggling to be “a good Muslim.” He had drifted away from his faith and I could see the turmoil it caused. He wanted to “go back” because this new path was drawing him away from being a better father, a better husband.

Then one day – three years ago – he woke up and said, “This is it. I’m done.” And he made a 180-degree turn in his life. He reset everything. Brutally.

It’s easy to call this cold turkey. But it wasn’t cold turkey when the transformation was already happening inside, when he had already recognised the turmoil.

Anyway, he has stayed on the path since. He’s not a good Muslim; he’s a better Muslim. Which, obviously, makes him happier – and certainly makes his children, his wife and his mother proud.

(What Muslims seem to fear the most is disappointing their mothers.)

“I am free, infidel!” he keeps telling me.

He calls me an infidel. I call him a camel abuser.

Anyway, the only reason I’m telling you this story is because it’s his birthday today. He turns 39. And I’m proud of him – of his transformation, his willpower, and his focus on walking the path he chose.

And I hope Allah never lets go of his hand on this journey, stills his spirit, and accords him grace – for himself and for others – when he stumbles.

And in the spirit of good Muslims, there is another friend of mine called Halake.

I met him in Juba, South Sudan, when I went there for work in 2018. He took me out at night to see how South Sudanese partied. (Guns under tables. Lousy dancers.) We bonded over books and running. He’s the type who read many books – because what else is there to do in Juba? – and ran even when he was fasting during Ramadhan.

He was skinny. Now he isn’t skinny. He has since quit running.

A few years ago, he invited me for a traditional ceremony in his hometown, Isiolo. He was being ordained as a Borana chief. I wore my kanzu and all, sat in a circle with a bunch of men, and ate with our hands.

As a mark of friendship, he later handed me the warm scrotum of a slaughtered cow – balls! – to take home.

Nobody had ever given me balls before.

I have him resaved on my phone: Halake, Paramount Chief.

He’s also a writer. He sent me something he has written, which I’m going to run as is.

Here goes.

By Mohamud Halake

My father never wore cologne. He didn’t need to. Nyali Bridge wore it for him. Mombasa wore it for him. When he hugged you, you carried him home on your shirt: old leather, salt air, sun-baked khaki, and that stubborn coastal smell that doesn’t ask permission. Even after he let you go, you found yourself speaking a little softer, standing a little straighter, like you’d just been told – without words – to behave.

He’s ninety-four now. My father. He shuffles to the bathroom in socks that slide on tiles. Sometimes there’s a small wet patch on the seat where he sat. Sometimes the smell arrives before he does. He calls me by another man’s name and waits for me to answer. I answer anyway. I’ve learned that dignity is not only something you keep; sometimes it’s something you lend.

But in my head, he’s still the young, chubby Ethiopian man who became a Kenyan traffic cop, pressed into a crisp uniform that made him look honest even before he opened his mouth. Before the toll station at Nyali Bridge, there was Garba Tulla. And Kinna. He married my mother, Kameh, when she was twelve.

You’d say twelve is chalk dust and scraped knees. It’s vowels whispered under your breath because you’re afraid you’ll forget them by morning. In my mind, I see my mother hunched over a slate, tongue peeping out in focus, tracing letters in the dirt and repeating them like a spell – as if the alphabet is a rope you hold so you don’t float away.

Then one day the house fills with women and warm water and instructions. Hair oiled and plaited. Cloth wrapped and re-wrapped. Henna drying on fingers that still look like a child’s. Aunties adjusting her headscarf, telling her to stop fidgeting, to sit still, to be “good.”

Outside, the sixties are happening and Kenya is still new enough to feel like it’s learning its own name. I suspect she even wore her skirt – the green, the red, the black and the white.

Three years later, at fifteen, my mother is in a different room learning a different lesson. A lantern hisses in the corner. Women crowd in. The midwife’s voice slices through the night with urgency. And before dawn, Khadija arrives -my elder sister- small, loud, alive; placed into arms that were still learning what it meant to hold the future.

That’s how some people enter adulthood: not by choice, but by weight.

My father was a cop all his life. In Nyali, at dusk, he’d come home with his pockets heavy – not with abundance, just work turned into money. He’d empty them onto the table and out would spill five-shilling notes: brown and tired, folded into themselves like secrets. Giraffes and buffaloes on the back. Shillingi Tano printed at the foot like a small oath.

We’d sit cross-legged on the floor and uncrumple them together. My job was easy: hold the corners, smooth the creases. His hands did the real work – thumb and forefinger flattening each note with a patience that felt endless. I loved the smell clinging to the bills: grease from steering wheels, ocean spray, sweat that had learned discipline.

Once I asked why he never brought home crisp notes. He didn’t look up. His fingers kept smoothing.

“So that you will be paid in new, crunchy notes,” he said.

I nodded the way children nod, accepting the sentence without understanding what was hidden inside it. At that age, you think money is the story. You don’t yet know sacrifice is the story.

Now, standing by the Nile, I understand.

A few metres away, an aid worker in a faded blue bib cups a child’s jaw and squeezes peanut paste into his mouth. He is all ribs and eyes. The paste sticks to his lips like a promise refusing to fall. His mother stands close, arms locked across her chest, watching with the kind of focus you only see when everything you love is fragile.

The Nile slides past us, muddy and indifferent, doing what rivers do: moving on.

In that small scene – paste, swallowing, a mother refusing to blink – I hear my father’s voice as clearly as if he’s behind me. I feel his calloused fingers again, smoothing paper, flattening a crease, turning something tired into a child’s dream.

Everything circles back: crumpled notes in Nyali, peanut paste in Malakal. The same sacrifice, just a different currency.

I first came here in September 2011. I stepped off a KQ flight with a full crop of hair and no grey in my beard, carrying too much optimism in my carry-on. South Sudan was two months old then – new flag, new slogans, that shiny newborn feeling that makes people speak in big words and forget what humans become when hunger and fear move into their ribs.

I was younger. I believed in nation-building the way young men believe in gym memberships: pay the fee, show up a few times, and transformation is guaranteed.

Now I’m forty-something, six feet tall and wiry, with a beard that has gone rogue. I’ve lived long enough in airports, suitcases and compounds to know the world rarely transforms on schedule. It transforms when it wants, and usually after it has broken a few things first.

I can also pass for almost any nationality if I keep quiet. My face – this tea-with-turmeric complexion – invites strangers to greet me in Amharic, Arabic, Somali, Tigrinya. Touareg even. Once, a Habesha man started speaking to me with the confidence of someone who had found his cousin; when I stared back blankly, he laughed, patted my shoulder, and tried another language like we were buying onions.

“I’m Kenyan,” I say.

They blink, recalibrating. They don’t know we Kenyans are an omnibus – cultures, traditions and faiths piled together, accents stacked like old suitcases – a country that can make your face belong to ten places at once. Sometimes that’s a gift. Other times it’s just another mask. Either way, you learn to wear it without letting it own you.

In Bor’s IDP camp, school-kids gathered around me like I was a visitor worth studying. Their uniforms were threadbare; their laughter wasn’t.

“Uncle,” the smallest girl asked, “do your children go to school?”

I nodded.

“Do they have goats?” another boy shouted, because children always ask about the real economy.

“Only when they visit the village,” I said.

They giggled like I’d handed them sweets.

We sat on a plastic mat and drew maps in the dirt – imaginary wild animals, rivers that disobeyed borders, lakes shaped like countries nobody has claimed yet. I asked them who invented subtraction.

“My mother,” a boy said, dust on his eyelashes, “when she takes food from my plate.”

I laughed sincerely. Then the laugh stopped when I looked at his wrists and the way his shirt hung on him like it was borrowed.

When I handed them pencils, they gripped them like candles. Not tools. Like something sacred. Like a vigil.

“Do your children have pencils?” the smallest girl whispered.

“Just one,” I lied.

It wasn’t clever. It was desperate – an attempt to shrink the distance between our lives for a second. The distance didn’t shrink. It just sat there, huge and rude. I looked past them toward the Nile because sometimes you need a horizon to hold your shame.

As I was leaving, a boy ran up with a mango the size of my fist, mottled yellow and green, bruised in places, warm from the sun.

“For your daughter,” he said, pressing it into my palm.

I froze. Which one? I wanted to ask. The question rose and stuck.

Instead, I bent to his height. “Shukran,” I whispered.

He grinned – teeth white against cracked lips – and ran back into the dust.

I kept that mango in my bag until it softened. For days, everything I owned smelled faintly sweet, like kindness refusing to leave.

Bentiu broke me in a quiet way. Mid-morning on a weekday – the hour when school bells should be ringing. Instead, children played hide-and-seek among freshly dug graves. Their laughter bounced off wooden crosses as if death were just another hiding place.

A boy sat on a mound of dirt, shaping a toy car from sticks, focused and calm, tongue slightly out like an engineer solving a hard equation.

I thought of my kids in Karen, Nairobi – cheeks chubby, shoes polished, blazers sharp, speaking English with that private-school British twang.

The contrast didn’t just hurt. It felt obscene.

Malakal taught me that war has a smell. Not just blood. Not just fear. In a burned hospital, melted plastic hung in the air like burnt sugar. Ash covered the floor like a grey carpet. Outside the paediatric wing, a human skull lay half-hidden, casual as litter.

Inside, the neonatal ward was a blackened shell. Beds stripped of purpose. Walls smoked into silence. On a filthy bedside table, someone had left behind a rhinestone-studded shoe – a single shoe, glittering stupidly in the ruin, as if beauty had wandered into violence and got lost.

War doesn’t only kill bodies; it kills the ordinary evidence that people once lived here. It burns memory. It erases the small things that prove a child was loved.

Violence isn’t just bullets and fire. It’s women slipping beyond razor wire to gather firewood. It’s crocodiles. Armed men. Children flinching when a soda bottle pops because their bodies have learned that sudden sound means danger.

I’ve seen men cry when they receive a small bag of sorghum. I’ve seen a doctor stand over a burned-out incubator and whisper, “There were twelve babies here,” as if the air might argue.

Privilege can bruise.

In my air-conditioned prefab, the AC hums like comfort. Outside, heat presses down like a palm. One afternoon I switched it off and let the room become honest. Sweat arrived immediately, as if it had been waiting in the corridor.

I folded my mosquito net and carried it outside. Under a thorn tree, a mother fanned her infant with a scrap of cardboard. The baby’s eyes were half-closed. The mother’s were fully open – those eyes that don’t get to rest.

“For your baby,” I said, handing her the net.

She stared at it, then at me, then back at it, as if gratitude were something you inspect for traps.

That night, mosquitoes buzzed in my room like small machines. I lay awake sweating, listening to the same heat the mother and baby were listening to outside. It wasn’t heroism. It was the closest I could get to truth without drowning in it.

When supply planes don’t come and food runs thin, I fast. Not as martyrdom – just mimicry. A way of letting my body briefly sit in the hunger that lives just beyond my door.

Hunger sharpens memory.

Growing up poor, our home was a cacophony of twenty-five siblings. My father – with six wives and one cop salary – shepherded us like a conductor trying to keep time with a broken orchestra. Dinner was elbows and knees and whispers. His peanut salary stretched like a rubber band; sometimes it snapped and we all heard the sound.

I sat the KCPE exams on an empty stomach and topped my class – not because I was special, but because failure was too expensive.

At Isiolo Boys, misery changed uniform: thin porridge, cold showers, torn socks. I clung to books like a life raft. Being top again got me to the University of Nairobi, Chiromo, where ambition smells like dust, ink and impatience.

Now I measure distance by airports. Doors open. People listen. They queue to shake your hand. Life does that strange thing where it drags you from smoothing crumpled notes on a floor to speaking in rooms that smell like carpet, policy and power.

In 2016, I built a three-bedroom bungalow for my parents. Cost a small fortune. The handover had no confetti – no speeches, no ribbon. Just keys passed into a calloused hand.

My father stood in the doorway like he wasn’t sure he was allowed. My mother checked the taps and sat in every room, trying to memorize the air. I heard her cry in the kitchen.

They never asked for anything. I couldn’t repay them. But I could give them this – my small way of saying their sacrifices landed somewhere solid. That they mattered.

Leyla, the mother of my children, holds our life together – four boys and little Chaaltu, homework and tantrums and birthdays, all the small daily emergencies that make a family.

When she asks, “How’s Juba?” I tell her about the heat that sits on your chest like a sleeping goat. About floodwater that never recedes. About campfires that make the night sky glow orange. I leave out the melted plastic. The charred incubator. She doesn’t need all my darkness.

After we buried Rufoh, our first daughter, I thought I had forgotten how to smile. Then Chaaltu arrived – a carbon copy, right down to the dimple – and stole my eyes the way her sister had.

When I sit by the Nile and watch fishermen cast nets into brown water, I think of her in Nairobi drawing circles in a sandpit, making worlds that don’t know war yet.

Grief and joy can sit on the same bench, shoulders touching, not speaking.

These scenes pile up like sandbags against a river. Some days they hold. Some days the river rises.

That’s why I tell you about my father’s crumpled notes, the mango in Bor, the burned hospital in Malakal. Details are life preservers. Grab enough and maybe you don’t drown.

I keep returning, in my head, to that floor in Mombasa: a boy, his father, five-shilling notes, patient hands.

A man smoothing out what the world kept crushing.

What is fatherhood, really, if not learning – again and again – to hold Rufoh’s memory in one arm and a starving child in Malakal in the other?

item.title: Big Deal
item.description:
We are blind men being led by the hands of life. We aren’t fully aware of where life leads us. Sometimes it leads you to Wote, Makueni – as I discovered yesterday. In Wote, this same life led us to our abode for the night, a hotel called – wait for it – Kusyombunguo.

Isn’t it amazing that someone – wealthy, most likely – can have the temerity to name a hotel with a name nobody can pronounce? That they sat in a meeting and said, “We are going to call it Kusyombunguo” and someone said. “Sir, I don’t think anyone will remember that name, let alone pronounce it.” And the boss probably growled, “They’ll remember it if we build a swimming pool!”

That’s how I found myself staring out at the swimming pool from my hotel room window last evening, having just dropped my backpack on the chair and taken a leak. The problem: I hadn’t packed swimming trunks. Which isn’t a problem if you are enslaved by shame.

I went downstairs anyway and asked for a towel from a very old, very bored pool attendant watching videos on his phone. He didn’t appreciate the interruption. “Tuna funga saa kumi na mbili,” he growled.

I glanced at my Garmin watch – because I’m a triathlete now; I don’t wear the watches you people wear – and said, “Niko na one hour.”

He handed me a towel so rough it could sand furniture. I stripped down to my boxers and stood at the edge of that luscious blue pool. That’s when he reappeared.

“Huna siruaru ya kuogele?”

He must have said something else, but I’m Luo, so I heard “siruaru.” I told him I didn’t carry any. He stared at my boxers – pink striped – sighed deeply, and walked away.

Anyway, I’m still in Makueni. Ashioya is holding fort this week. He lost his mother, and he’s now doing drugs. He is hurting, so we will pretend that we aren’t concerned.

By Eddy Ashioya

When paying for cocaine at K-town’s catty dealer, gentlemen, it is imperative that you don’t ask too many questions. You are less suspicious, as any drug dealer worth the jailtime would tell you, and they may even like you, stretch your shillings to its elastic limit. Eight neat lines lay chopped on my switched-off Oppo phone, an Equity Gold debit card beside them, the white powder arranged like a row of cirrus clouds. I remember thinking there was something obscene-looking about that scene.

K-Town is an abject, ugly town with all its dirty laundry available for inspection—matatus that are driven by psychiatric candidates, nduthis that are ridden by psychiatric fugitives and pedestrians on psychosis.  Sheesh, it’s annoying. Or, in modern parlance, triggering. But this is Nairobi, and there’s no law against being annoying.

We are here in one of those estates that you buy only after listening to that morning radio duo, Maina and his sidekick King’ang’i wailing on the radio, telling you, what is it they are telling you?  Land banking, they say. Big deal! Get yourself this prime property, just four hours from the beach! Don’t wait to buy; buy and wait. Digehota! And then they laugh. Is it you they are laughing at? Hard to say.

None of this is important, really. You probably just want to know why it is I am doing cocaine on a Tuesday evening. The short answer is I don’t know. Or maybe I just don’t care. No, that isn’t true, although it’s what I have told myself from time to time as an excuse. There is a drug for every reason and a reason for every drug. When you think about it, it’s mighty crazy how accessible all these drugs are, with a plug a phone away. If you get too parochial about it, you might even consider doing random drug tests for your children, but it’s too late. You cannot eradicate; you can only hope to contain. Some people get punished. Some of us, we get away with murder. You know how it is. The appearance of the law must be upheld, especially while it’s being broken.

The array of drugs is laid out. Molly, acid, coke, weed…and KC Ginger. Dealer’s choice, if you can pardon the pun. I am pretty much disciplined, believe it or not, so I steer clear of anything that will inhibit my inhibitions. In other words, KC Ginger has to go. I am half-disappointed when they don’t remove a knife and stab the coke and put it close to their nose like Pablo Escobar said should be done, or perhaps I have watched too much DJ Afro. Instead, they roll an American dollar bill, which they kept calling a Washington, something I suppose only cool cats do, and then they offer me first rites. Virginity has its perks.

On the boombox, they are playing Toxic Lyricali. Because drugs hit harder when the music is hard; hence some “Backbencher ndani ya S class. Chuo tulipata E…” I keep quiet on the “E” part cause I actually passed my exams, A student that I am. But I wouldn’t mind an S Class. I consider asking them to play Otile Brown, whose voice is like raw heartache in Jeraha, because that’s love, that was the way love was – but I decide against it. No self-respecting crackhead listens to Otile.

The first line almost took my head off. I feel a tingling buzz that’s like the first wave of a coke rush. An assault on my senses, like a thief picking a lock. No joke. Some girl waltz in. Her name’s Petty or Pretty or Petra. Some name with a vowel in it. She had large, Fricano eyes, full of a certain amount of smoke and mystery and bad luck. Later, I learn she is the drug dealer’s piece, as if the handholding and fondling and frolicking isn’t enough clue. Not that I care. She couldn’t be any older than 23, 24 if I am being generous, a snake tattoo slithering from the small of her back. She snorts her first line and a smile cracks her face. She does two more lines in quick succession, and my mouth forms an invisible Wow. The prospect of overdosing did not deter her. She was up for whatever. When she comes back for air, white freckles like dirty raindrops lay siege on her nostrils. I knew exactly what every nigger in the room was thinking because I was thinking it too. Her eyes meet mine, and I feel something fall apart inside me.

My drug lord has been doing this for a while now, a drug dealer who got God on their side. To paraphrase Bruce Lee, don’t fear the man who has cut 10,000 lines once, but the man who has cut one line 10,000 times. He tells me how much a gram is. He shows me his tattoos, which run from the nape of his neck all the way to his ankles. He takes off his T-shirt, and I look away, because I am respectful like that. I don’t know if he knows this, but I don’t like him like that, and besides, I prefer my men with a vagina instead. I may be reckless, but I am not dumb. Thankfully, he just wants to show me more tattoos – funny what you could bond over – most of which are gang signs and guns and a Bible verse. Such a cliché. What is it with gangsters and Bible verses? I am not impressed, especially because he picked the most pickable verse in the world. John 3:16. No shit.

It felt good to be doing drugs; it was like being immortal and unbeatable and unbwogable, like Eve tasting the apple, like a bee suffering from diabetes, like a virgin fondling with a small phallus. Or something better than happiness. Peace. So why am I suddenly missing my mother at 2-something AM, or so? I have pretended I don’t remember a thing about that time when I would visit Ma in the hospital, and she would remind me that when I was seven or eight, I promised to buy her a Land Rover Defender, so cheer up, son, I am not dying any time soon, one of those throwaway things mothers say. But then mothers break your heart. Mothers die. Mothers die every day. Big deal. You wish you could have just one more conversation, no matter how awful it was, and even though you are not much of a talker, you’d never shut up, wearing out the Grim Reaper, because even the worst moment is better than knowing there never will be any others. Hospitals have a certain inevitability about them, you see. Either you make it, or you don’t. She didn’t. You’d think I would tire of that last conversation with the days passing, but I don’t. When you lose someone from your life, you want to remember some big, important things they said, but sometimes all you come up with are throwaway lines.

Once, on campus, I read in a Joyce Carol Oates book that anything a man cares for, after he’s dead, seems like some weakness of his. Being dead is a weakness, you see. You can’t speak for yourself any longer; everybody else is gabbing and yammering and making speeches over you like they are chewing you up and getting set to swallow. Ma always encouraged us to read and eat books and become whatever it is we were supposed to be. “Chuo tulipata E…” the niggers are shouting; trust a Kenyan with bad timing.

In therapy, they tell you that no one can own your story better than you. They teach us that when you own your story, it loses its power over you, blame has nothing to do with it, they teach us, and, like you, the first time I heard such absurdities, I laughed. Therapy speak. Nonsense isn’t the right word, but it’s the first word that comes to mind. And you’d talk. My God. All that incessant chatter, parsing through cobwebs of your childhood, through the libidinous years of teenage that hardened the exoskeleton of your adult life, the therapist nodding along, never in a hurry, watching you disintegrate in her Venus flytrap, the only way out was to use your words, which she replied only with a ‘Mmh’ or ‘And…’ or ‘Go on…’. Then only the demons inhabiting us could be seen. I think this is what adulting really is. The desire to hold on to your childhood. Yet, for each drop of water one received, one repaid with a well.

Ras, one more?

They have laid out fresh lines. Toxic, on the boombox, insists he hasn’t changed his number. “Namba ni jamo bado sijai badilisha…”

What harm could one more line do? Cocaine may not be the most popular drug around, but it has the best celebrity endorsement. Kurt Cobain. Amy Winehouse. Whitney Houston. Say what you want, I am in the realm of the greats. So…what is this millennial ennui tightening my throat? This tendency to think too hard and do too little. That no matter how good life was, there is always the nagging worry that you are missing a more interesting one. We had that helpless, destined feeling, like the water got poisoned and we got used to the taste. You might say that life itself is an answer unto itself, that life has a way of getting in the way of, erm, life, that somehow, one will always miss out on something, but I don’t think I could agree with that. Ah, fuck it. Life is for the living. Nothing mattered except that we were alive. If you believe in God, you believe that. And if you don’t believe in God, well, it’s obvious.

So what’s one more line? Big deal. I can quit anytime I want, I tell myself. Like that. By the end of this sentence.

item.title: What Do You Think?
item.description:
Yesterday, way before the sun would come up, I picked up two teenage girls on the road.

I had set off from the village at 5 am on an 8-hour journey back to Nairobi. Most of that early morning drive happens in darkness, the road rising and plunging, the lake glistering on the left. Otile Brown was playing on my stereo, some song about betrayal, about love.

By the roadside, I’d occasionally happen upon two or three groups of school kids walking. High schoolers who perhaps were expected to start class at 6 am. As I finished a small hill, where the road curved right, my headlights fell on a figure standing by the roadside. A girl with a backpack on her back. Closer, I realised it was a schoolgirl. Just standing there in darkness, waiting for God knows what.

I stopped right before her, rolled down the passenger window and switched on the overhead light so she could see that I was only an SDA boy. I lowered Otile Brown and said hello. She regarded me, looked down the road at the darkness, and said a shy hello. I asked her if she wanted a ride. She hesitated and said, “OK.” Then she jumped in. She smelled of soap and a faint hint of sweat. I asked her if she wasn’t scared of the darkness. Where she schooled. (Waondo Mixed Day). What form she was in. If she liked school. She mumbled her responses from the back. I felt her stiffness, alertness.

Further down, I stopped for another girl who also jumped in the back. “Do you guys know each other?” I asked the new girl as we set off, and she said yeah. “So how come you didn’t say hello to each other?” They said hello to each other. I grinned in the dark.

They weren’t very chatty, the pair, and I was happy to listen to Otile. We drove in silence. Then I dropped them off ten minutes later, at another dark stretch of road, opposite a path that led to the school. More students were trooping in now, in that weak morning light, like soldiers off to an ambush.

I thought, these kids can’t be any older than 15. They are younger than the blog.

The blog is 16 years old this year. Can you believe it? Each year, I have tried to do a themed something. This year I’m out of ideas, so I’m putting it to you guys – the Gang.

I was thinking of doing something around the jobs people do. Going to watch a surgeon cut open a brain. A mortician embalm a body. A lawyer in court. A pastry chef in a big hotel. The worlds people disappear into every day that we never see. But I need it to have legs, and I’m not sure it does – so I’m opening it up.

What do you want to read this year? The most requested idea is what I will run with. Democracy and all that jazz.

Over to you.

item.title: No Women For Old Men
item.description:
Whatever happened to Anonymous?” A friend of mine I was chatting with last week, asked me. Anonymous is this writer fellow that I know. We all used to read him when we were coming up as writers. He always sounded weird/quirky on paper. Someone who woke up to write in his underwear or naked, a bottle of vodka by his elbow and a skinny naked girl sleeping, face down, on his bed nearby, one hand dangling from the bed’s edge. A quintessential writer of lore. The last of his kind. He reminds me of  Charles Bukowski, in many ways. And we know Charles was off his rocker.

And when I saw him for the first time – someone pointed him out at an event – he looked like a typical writer. He had a drink in hand, was holding court in a group that gathered around him in a semi-circle, and they were laughing at whatever he was saying. He was writing books and things, and both myth and notoriety followed him in each room. I didn’t know it was possible to make an acquaintance of someone like that, I didn’t befriend edgy people like that, but eventually our stars soon collided one day as they were meant to be (Fatherly hand on shoulder: Oh you are the mysterious zulu man! ) and it turned out he was everything I expected; weird, quirky, witty and sharp like an Ahlspiess. He was a typical writer; he carried a backpack on his back, which I could have paid many good pieces of silver to rummage through and write about its contents, and always had a bottle of soda, which any fool would know wasn’t a soda. He wrote his thoughts and drafts in this dog-eared notebook, which I could have paid the remaining pieces of silver to read.
Anyway, I Whatsapped him last week after my friend asked me whatever happened to him. He responded immediately, “I’m good, brother Biko.” [He calls me that, as if I own a church.] “I am in Guangdong now. I turned 50, you know.” I immediately Googled what a writer would be doing in Guangdong.

We had a little light banter. [I always chuckle reading his messages. He’s a bit mad, this fellow]. Conversation swerved slightly into a ditch that is Valentine’s Day, where our wheels whirred uncontrollably, which led him to say, “I could write something.” I had been scheduled to interview a gambler lawyer fellow who ghosted me, so I had nothing complete this week. I said, “Don’t you say you will write something then you don’t come through, boss.”

He said. “I’m a man of honour, brother Biko.”

And who better to write a love story?

Here, joining this week’s podcast (he-he) is Anonymous.

There are no women in this town

By Anonymous

Women are always complaining that there are no men in Nairobi – by which they mean that there is no man who fits the ideal in their head, which is why most of them won’t be all red dresses flowing on city streets with flowers of bouquets floating above salon-coiffed heads this coming Saturday. Fact: Some are actively anti-Valentine, and there’s a suspicious amount of activities planned this coming weekend that don’t have the theme of ‘love’ (ooo, sweet love) featuring in them.

There’s a ‘Shoot your Shot’ by one Amakove, and it sounds like playing pool – or rather, playing in the dating pool.

“I’m a 44-year-old lady based in Nairobi, interested in meeting a healed 44-50 year old man with a kind heart, growth driven, has purpose and direction in his life, and has a well-established career or business. I’m interested in a connection that will lead to marriage. I’ve never been married myself, don’t have kids, but I have an established career. Email me at innerchild@gmail.com + your full photo.”

I fit the bill – and just when a man is calculating mailing this lady, here comes one Aliet with the cynical warning that the sub-text of this woman’s message is this:

“I’ve dated dozens of damaged dudes, and now ready to settle with one who will fulfil all my needs without question, and is able to fund my lifestyle and pay all the bills. I have not yet met any mate worth me, but maybe you’ll get lucky, mate; and now, too old for kids, I still want a ‘retirement’ companion who is still tall, dark and handsome, looks good on IG, and gives me ‘baby girl’ treatment, (because her email name is ‘Inner Child’).” So I don’t email her.

As a fifty-year-old “Mubaba”, I can equally say, and with confidence, that “there are no women in this town.”

Of course, there are many women in Kenya – 28.5 million, and 18 million of them are adult females, so presumably marriageable. The greater Nairobi metropolitan area has 6 million folks, and of these ones, there are almost two million adult females. (Sorry if I’m coming across sounding like wale watu wa census).

But even with two million of them roaming the Nairobi streets, there are still no women in this town.

At least not since Lorraine, or Lora as I called her.

Our story began a month after my (ex) wife walked out of our house on the Labour Day of 2021, although technically, it could have been on any of the preceding days of the week that I was away on a business conference in Marrakesh.

What I’ll never forget is landing at the Jomo Kenyatta Intl. Airport, and Uber driving me to my apartment, me ringing the doorbell on the ninth floor (I like city views), and when there was no answer, using my key to get in – and the smell of emptiness hitting my nostrils like fish gone bad, or eggs given in to stench.

It wasn’t technically empty – she had left my bed, hadn’t burnt my clothes (asante, mama), and her departure note wasn’t stuck on the refrigerator like the movies – because she had “kuhama’d na fridge” – but it was in the kitchen nonetheless.

In the drawer where she had left one plate, one knife, one spoon, one fork, and two spoons – one table, the other tea…

“If you want to invite any of your side-dishes here,” the note read, and I was sure the pun was unintended, as my Ex isn’t the word-jester type, “they’ll have to bring their own cutlery.”

That was my Ex, both cruel and considerate. Still is.

In the same spirit, she’d cleared the living room of everything, kila kitu, except my large armchair and the giant screen T.V. that I loved watching the EPL / CL on.

I switched on the T.V., and because it was Labour Day, Atwoli’s round mug, which I find extremely unappealing, filled the screen; as that grating, querulous voice screeched in my ears. To date, when I see the chap on TV, it brings that sickening Saturday of my life when my wife of ten years abandoned ship.

A month later, exactly, at a Madaraka Day concert, I ran into Lorraine, literally, at one of those temporary bars that they create for those kinds of events, from tents.

I was still distraught from my “divorce”, where I had also lost my nine-year-old daughter, and although I don’t like concerts, I was going out to one every weekend, just so as not to chill in the chill of my crib that was no longer a crib. It had become just a digs, and when I lay in my king-size bed at night, it felt like I’d gotten drunk and slipped into a ditch.

Now I was buzzed at the concert, and aiming for half-blind drunk, and as I charged at the bar, a tall, chocolate-skinned lass in a bright blue blouse that showed a bare waist with a dancer’s ring and navel piercings (I donno what they’re all called), and those flared jeans, very wide at the bottom, and bright pink sandals with rhinestones, and a proper Afro like a crown, with an actual jasmine tucked behind her ear – this girl turned with two cans in her hands – and I barged into her, and down went drinks, drowning in grass!

“I’m sorry –” I started, but she cut me off with a –

“Just because I’m tipsy doesn’t mean you have to nibble my nipple…”

“I’m sorry, what did you say?” I said, thinking me drunken.

“Topple my tipple,” she said. “I did tell you I was wee tipsy.”

And only then did I know that this girl, who looked to be in her mid-twenties, was teasing.

Naturally, I bought her her cans, Guaranas, and got my Black Label, and we sat together and ignored the concert – turned out later, she was concert-obsessed, but had made a concession for me that day, by way of confession; and that she was a Human Rights lawyer with some N.G.O. and a poet (toppling tipples, nibbling nipples) and noted I had never met anyone, girl or guy, who spoke as sparklingly as she did and I consider myself a pretty witty chap, myself;  in my youth I even appeared in a skit with ‘Redykyulas’ when I was a fresher in K.U., which got me laid by a Third Year lady  – (and that is all Kiarie John has ever done for me, even now as my current M.P.; not that I don’t really like the guy, I do)!!

Lorraine told me she believed in fate and astrology. I think ‘stars’ are a bunch of hogwash and burning suns, and asked me what star sign I was. It went like so:

“I’m Cancer. What are you?”

“Non-cancerous, na tuna shukuru Mungu…”

“Seriously, what date is your birthday?”

“Exactly a month from today.”

“July 1st,” she said, looking star-struck or shell-shocked.

“I am July 1st, 1995.”

“Well,” I said, sipping my drink, “if that’s true, and though I’m twenty years older than you, to the dot, I suppose that makes us soulmates…”

“It just makes us Happy Birthday mates,” Lora said.

“I thought you believed in constellation signs, and all that…”

“I do,” Lorraine said, “but wewe si type yangu.”

Surprisingly, that hurt more because it wasn’t supposed to.

“I like my guys tall, dark and handsome,” she said.

“And I like my girls shorter, hotter, and a little older.”

“Touche,” she said, with a cute finger-tip  salute, like she was tipping a cap,  and I ended up dropping her home – or at least near her home – “because,” Lora said, “you may be a serial killer, so I don’t want you to know my S.Q.”

“I am a serial killer,” I said. “That’s why I never go to these malls where they say boss, fungua ‘boot’…”

Her happy laughter stayed ringing in my ears, long after I had driven off, with the name ‘Lorraine’ ringing on my mind.

I waited a week to hear from her, then when I didn’t, sent her a ‘casual’ text on WhatsApp chat. She replied right away:

“Mzeaddy, you mean I didn’t BLOCK you?”

Three weeks later, we had a fancy joint birthday dinner together, my treat, About Thyme, and then spent Saturday afternoons that July doing relatively tame outings: a SLAM poetry afternoon, watching a LIVE soccer game at Nyayo stadium, going for a movie called ‘Cruella’ about some young grafter called Estella, whom during the 1970s London punk rock revolution, transforms herself into the raucous hell-bent-for-revenge, Cruella de Vil.

Lorraine loved that film, me not as much, and we debated over drinks at the same cinema-mall, at the end of which she called a Bolt, and bolted.

“But I can drop you home, Lora,” I said.

“You are drunk!”

“So, what happens to me if I’m too drunk to drive?”

“Then you’ll be dead drunk,” she said, gave me a peck, and bounced.

Maybe that was the moment, watching her sashay away, that I realised how deeply ‘into’ Lorraine, as we Ole Skoolers call it, that I was – and I was scared.

That next Sunday of August 1st, exactly two months after we met, we slept together for the first of perhaps one thousand times, or maybe 665, sijui …

It was the first time she ever came to my place, and I poured her and me a whiskey, placing the bottle – and the Sprite she insisted on spoiling the single malt with – on my recently acquired coffee table.

Then she perched her long, lithe, slim self on the edge of my armchair, tush next to my elbow, as I switched on the TV to a local station where there was a documentary on the 1982 attempted coup going on.

Lora, who wasn’t a fan of local history of anything that happened before the PEV of January 2008 – but perversely obsessive of everything that has happened since – mock yawned ‘b.o. ring’, and next thing I know, clothes are getting ripped off bodies … and bodies are tumbling about crazily in the bedroom like bang bangles.

From that moment on, every moment that I wasn’t elsewhere, I was with Lora.

It wasn’t just that the lass was a sweet, great lover, but that she literally filled my days with light and laughter, with that wicked sense of humour that played with words, the way Mozart mused with pianos.

I suppose I am a sapio-sexual.

Also, every three or four months, we took this weekend ‘Tembea Kenya’trips – first to Mombasa, ‘coz that’s a must’, then to Tsavo West (which makes other safaris seem tame), then to Watamu, then another time to Shela Beach, then Voi, and Kilifi, and then Malindi, which I loved best.

Lorraine was exactly 20 years younger than I, but we spoke as equals, sharing our dreams, fears, hopes, ambitions – and actually helping each other be the best versions of ourselves.

My birthday mate was actually my soulmate.

And then on June 1st, 2024, on the third anniversary of when we’d first met, Lora said she was treating me for dinner at the place where we’d celebrated her 26th birthday, and my 46th birthday, three years before; and when dinner was done, she took both my hands in her long arms, and said: “Soul-Mate (that’s what we called each other instead of ‘sweetheart’, or just ‘soul’),  I just want to say I applied for a scholarship for my Masters’ last year, and I got it! Full scholarship!”

My heart was hammering in my chest like a heart attack. But I smiled and said, “Congratulations, soulmate.”

Her hands gripped mine harder. “It’s in Australia.”

An image of those ‘Men at Work’ guys in “Land Down Under” jumping around in pyjamas like kangaroos came to mind – (and if you’ve no idea what I’m talking about, YouTube, dammit!)

But all I said, stupidly so, was: “Do you know that the year you were born, Biwott was the bull of Auckland?”

Now she let go of my hands, cracking up – “Be waaaat?”

And in spite of being smart as a whip, and a HR-lawyer, I immediately knew Lorraine had no idea who Biwott had been, perhaps because ‘Total Man’ lost his Keiyo seat in 2007, and Kenyan history for Lorraine begins on January 1st, 2008, when the country convulses into PEV conflagration.

Our final week-long trip, very early August, was to Mbita, that Victoria Sands place, which isn’t too far from where Bikozulu here has built his place, so the owner informed us. It was the most bittersweet holiday we’d ever had – Lora spent almost as much time crying as she did, cracking me up, and even as she split my ribs, I felt the heart beneath them break, break, break, into a billion pieces.

And on August 14th, I dropped her off at JKIA. Ciao, ciao, Lora.

Dasvidanya, my darling damsel!

It’s been eighteen months since Lorraine left, and the rain of pain is still beating in my heart – pounding my head.

Two months after she left, one midnight, a Somali neighbour in her late-20s pounded on my door. When I opened it, Fatush spilled in, blood pouring from her forehead.

“My big sis has slashed me, saying I sleppin’ wit’ boyfriend.”

I helped clean up Fatush’s head, then drove her to a nearby proper small hospital where they stitched her up; and they offered to give her an assault medical report for the P2 form to get her big sister arrested.

“No, no, I deal with family in my s’bezo way…”

That night, I spared Fatush my couch – yes, I had bought more furniture – and the next morning, left her sleeping as I went to work.

Sometime in the day, the caretaker called me, saying that Fatush had cracked her sister’s head with a bottle of whisky (my 12-year-old whisky!), and locked herself in my house; and there were three cops outside my digs, demanding I be called so that they could be let in, and arrest Fatush.

That December of 2024, I also met a fading beauty of 39, who was dressed in a dera, and proclaimed love at first sight.

CYPRIA.

By evening, she was asking I send Shs. 5K for gas. Turns out that when she was in campus in her early 20s, she had been a side-dish of the late Cyrus Jirongo, and eventually dropped out of college, as he’d said he will marry her.

He didn’t, and she had lived off her looks, rather than her wits, since then, and guys like me were the gentlemen at the end of the ruined rail line that leads to Cypria.

Last year, I also ran into a high school crush called Angel at a country club in Karen, and after a couple of ‘catching up’ lunches, she gave me the ‘hole’ of her life – married some rich guy at 33, got twin boys (now turning 18), became a Karen housewife, now divorced – (incredibly, also in mid-2021)  I, myself,  have since become good friends /co-parents with my Ex, now a fiercely single corporate chieftain.

From her Shs. 10,000 per bottle Martell and interests in my financials, I soon gathered that I certainly could not afford to maintain Angel in the lifestyle her ex-husband “had accustomed her to…” So, in spite of having day-dreamed of this damsel daily, between 1990 and 1999, I ghosted her like she’d died in nineteen ninety nine.

I’m kind-hearted, but I’m not always a nice guy!

Then, at some Book Fair, I met a 44-year-old kindergarten teacher from ‘one of those international brats’ academies; now that was a nice woman, sickeningly sweet like syrup.

She has taught nursery school since the year 2000, straight out of high school, and into a world of kids and kindergartens, and Olive was the most obviously weirdly boring woman I have ever met.

“She spoke in this soft sing-song voice, said kindly obvious shit-like, ‘Oh, look, the sky is so very blue today!’”

Combine her simpleness with a certain moralising Christianity – she just realised, aha, at forty-something, that she might want kids of (her) own, inside a strong Christian marriage – I swear on the Bible, her very words, and the witless hap was on the direct spectrum end of Lora’s glittering wit.

I guess that’s what happens when you spend a quarter-century, daily, hanging out with three to five-year-old babies.

“You must wash your hands before you eat…”

“You need to look left, look right, look left again, before you cross the road,” she told a tipsy me one day.

And that was the end of the fairy tale.

There was Gertie, 55, a widow and mom of adult kids (a daughter she was estranged from, and a son who seemed to stay in touch only out of obligation). She is the Deputy Consul of a certain consulate in this city – from whom I sensed a deep grief and loneliness, and bitterness, who spoke of buying a small villa near the sea and retiring there when her posting here was over – (living by the Indian Ocean is something we, once in a while, half-jokingly spoke about with Lora).

In the end, the Deputy Consul was just too blue for good company.

It was like, in spite of her outward success, an inner light in her had gone out, long before I met her – and nothing could ever switch it on again.

You had dinner with her, she fed you all these tales of woe about those who had left, or were departing the world, and you came away feeling slightly depressed.

Now imagine being with Gertie for the rest of one’s life.

In the end, I just told her I was in love with a girl in Australia, and before I could explain further, she snapped: “You black boys. Always in love with dem damn white girls. Me first husband lef’ me for one o’ dem.”

I hadn’t even known Gertie had had a first husband, who left her for a white lass; or did he leave her for the whitey, before leaving everyone, forever, for the “good nightie”, as the poet Dylan Thomas, whose work Lorraine introduced me to, used to call eternity?

There is,  however, one whom I speak with at least once a week, coming over from the city of Adelaide in May, and staying till September, before she has to join the Ph.D. program of some university in Mid-West America; “in the fall semester,” as she puts it.

“Tafta bibi, wewe Mzeeaddy,” she’s always teasing at call end.

“There are no women in this town,” I tell her, sounding plaintive.

“Basi lipa one million ya dowry niwambie nyumbani kwangu nimepata bwana, na tunakuja na gari yao for blessings presided over by Prophet Owuor, (who talks to ‘God’ on WhatsApp where the ‘Lord’ accepted the invite from Prophet Owuor) …,” she recently told me. With her, you’re never quite sure if she’s joking, so I’ve been looking at what used cars a million bob gets you now in Kenya –  Toyota Voxy 2010, Mazda Demio 2016, Toyota Estima 2012, Toyota Ractis 2015; or I just look for Shs. 120k more, and we get Lorraine’s parents a silver Mercedes-Benz C200, 2008 model?

In 2008, Lora was thirteen, which is the current age of my daughter.

She, my daughter, on Saturday will send me a “Best Dad Ever” card – as she always has since she was ten, the year after the split – or should I call it ‘Run-away Day’ as Lorraine called it, saying “your Ex got tired of the Labour of Love that you are, Laban.”

(I lie about Laban, I’m not called ‘Laban’, so get away from me, Satan!)

But love, or at least looking for it, is lots of labour.

I am now retired from it, at fifty.

At first, it was not easy to keep to the celibacy vow I gave myself when I turned fifty last year, and I must thank a certain adult website for walking this journey with me these many months.

This Saturday, I have one ticket for the HSBC  Women’s Rugby Sevens at the Nyayo National Stadium.

I’m tired of picking up women, so I want a woman who can pick me up, like a large female rugby player is the perfect picker-up, as opposed to a pick-me-up.

Someone with whom, after drinks and dinner, we can have a bit of a scrum in the sitting room, before I race for the bedroom, with her hot on my (shoeless) heels.

Then, before I can make a touchdown on the bed, BAM, she has slammed into me, and I have whacked my head on the bed-board, and blacked out. And in the morning, when I wake up with a post-Vale headache and black eye, I can mutter: “Akia Mungu — I tell you.  There are no women in this town.”

***

Gentlemen, have you read You Should Date A Girl Who Reads by Rosemarie Urquico? Google it. But before you do, get that girl a book for Valentine’s Day. Not just any other book but one of my own. I will write any special message you want on it. Seal it. Hell, I can even spray it with a perfume like we did in high school. Grab a copy HERE.

item.title: A Small Death For Small Lives
item.description:
The girl who snitched on her was witchy-looking: small eyes set close together and a mouth shaped like the devil’s spittle. She was called Marion. The school suspended her. Her mom left her job at the bank and came for her to school wearing red high heels and a very tight-fitting grey plaited skirt that suddenly made her walk with tiny unnatural steps. She scolded her bitterly in the car (“What deviant are you becoming, Linda?”) as she looked outside, thinking about the terrible fate that would befall Marion. The two weeks she was home, her father pretended she wasn’t there. Treated her like an empty can of soda that someone had left on top of the kitchen counter.

In Form 2, she joined a band of Forth Formers who would occasionally sneak out of the dormitories at night to smoke in the corner of the school compound. The group was led by a girl whom everybody called Nekesa, but that wasn’t her real name. Word was she was a lesbian. She also played netball, which has got nothing with being a lesbian, although many lesbians played netball in her school. Nekesa’s father was a politician, which meant that most of the harsh rules that applied to the rest didn’t apply to her. Her father kept, in his pocket, the other fathers who sat on the school board.

One night, they were all out smoking in the very darkened area between the long strip of outside toilets that were used when water ran out and the massive grain store that led down to the school farm. They must have been six girls, sweaters off, silently passing around two cigarettes. It was after lights out, close to midnight, Thursday night she remembers. The fight started when Nekesa mentioned casually that she was holding too long on the cigarettes. She could barely see her face in the darkness, of course, which made it easier for her to roll her eyes. “She claims I made a rude sound. A click or whatever. I insisted I didn’t.” Linda remembers. “She said that I had a ‘foul attitude.’ That’s how she spoke, like she owned servants.”

So anyway, she – Linda – has never been one to shut up, so she told her she needed to have her ears checked because she heard her own things. “I could hear a collective holding of breath amongst the girls.” Nobody spoke to Nekesa like that. Nobody. Certainly not a Form 2. The smoking group was hers. It was unspoken. She could evict you from it. “Last time you are coming here with us,” Nekesa hissed into the darkness. So Linda started her own smoking group. A better one, because later in Form Four, they introduced weed in it.

Anybody who remembers her from high school says they remember the day she stood up against a bully teacher, Ms Ogana. How they grabbed each other by their collars and scuffled about, only Ms Ogana tripped and fell in the brief tussle, her skirt riding up to reveal the football shorts she wore underneath. The gathered girls howled. So it looked like she had beaten her ass down. A teacher! She faced expulsion, but because she had by then become the de facto freedom fighter for those without voices in school, everybody gave grave testimonies against Ms Ogana, and there was great tension and rumours of a protest if she was expelled. That saved her skin. She was suspended again and punished by cleaning the entire classroom block on Block E for an entire week. “I had become a hero. Untouchable.” Ms Ogana hated her. “I didn’t hate her,” Linda says. “I just thought she was weak, picking fights with high school girls at her big age.”

They also remember how she played most sports (except netball for obvious reasons – it belonged to the Mafia, Nekesa being the captain), how she led debate clubs, and how in Form 3 she led vigorous lobbying that saw the administration change their Sunday diet. It’s also in Form 3 that she took a train to Mombasa after a fight with her mom and stayed with a stranger in a YWCA hostel in Likoni as they looked for her desperately, thinking she had died. Nonetheless, nobody was surprised at her KCSE grades; an A minus, missing an A by one point. But everybody was surprised when she said she wanted to study veterinary medicine because nobody knew her to be an animal lover, not even herself. Her parents tried to convince her to change her mind. “You want to treat dogs!” Her father, a very emotional man, cried.

“Yes, father, dogs and cats and horses and rabbits and sheep and whales and giraffes and birds…”

“Whales.”

I thought animals needed saving from humans, she says. “I never grew up with any pets because my mom hates pets, so I had no experience with animals at all except hearing the neighbours’ dogs bark at night. The first time I carried a kitten on my lap, I was 19. The first time a dog licked my hands, I was 20. But I felt I could make a good veterinary doctor. It was whimsical, as most things I have done in my life – and done very well.”

When she was in her second year, she still desired animals to be saved, just not by her. So she quit university and got into the curio business. “My parents went berserk. Curio business was ten times worse than treating dogs. It was for failures, not unlike hawking in buses, my dad said. But I didn’t care. I was very good at convincing white people to buy shit that they thought was Africa – not that they needed a lot of convincing, to be honest.” She laughs.

She started a company together with a penpal (yes, children, there was a time not long ago when you could correspond with someone you had never met or seen, only it took weeks for them to reply). The penpal, from Norway, was called Hedvig. “By 21, I had made my first million, and I was driving an old second-hand Toyota. I also moved out of my parents’ house because I couldn’t bear to hear them moan about how I needed a university education.”

At 23, a boy moved in with her in her small flat in Kileleshwa, and together they played house. “Jamo was a sculptor, dreadlocked, with Bob Marley’s facial bone structure. His face was one of the things I liked most about him, even though I didn’t listen to reggae. Our relationship was a cliché; he had grown up rough in Mbotela or Jericho – or one of those places I had never set foot in. I hadn’t.” She pauses. “He was quiet, and he was very good with his hands. He was only 2,6 but it felt like he was much older than me, in retrospect. He was sweet. When he came to live with me, he didn’t know how to use the water kettle or the gas cooker. He’d never been in a lift before, and didn’t know the difference between a fish knife and a steak knife. But he was very kind and loving and went about his life with an innocence I found reckless even at my young age. We smoked a lot of weed. Eventually, I kicked him out after a year and some months. The novelty of being with someone very different wore off.”

The novelty of curios also wore off. “I was making good money from it, but I was bored. So I hired someone to do the running around while I dealt with expanding our markets abroad. Hedvig later died from falling off a cliff while mountaineering. I was devastated, even though we had never met.”

She then got into mobile telephony, importing mobile phones as a supplier and setting up M-Pesa shops. “That made me very rich in a way I hadn’t anticipated. While the friends I was with in medical school were busting their heads dissecting dead bodies, I was already driving a Harrier and living in a two-bedroom apartment in Lavington. My parents still thought I should do a degree course, but I was already doing a degree in life. I was very good with people, with selling ideas to people. If you let me into a room, you were sold. My confidence has always been very high, my enthusiasm so infectious. People listened to me, trusted me. And I was bold. I dressed in very colourful clothes, sometimes hats that didn’t match my outfit. I wore short skirts, very short skirts. I was unafraid. I joined a country club at 27 and sold whatever I was into at that time to the old-moneyed men in those clubs. They liked me – at least the ones who didn’t try to get into my pants. I was doing extremely well with myself by 27, upwardly mobile, you’d say – except for one thing; I wasn’t sleeping very well!”

Sleep had always been something she never prioritised, that never came naturally. Not even as far back as primary school. In high school, girls constantly got into trouble for sleeping in. She was always up before the morning prep bell went off, up and walking to class – and not because she was studious but because sleeping bored her. She was up early, even on weekends when most slept in. In adulthood, she always burnt the candle from both ends. “I’d work late into the night and get up early to continue working or reading. Sleep was something I did because everybody was asleep, not because I needed it. It was an inconvenience, a waste of momentum. I felt alive constantly. I would clean my room in the middle of the night, playing orchestra music. Or text people at 2 am. Or read and read until my body would crumble and I’d pass out. I was happy to do four hours. I thought lazy people slept a lot.”

It’s Tom, a telecom engineer she was engaged to at 31, who first said it. “You might have a sleeping disorder. I know someone who can help you.” She saw the doctor in a clinic in Karen. He prescribed some drugs, some supplements and told her to change her curtains. That didn’t work. When Tom would come back home late in the night or early in the morning from work, he would find her sitting up reading or watching TV. It drove him insane.

He took her to see two more doctors; the last one suggested she stop smoking weed. Linda offered the smile she reserves for small-minded suggestions.

“I don’t have a drug problem,” she said. “I have ideas.”

The doctor didn’t smile back.

“Cannabis can destabilise mood. Especially when sleep is already fragile.”

“My mood isn’t fragile. It’s productive.” She leaned back in her chair, legs crossed.

“Sometimes productivity is the symptom.”

A pause. Clinical. She stared at him.

“He should stop practising medicine.” She told Tom when they walked out. Ironically, even though she wasn’t sleeping, her businesses were thriving. She had since thrown herself aggressively at financial investments on top of everything else she was doing. Tom was fascinated by her drive. Her relentlessness and the risks she took. “He was a risk-averse individual; he liked to plan and know his next steps before he made a move. His engineering brain would constantly drive me insane. I was from the ‘fuck-it’ school of thought.” She laughs.

They got married in a small garden wedding with a few friends to witness. Her favourite uncle, an alcoholic clergyman, officiated the event. “When I said I do, I had slept a collective four hours in the past three days. I remember my father telling me that I smelled of ‘smoke’ as he walked me down the aisle. The smoke was weed. He could never tell the difference. Mom could. Mom was a thug.”

One day, when their daughter was one, she couldn’t sleep for three days. “That’s when I set up meetings and booked a flight to China online, and when my husband woke up, he found me packing, throwing things in my suitcase, pulling down my dresses from the wardrobe. My skin was tingling. I felt buoyant and charged. I don’t remember the details of this part of the story, and everything I’m telling you now is what Tom told me happened.”

That early morning – it was 4 am – Tom leaned up on his elbow in bed, blinking.

“Where are you going?”

“China.” She turned to look at him, bright-eyed. “I’m going to China.”

He watched her for a moment, then slowly got out of bed and held her firmly by the shoulder. “Stop, stop, just stop. Linda. Stop for a second.” She stopped moving and looked up at him with big, wide eyes.

“Are you going to China, the country?”

“Yes! Is there any other?” She smiled.

“When we went to bed, you didn’t have these plans.”

“Yes, but now I do. Great plans come in the night.”

“OK.” He steadied his voice. “What’s happening in China?”

“Oh, thank you. I was afraid you were not going to ask.” She pulled him to sit at the edge of the bed.

She rattled on about a fantastic business opportunity, something about a customised, lab-cultured protein feed for exotic pets. “Rare birds, dogs, cats, reptiles… We’ll eliminate traditional supply chains. Precision feed. Ethically sourced insect protein, of course, because we have to be kind to living things and all that. Blockchain traceability. I have a background in veterinary medicine; this will be revolutionary!” She sprang up and started packing again. “I have a contact who will manufacture this cheaply in Shenzhen, and we will then sell it across Africa via online subscription.”

Tom’s head dropped. He stared hard at the carpet.

He stepped out of the room and called her mother from the kitchen balcony. She arrived when Linda was all packed and singing in the shower. When she came out to find her mother seated on the bed, her face opened up.

“Mother! I see Tom has told you about this business opportunity. Perfect. What do you know about bio-tech and blockchain traceability?”

She was hospitalised. She was a danger to herself, they said. “I slept the longest I have in my adult life. When I woke up, I felt weird – confused and embarrassed to find my mother and father seated next to my hospital bed, whispering to each other. When I asked why I was in the hospital, my mother said I had wanted to go to China.”

“China?” she asked groggily. “For what?”

“To buy lab-cultured proteins for animals.” Her mother’s voice was sad and flat.

“That sounds interesting, mother.” She looked across at her father. “No, dad?” And he started weeping. “I was so confused.”

In another room – cool, open windows, white walls – a doctor with a very sombre look diagnosed her. He spat the words fast: bipolar spectrum disorder, hypomania, sleep deprivation, escalating risk. She sat between her husband and her mother, the three of them arranged like a painting nobody wanted to be in.

Mood stabilisers were discussed. Side effects listed with bureaucratic calm.

“Flattening?” she repeated.

“Reducing extremes. Protecting your sleep.”

“I don’t need protection.”

“You haven’t slept properly in days.”

“That’s called focus.”

He studied her for a long moment.

“Focus doesn’t usually come with a packed suitcase and a midnight ticket to China.”

She looked away first.

“Of course, I refused long-term medication,” she sighs. “It would dull me. I would be those dull babes who take tea and sleep at 10. Very housewifey stuff. Very safe and unexciting.”

She is not convinced she is broken.

She sent me a long text after this interview. Here is part of it.

I have no desire to be normal. I have no desire for my children to be normal. I want them awake to the world. I want them curious and slightly unruly and unafraid of their own voltage. I know now that I have a chemical imbalance. I know my brain doesn’t idle where other brains idle. I see patterns faster. I feel everything louder. The highs arrive like cavalry; the lows like weather fronts you can see building but cannot outrun. I understand the science of it. What I don’t understand is why the solution must feel like subtraction.

I don’t want to be turned into a person who does normal things and thinks normal thoughts and goes to bed at normal hours with normal dreams. I don’t want my edges sanded down until I am safe for public consumption. I don’t want my brain dulled.

She sent that message at 2:34 am.

**

I enjoyed talking to this girl. I enjoy talking to oddballs and squarepegs. It’s like going on a rollercoaster. Do you have a story you want told? Do you do an interesting job you want to invite me to see? Do you have an experience you want to share? Are you in remand, and you want to tell me how you ended up there? I can come with bread and milk, and we can speak between the bars? Anything. Email me: bikozulu@gmail.com.
