item.title: A Long Road
item.description:
At the Tanzania-Zambia border, in a beige small town called Tunduma, a thin-lipped immigration officer studied her passport and those of her four children and asked suspiciously, “Where is the father of these children?”

The father of those children was back in Nairobi. And she was running away from him. From the marriage. She was taking flight from a life that had turned tumultuous and increasingly abusive and violent. Ciku was on the run. And like most women on the run from their marriages – to mean, men – she was scarred, scared but hopeful. She didn’t have a plan. She only wanted to put as much distance between herself and whatever she was leaving behind.

She had thought about Tanzania because it’s next door. So one day, on a whim, she went down to River Road to inquire about buses and was told there was one leaving later that day. A little voice in her head said, why not? She bought five tickets. Back seats. She went back to her friend’s house, where she had taken refuge and told the kids: We are leaving for an adventure. Clothes went into three rucksacks. The rest she told her friend to donate. She had closed her business and had a little money. They ended up living in Tanzania for a month, mostly in affordable hotels, homeschooling the kids. When the father realised the children were gone, he immediately got a court order. It got ugly. [Case still in court]

Determined to be a moving target, she moved again. That’s how she found herself at the border of Zambia.

“It’s unfortunate to be a woman in that circumstance,” she reflects now. “Legally, I’m not supposed to leave the country without the consent of their father, but nobody protects me from an abuser. I had been in domestic situations where I was physically assaulted, and when the cops came, I turned out to be the villain. The charge sheet read that I was disturbing the peace. So you feel powerless. Desperate. Alone. And you want to do what’s right by you and your children, but your natural instincts as a mother conflict with the law.”

“The father of these children,” the officer asked again, “where is he?”

“The father is not in the picture.”

“So where is the parental consent?”

“We are separated. We are not even on talking terms.”

“And where are you going?”

“I don’t know. I’m not sure. The furthest I can go.”

He paused and regarded her like he knew her, or knew women like her, and handed back the passports. “I usually don’t do this, but I understand where you’re coming from. Proceed with your journey. Be safe.”

They got onto an old train called Tazara and chugged off to Zambia, later breaking down along the way.

A night in Lusaka. Next morning, another bus – passing landscapes, trees and hills – to Mozambique through the Cassacatiza border. A night in a sketchy lodging with a long-drop toilet. The kids had never seen anything like it. Standing around the hole, they asked, “Mum, how do you use this?” She comes from Nyeri. “Even I had never used a toilet like that before.” But they figured it out, which was what the trip was teaching them.

Another bus to Tete. [‘Tete was hot in a way I had never experienced.’] Then another bus to Chimoio, the fifth largest city in Mozambique. Then, Maputo, for a month, hosted by a Kenyan friend. Maputo surprised her. “It’s beautiful in a way that catches you off guard. Wide streets, jacaranda trees, extraordinary seafood.” She’d set the kids up with their schoolwork each morning and sit nearby with her notebook, trying to figure out what came next. “I still didn’t have a plan. But for the first time since leaving Nairobi, I felt like I could breathe and think.”

After thirty days, they crossed the Lebombo-Komatipoort border into South Africa. Pretoria for three months. Then Cape Town. “Cape Town was where I finally exhaled.”

Not long after, she met a man, loved him, and he loved her, and they travelled together and camped in the open, until he died and she had him cremated. Then the shit-show started.

But before we get to the shit-show.

I asked how it felt almost natural to just pack and run, to face south and go through borders, to live in towns she had never heard of and start over somewhere very far and very unfamiliar. Where did that muscle come from?

“I was born to a teenage mother in Nyeri. When I was five, my mom married a man we called Daddy, and he lived in Garissa. Daddy was a crop scientist, and his job took him to farflung corners of Northern Kenya – Ijara, Garsen, Abakore, Qara, Dambas, Biyamadhow – places most people haven’t heard of. He drove an old Land Rover. Sometimes he’d take Mum and me. Sometimes just me. Imagine taking a child to those brutal, harsh places. No roads. We’d drive through sand, through rivers, under the bluest skies – the hottest blues. He’d put me in the backseat to sleep, cover me with a shuka, and point out trees as we drove: baobab, acacia, desert date, white flame. He’d say, ‘Notice how the soil has changed here? You will see, it will change again.’ Fascinating man. A genius, really. And maybe that’s where I learnt that travel was about courage – to go into the unknown with everything you know, hoping you’ll learn more. I have never hesitated to pack a bag. When I was 24, my best friend and I went to South Africa for three years. She came back after the post-election violence. I stayed until my dad died, and I had to come bury him. Travel for me is just: get up and go. So booking tickets to Tanzania and packing my life and my children – it seemed natural. Not as scary as going through bandit land.”

They had met through a WhatsApp book club during Covid. Kenyans living wherever – in Kenya, outside Kenya – gathering every Saturday morning to discuss a book. He was one of them. “Just a WhatsApp group member. Healthy discussions. Nothing special.” When he launched his book, Troubled Heart, in 2023, he looked for her. She was in Cape Town. He was in Nairobi. She couldn’t attend. Late,r he saw her travel photos from the Philippines on Facebook and slid into her inbox asking how she had arranged the trip. Normal chit-chat.

In 2024, she posted a photo of herself and the children outside the Pretoria Museum. He recognised it immediately. How are you in my country and you’re not reaching out?  She told him she’d been busy, hadn’t thought about him, had two weeks left. He told her two weeks was a long time and invited her to his town. Port Elizabeth. 1,500 kilometres away.

“I thought I wasn’t ready for that.” But after some back and forth, she agreed. He sent return tickets.

She wasn’t prepared for him. He picked them up on an early morning flight and took them to his house while the Airbnb was being readied. He had a Kenyan flag on his gate. Another in his living room. He made breakfast: eggs and things. The kids went out to play in his big compound while he and Ciku talked – banter – until she remembered she had a court session. Her divorce was still ongoing. He drove her somewhere quiet and took the children with him. He came back an hour later with the kids loaded with toys and balls he had bought them.

“That was my first impression of him; someone kind and gentle.”

Two weeks became four, then six. He kept asking how she could extend her stay. They discovered she could pay to extend beyond the 90 visa-free days. The process started almost before she had decided anything consciously. He engaged seriously with the homeschooling, even shared a curriculum he had developed himself, having once wanted to open a school. He suggested enrolling the four-year-old in a local crèche. “That’s how we started life together.”

“The children took to him. They had been through a lot. They were guarded. He didn’t try too hard – he just showed up consistently and let them come to him at their own pace.”

It was a second chance at love in her 40s, built quietly in a city she had never planned to be in. They travelled together, camped in the open, moved through the world the way she had always believed it should be moved through – with curiosity and without too much luggage. She had known him five years, but they had lived together only fifteen months. Not long enough, and yet long enough to rebuild something she thought the first marriage had permanently destroyed: her belief that she deserved to be loved well.

On Saturday, October 11th 2025 –  nine days before his 55th birthday – he left for his usual 21km run. She left for her walk. They went in different directions, the way people do when they trust they’ll find each other again on the other side.

“That day I had decided to try a new route.” He got back before her. She called to say she was lost and sent him a pin. He asked if she wanted him to come fetch her. She said she’d call when she found the main road. The next call was from her son. Papa is on the floor. She went to the video immediately. He was lying on his belly. “I could hear him groan.” A neighbour was called, and he was rushed to hospital. “When I got there, he was dead. He was just lying there, like he was sleeping.” He was the fittest person she knew. Healthy as a horse. She was devastated. 

“I knew I was in trouble that evening, on the phone with his cousin. He asked me, could it be something he ate? I told him he had been holding an avocado. Then a pastor friend of the family got on the line. ‘Do you think the avocado was poisoned?’ That’s when I knew. If someone is already thinking the avocado was poisoned, trouble is coming.” She pauses. “By the next day, trouble had arrived.”

Grief, it turns out, does not pause the administrative requirements of death. There were forms. Queues to stand in. The world does not lower its voice just because yours has gone quiet. Nothing happens in government facilities over the weekend. She went back on Monday, was told an autopsy was required, paid, was put on a waiting list, and was assigned for Wednesday. Between his death on Saturday and the autopsy on Wednesday, not one of his relatives had shown up. “Five days. Nobody.”

After the autopsy, she was asked: burial or cremation? She already knew. He had told her the day before he died, in fact, not because either of them knew what was coming. You have those conversations because death is a someday thing, not a tomorrow thing. “I trust you to do this,” he had said. “You know what this is.” His family pushed back hard; phone calls, not all of them friendly.  She waited. Nobody came to Mozambique. On the day of the cremation, one relative finally arrived. She went ahead anyway.

The day after, she went to collect the autopsy report, leaving the children waiting in the car. Inside, as the report was about to be handed over, someone said: Before we give you this, you need to go with these people. They put her in a car. Five kilometres later, even in Portuguese, she could read the building well enough. Criminal investigation. Something.

“Why am I here?”

The family, through the Kenyan Embassy, had requested an investigation. The officer read the report. Natural causes. Cardiac arrest. No case, technically, but the procedure required them to proceed. She sat for five hours: who was she, where had they met, where had they lived, had he been sick. Then they wanted to see the house without her present. She called a cab driver she trusted – the one she sent to the supermarket – and he drove the CID officers while she waited.

“They had already made up their minds. It didn’t matter what I said.”

The autopsy report was handwritten –  that is how the government pathologist in Mozambique produces them, by hand, in Portuguese. The family declared it fake. The story ran in the media. Kenyan blogs said she had poisoned him with the avocado to inherit his wealth. “And it doesn’t help that I’m Kikuyu and he was Luhya. That I was a divorced woman with four children. So I wasn’t good enough for him, and then I killed him.”

She says this last part without bitterness. In the flat tone of someone who has repeated an absurdity so many times it has lost the power to shock.

So after everything – the interrogation, the pushback, the blogs, the poisoned avocado – she cremated him as he had asked. She packed the urn into her suitcase among her clothes and flew with her four children to Bali. She did not declare it at check-in. You’re probably not supposed to travel with human remains tucked between your blouses, but there are moments in life when the rules feel written for people whose lives are proceeding normally.

They had been in Bali for four days when the morning came. It had rained every single day, but that morning the forecast said it would pass early and the rest of the day would be clear. She had always wanted to bring her children to Potato Head, a resort on the beach about an hour away. She had been there with friends once and thought: If I ever come back, I’m bringing them. She tucked the urn into her bag. They got an Uber. After lunch, they set out on the beach. They already knew what the day was for. She had told them that morning. This is the last thing we do for Papa. The final thing.

They found a spot that felt right. It seemed calm enough, a place to release someone. The ocean was calm, the Indian Ocean flat like paper, the way it gets on windless mornings. She reached into her bag and took out the urn. She opened it. She poured. Nobody said anything. They walked back along the beach in silence.

“It was a feeling of…it is done,” she says. “There had been so much pushback. And I had finally honoured him. In the way he asked to be honoured.” She pauses. “But also finality. The ash is gone. It is so done.”

This was not the first time. In 2022, she had cremated her mother and brought the children to scatter her ashes in the ocean in Mombasa. 

“I’m still being hounded.” She says now. The relatives want answers she has already given. She gets the feeling sometimes that she is being watched, followed. “I feel like I need to take off again. To protect myself and my children.”

What she wants is simple and should not be radical: for women to be allowed to carry out their partner’s last wishes in peace. “There’s a reason why they tell us these things. There’s a reason why they trust us. I didn’t apply to be Kikuyu. I didn’t apply to be a divorced mother of four.” 

***

She wrote a book. The Soft Place After The Storm. It is available at Nuria Bookstore in Nairobi and Nyali, Soma Nami Bookstore on Ngong Road, and Wine and Spine Bookstore in Nanyuki. And on Amazon.

item.title: Fourth Time’s A Charm
item.description:
The first time I was married, I had no choice in that matter. I was in university – KU – when a girl I wasn’t even crazy about, a girl I was just having fun with, said she was pregnant with my baby. I was in my final year of Biomedical Engineering, barely having time for much less. (Clearly, I had time for sex). She freaked out, completely lost her shit. She said her father would kill her. She was Kisii, so I believed her. I had heard things about the violence of Kisii men. The boy who lived next door in the hostels when I was in second year was expelled when he cut his roommate with a knife. He was Kisii, and very temperamental. So I believed her.

Shaken – for I didn’t imagine I would make anyone pregnant – I went back home to consult my father. My father was almost retiring then from Kenya Railways, where he was an engineer. We lived in an old government house, probably the only benefit he had for working for the government, and he had time to consult for his side gigs. I am the last-born, the age gap between me and the sibling I follow is about 9 years. That’s because my dad remarried when his first wife passed on. I never met her, but I was told she resembled my stepsisters, who are such amazing human beings. I speak of this because, as the last-born, I was very close to my father. I’d take him to work during school holidays. I liked the smell of his office. I liked to go to the workshop and touch tools and watch men in the workshop pound steel with hammers, or cut wood with saws. My idea of manhood was informed by watching men use their hands. Of my father in overalls, grease on his hands.

I remember him staring at our old carpet for a long time. That’s how he thought; in these long interludes where he stared at something. It could be the TV off in the wall unit, or his cup of tea on the table. It could get uncomfortable if you didn’t know him. You’d be tempted to say something – a mistake. We knew to give him time, to allow and sit in this silence.

When he looked up, he said, “Tom, you have to do the right thing.”

He fell into another brief silence. Then he said, “You have to take responsibility.”

“But I don’t have a job.”

“Does the baby have a job?” he asked me calmly. “Will it come out with a job? How do you think it will eat and where will it sleep?”

I was silent.

“We will go to their parents and tell them…”

“Her parents will kill her.”

“No, they will do no such thing.”

“Dad, they are Kisiis.”

I gave my dad her dad’s number, and I guess they met together, a meeting that went as well as it did because later, another meeting was organised between me, Aggie, my parents, and Aggie’s parents. In the meeting, at a café I don’t recall in town, one of those small ones on a squeezed street, we sat at a small table, the six of us, and the men spoke. Her father was a short man with a very soft, round face, the dangerous type. I couldn’t look him in the eye. Her mother was quiet but wise. I could tell.

It was decided for us that we would move in together and figure out our lives. It came across like punishment; you kids wanted to have sex, irresponsible sex, these are the repercussions, so live with it. Or live together.

We moved in together.

So I got married at 24, and I was a father at 25.

I don’t recall the bits of fatherhood in those initial years other than feeling like I was an eel and I was stuck between two stones at the bottom of the ocean. Aggie was happy to be a mother. Or seemed happy. I secured employment almost immediately after university, while she took a year off university when the baby came. She would later resume, finish, and secure a job. She was a talented architect. Very artistic.

To run away from the life that I had found myself in, I secured a scholarship in Germany for a year. Then I extended it by another year. When I came back home, I was different. Aggie was different, too, mostly because she was having an affair with this guy called Ndolo. I discovered this from a note he had written to her, some sort of a love letter with terrible handwriting, which I had found in her purse when I went rummaging for Vaseline because my lips get dry. I knew this Ndolo fellow from university. She was seeing him casually back then. He studied Environmental Science or Education or one of those arts courses. All I know is that he had a lot of time on his hands and he was always hanging around the oddball artistic types in uni who didn’t care to comb their hair.

I wasn’t mad. OK, I was mad, but not as mad as I pretended to be. Deep down, I felt relief. It was a confirmation that I wasn’t the only one who was blindsided in the marriage. Besides, it’s not like I was living in a monastery in Germany. So I confronted her. I banged on a few doors. I shouted. I said things like, “You have no respect for me or for yourself, shame on you!” I didn’t mean any of these things.

I haven’t mentioned anything about my son because after that affair, I did a paternity test one day and discovered that he wasn’t mine. Most probably Ndolo’s. It turns out that the person who had no self-respect, one who should have been ashamed of himself, was Ndolo, making another man raise his child.

When I told my dad that the boy wasn’t mine, he stayed at a spot on the table for a long time before saying, “You know, do you love your son and your wife enough to look away from this fact?”

“I don’t love either of them,” I said from the coldest depths of my heart.

“I don’t believe you,” he said, “but you should do what you want to do now.”

My mom shook her head and said, “Children don’t ask for the parents they get. You can’t abandon your son.”

“He has a father, Mom,” I told her. “I can’t stand in the way of their relationship.”

I was free.

I worked hard and dated hard. I felt like I had been given a second chance at life. I was careful not to botch it this time. I used condoms diligently and disposed of them myself. I didn’t trust any woman who said, “I’m on the pill.” Neither did I trust the pill. I only trusted myself.

Things were going great until I went and fell in love with Angela at 32. It was what romance novels call a whirlwind romance. Something that blows you away and takes you to the clouds, where the sun doesn’t stop shining. My career was going very well. She was ambitious and fun, a very courageous woman. By 34 I was married again. It felt right. I felt ready. I was determined to do this right. We had a church wedding, which my mother didn’t attend because she died the previous year of cervical cancer. “I’m your mother now,” Angela’s mom – a glamorous lady with an even bigger personality – told me during the wedding. I tried not to cry. Angela’s mother smoked cigarettes and went on solo holidays. My mother would have disapproved. God knows she scared my dad.

We had a son the following year. And a daughter a year later. Our Irish twins. We were happy. The problem with marrying a very ambitious woman is that they get restless, ants in their pants. When our last-born was barely old enough to hold a sippy cup, Angela was gone to the UK to do her Master’s. It wasn’t a discussion because if you knew her, you knew that career and her own self-development were not negotiable. She went to study MSc Medical Physics at the University of Surrey. I was left to play mummy and daddy, even though her mother basically ran our home with the help of a very capable nanny who spoke English better than many people I knew. She was a trained nurse. The nanny – Prudent – was the James Bond of nannies. She could drive a car, do mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, cook a beef stroganoff, and do math homework. I bet she also had hidden talents like fighting thieves with her black belt if need arose. I would be a liar if I claimed it was a very difficult time handling the home when my wife took off. Things simply happened around me. Like I was in a magic show. Even though I admired my wife, I was also jealous of her. Jealous that she had to be the one who left. Jealous of her ambition and the support she was receiving from her parents. I felt like she had gone off into the future and left me in the past. After a year, she was a medical physicist who, in case you are wondering, is the brain behind those machines that see inside us, through bone and shadow, calculating invisible forces so the images come out sharp. And as a biomedical engineer, I knew what that meant. She was optimizing technology.

Our marriage took a turn when she called me one day and said, “Tom, I got an opportunity here to work. Would you be comfortable relocating? It’s a great deal. You could get a job here with your qualifications, the children could start a great life here.”

I wish I were someone like my father, who takes a long pause when asked a question, because then I wouldn’t have said quickly, “I hate the UK.”

“But how can you hate it? You have never lived here,” she said.

“I visited it once when I was in Germany. It rained all the time. And I hated the food.”

“Think of the big picture,” she urged.

“I love my job. I can’t just leave my job. My life is here. Our life is here.”

So we talked about it for days. My dad wasn’t for the idea. Her mom shrugged and said cryptically, “Angela is like a dog with a bone.” Her father, whose opinion nobody seemed to seek, never said a word about it. I think he had long learned that marriage to a woman like Angela’s mom was life wearing handcuffs; the more you struggled, the more uncomfortable it got.

When Angela flew in two weeks later, wearing this odd hat, I knew there was a problem because she said, “I signed the contract. And now we have to figure out how we can move from there.”

Only we never really moved from there. We couldn’t move from there because I refused to move. I was mad. And I wasn’t pretending this time. She had made her decision without consulting me. I was a mere footnote for her. I also refused to have her move with the children. “You go build your career,” I told her bitterly. “I will rebuild whatever is left of this family here.”

She eventually left for the UK because she is a dog with a bone. And even though she would come back to see the kids every six months or so (she had a great job with perks), things never got any better. We just became two people who were married on different continents. In fact, I was closer to our James Bond nanny than to her. I know what you are thinking. “Oh God, he didn’t marry the nanny! God, he didn’t!” Well, of course I didn’t. What do you take me for?

The marriage pretty much crumbled in under three years. You should see our email correspondence. I was reading it the other day; we sound like child traffickers, talking about our children. That’s all we talked about. Our emails started with “Hello,” no names mentioned, in case Interpol was reading our mail. I never asked how she was coping in that rain and darkness, and she never asked if I was safe from the government abductions and disappearances.

Before the courts set us free, I was already waist-deep in a relationship with Roseline. She was a lawyer with a baby daddy who was on and off like a faulty bulb. She had one child, a sweet little, curious girl who couldn’t stop talking and asking questions: My daddy flies planes. They won’t let us play in the school field because they are planting grass. Why do you shave your hair like that? How come you don’t like eating onions? I like purple and green. What is your favourite colour? My dad lost his hat one time… On and on. I liked her as much as I liked her mother. And I wanted to be her stepfather. Sometimes the child makes the decision for you. I once dated a woman with a child – a boy of about 10 years – who had the personality of a hyena. I couldn’t just see myself with her because of her son. A child makes or breaks. This sweet little girl was the bow to the relationship.

I emailed Angela and told her about Roseline and my life’s plan with her. She emailed back and said, “I’m happy you are finding leverage in your social life. What does that mean for the future of our children?” She sounded like our children would become homeless if I got married. She suggested that I let her have the children. That they would get a better life there, a great education, and “a new cultural experience.” You really should read our emails. I couldn’t bear to live without our children. They had a great life in Nairobi. To me, they were my life. Her mother talked to me. She said, “I’m not even here as the mother of your ex-wife, but she makes a great case, don’t you think?” I agonised over it. I spoke to the children about it, and they wanted to go. They were charmed by the romance of life abroad. I spoke to my father, who thought I should think of the children. “Besides, children are nurtured better by their mother.” Eventually, we agreed the children would go live with her in the UK and each holiday I’d have them. Off they went, our Irish twins.

I was crushed to see them go. I cried at the airport when I knelt to hold both of them in a hug. I wondered if I would ever see them again. If they would forget me entirely. If they would call Angela’s man “Dad.” Or like him more. My youngest, my little pawpaw, my strawberry, said in her small voice, “Daddy, don’t cry. We will see you soon. We love you.” And her brother repeated like an adult, “We love you, Daddy.” I cried even harder. I cried in the car on my way home. I cried when I went to their bedroom and looked at their rumpled beds, things strewn all around, an odd toy, an old pair of shoes, a piece of sock. I lay on my daughter’s bed and stared at the ceiling, my eyes red. The whole room smelled of my children and I never wanted to forget that smell.

We started a married life with Roseline and our little baby girl. I was now in my early forties. I liked and loved Roseline. She was very sober-headed, a great planner with great wit. We were a great fit because we both wanted the same things. I wanted stability; I have always wanted stability. She wanted someone who was reliable and dependable. “I don’t want a father for my daughter, she already has one,” she told me. “I want someone for me.”

I would like to say the life we were building together was a complete life, but how could it be complete when half of my heart was living abroad? It was never going to be complete. I loved Roseline and our daughter and our life, but I was also a man in mourning. At some point I felt that I had made a grave mistake letting my children go. In a genius masterstroke, I convinced both my ex-wife and Prudent for her to go to the UK since my ex-wife was very busy. She could also further her nursing studies, maybe get herself a job in a nursing home, or set up one herself when the children were big enough. OK, it wasn’t me who convinced her; it was my mother-in-law who suggested it “in passing.” I felt very comfortable with that idea. I felt like I was planting a spy, an agent in that home, to be my eye on the children.

I wouldn’t say them going was entirely a bad idea. There are great benefits over and above my own depraved feelings. After two years, I was at Aga Khan waiting outside the delivery room for the third time. (I never go inside; it’s unnatural for men to be in the delivery room. The concept is very foreign, to me white. It’s like sleeping with a dog in the same bed).

We got a son. A bouncing one. Looking at him filled my heart with small little flowers that were sprouting open. I have that feeling even now. He was a perfect boy, from a perfect relationship. So there, I had two sets of boys and girls. My world felt balanced in some way. My work was going great. Suddenly, I was also very liquid, seeing as I had stopped paying fees for my two children. However, I was sending money for their other needs, which isn’t as much as the fees still. I now possessed significant disposable income. Maybe it was the extra money or the grief, but eventually Roseline started complaining that I was drinking too much. I was never much of a drinker to start with, and I didn’t feel I was. It got progressively bad by the time my son was getting into kindergarten.

One time, I crashed the car and was in a neck brace. When I came to on a hospital bed, Roseline was sitting there watching TV with the volume very low. She told me, “I won’t bury you, Tom. I’m too young to bury a husband. But I’m young enough to bury an ex-husband.” That’s who she was, a straight shooter. When I came out of hospital I hadn’t learnt my lesson; I drank in the neck brace. Then, when Roseline found out about some messages I was sharing with some 28-year-old girl from work, she didn’t make a fuss. She packed her bags and left with our children. I thought it was just her throwing her toys from the pram and would soon come back home. But she wouldn’t. She said, “My father was a drunkard. I won’t live my mother’s life, Tom.”

By the time I was waking up to the reality that Roseline was serious and that I would lose everything, it was rather late. She had quickly filed for divorce. I took a sabbatical from work and checked myself into rehab, where I dried out for three months. My rehab chapter of my life is another story altogether. But I remember walking into the visitors’ room in my final month to find my ex-wife, Angela, sitting there, prim and proper, looking like a very wealthy woman. I was both touched and shocked.

“What’s with these hats, Anj’?” was the first thing I asked her. We laughed –  that thin, careful laugh of people standing at the edge of something. Phones weren’t allowed, so she had printed the children’s photos and spread them out in the main office like evidence of a life still in motion. I covered my face and wept quietly. “Do they ask about me?” I said. She told me the children missed me. They sent their love. Their well wishes. My daughter also made a little paper flower. (I still keep it to date, the most precious gift I have ever received).

I had reached the belly of the beast and clawed my way back up; now there was light, actual light, and something that felt like hope. I felt stronger. Clearer. Renewed in body, yes, but also in spirit. I had been reading Buddhism and Islam, filling my head with doctrine and discipline, which I told Angela about — as if I’d been away studying the architecture of faith and had come back carrying blueprints. She listened and asked questions, and when she prayed for me before she departed, she said, “…heal Tom so that he can enjoy the joyous richness of his children.”

When I came out of rehab, I went after Roseline. Wooed her. Relentlessly. For a year. We had long conversations about what I wanted, who she was, and where we were and how those two could triangulate. We saw a counsellor, some man who looked like a village pastor in his dreadful suits, but who had great insight and wisdom on couples. For a year we didn’t get intimate, didn’t spend the night in the same room. I did the heavy lifting, I dated her, I threw myself into being a dad again to our kids and my kids abroad. When I travelled to the UK to visit my children, I found them so grown I didn’t know how to talk to them. They asked me why I was in the hospital. I told them I was struggling with addiction. They knew what addiction was. That’s how grown they were. “How do you become addicted?” my son asked. “Is it something inside you?” I said sometimes it is. Sometimes it’s bad habits. I was staying in an Airbnb nearby and we spent a great deal of time in that small apartment. They scared me, how much they had changed. They called Angela’s husband “Peter” by his first name. That gave me relief. “Peter says that the best time to get a pet is during winter. Because then you spend a lot of time knowing each other.” I liked Peter too; a big man, red-cheeked, ginger beard. He seemed like a solid fellow.

After one year, Roseline and I got married again. My fourth marriage. And hopefully my last. I don’t have another one in me. I’m all married out.

I’ve been sober for close to three years now. My life is largely what I expect it to be because of what I put into it. When things go sideways, it’s not always sabotage; sometimes it’s just the universe shifting on its axis. And I let it.

I am content now. Not euphoric. Just steadier.

But contentment doesn’t cancel worry. I worry about money. I worry about my children – the ones in the UK, whether they’ll be safe from drugs, from forgetting me. I worry about the ones here – whether I did permanent damage during my drinking years, whether they look at me and see a father or a man recovering from himself.

I worry about my heart and its appetites. I worry whether Roseline is happy enough to stay. Whether I am enough for her today. Tomorrow.

I worry about my father. He is very old now. Sickly. I cannot imagine a world without him. I cannot imagine not being able to sit across from him while he stares at a spot on the table, thinking. He is my ChatGPT of life. The place I go when I don’t know what to do.

But I’m learning that worry is a form of arrogance – as if I can outthink fate.

So I try to live.

***

item.title: Her Seven Men
item.description:
Can the men you knew as a child follow you into your adulthood? Even if many of them were nameless and are now faceless. Even if what you remember most are their moans, how they breathed at night behind the curtain. Men who didn’t hurt you but took away pieces of your childhood simply by being there. And then the other men – the good ones – the ones who hugged you, extended kindness.

Her childhood is full of these men. Men her mother introduced into her life, and men life introduced on its own.

Where do you keep these men?

The truth is, they aren’t your men to keep. Most of them were your mother’s men. She let them in. And perhaps this is where the story begins, not with the men but with your mother.

“I love her so much,” Bosibori* says behind her massive, perspiring glass of lemonade. “She is my reason for living.”

We are at CJ’s on James Gichuru, the Sunday crowd trooping in from church, still carrying their spiritual nourishment. She’s wearing an elegant burnt orange shawl. I tell her I’d like to picture her mother. “She’s big now, but she was never big. She is light, but she enhanced it by bleaching herself. She looks good though,’ she chuckles, raising her hand, “not like those people who bleach and their knuckles remain dark. She wasn’t dark before, so the bleaching turned out well for her.

Her mother’s story starts with incest.

Omwenga

When she was a young girl, her mother had planned to meet her boyfriend at her cousin’s place for a tryst. It was a Saturday. Kisii rain is ferocious, and when it came down that afternoon, her boyfriend couldn’t show up. She was stranded. That night, with the rain loud on the roof and nowhere to go, something happened between her and her cousin that neither of them would ever name out loud.

When she discovered she was pregnant, her mother was furious. To spare the family embarrassment, she was banished to Kisii town after giving birth, where she secured a job as a house help for a rich pastor who owned matatus. She left her son behind. Soon enough, she fell in love with Omwenga, one of the drivers. She fell pregnant and moved in with him, and that is how Bosibori came into the world – our lady in the burnt orange shawl, seated here with her massive lemonade.

Omwenga was a violent man. He beat her mother, and her mother, being mouthy and unwilling to take anything lying down, fought back. The house was a war zone. Eventually, her mother packed Bosibori and left, returning to her own mother, who didn’t want her there either – too much shame, too much noise. So she kept moving, landing finally in a one-roomed house in Kisumu’s Railway Staff Quarters, doing odd jobs: Mama fua. Kibanda cooking. Casual labour. It wasn’t enough. So she sent for Bosibori’s brother and got into sex work, needing someone to stay with the child at night while she was out.

“What do you remember of those nights before your mom would leave the house for work?” I ask.

“I remember her looking around the house for her eye pencil. She’d hold up a small mirror and run wanja – what she called eye pencil – around her eyebrows and lips, then wear a bright red lipstick. She’d wear a very short jeans skirt, tell us not to open the door for anyone until she was back, then step outside into the darkness and be gone.”

“Where would she tell you she has gone to?”

“To buy bread.” She says. “Nimeenda kununua mkate.”

At around 2am she would knock, calling out. “She called me Mam. I’d hear her – Mam, mam, open up, it’s me.” Her brother would scramble out of bed and open the door. “Kuna mgeni,” she would announce, as a warning. There was always a different man standing behind her. Sometimes finishing a cigarette before stepping in. Sometimes swaying, drunk. Sometimes sober. Tall men. Short men. Fat men. Men in hats. Bald men. Her mother would drop a mattress on the floor and disappear behind the curtain with the man.

Mogeni

“In class seven, my brother Mogeni got into depression, drugs and alcohol and moved out,” Bosi says. “He couldn’t stand it. He couldn’t stand being in the house where my mother brought in men.” They lived in a plot, and when her mother fought with neighbours –  which was often, her mother being tempestuous – the neighbours would hurl the word malaya at her like a stone meant to maim. Only it hurt her children more. Mogeni couldn’t bear that environment. So when he was 13, he left, and it was just her and her mother.

“Would you be able to go back to sleep when she brought the men home?” I ask.

She shakes her head. “No. I’d hear them.” A pause. “I’d hear her moan. I was a child, maybe class one or two, so I thought they were hurting my mom. It would make me cry, but I couldn’t cry loudly because my mother was a very angry woman, and I was afraid she would hear me and beat me up. So I’d cry until the moaning stopped, then wake up very early and run off to school. School was a refuge for me.” She pauses again and stares at her drink. “Now that I’m an adult, I know it wasn’t normal sex. I think it was BDSM.”

“Why do you think so?”

“Because it was just – ” I can hear her shake her leg under the table. “Very… extreme.”

She pauses and then smiles, the saddest smile you can see on a girl on a Sunday. “I think she used female condoms at some point, and once it got stuck, and I could hear her crying as the man tried to remove it. It must have been painful. They really tried for a while, her crying…”

Another time, she parted the curtain to ask her mother for break-time money, and the man who turned around in bed – to her dismay – was her math teacher. “Our eyes met and he turned away. I cried all the way to school. We held teachers in such high regard. And there was mine, in bed with my mother. It crumbled things I thought were solid.” A secret formed between them after that – unspoken, never acknowledged. He never punished her in class again. She was bright enough that it didn’t matter, but they both knew it wasn’t about brightness.

She never knew what state her mother would come home in. Beaten by cops – the police had no softness for sex workers. Drunk. Sometimes both.

In class six, her mother sat her down. “I want you to go live with your father.” Bosi was confused – her mother had always told her he was dead. But nobody questioned her mother. She was handed 500 shillings and put on a bus. When you get to the stage, ask for the butchery. That’s your grandfather’s butchery. He’ll take you to your father.

“I hated him immediately when I saw him- my father. He wasn’t there when I needed protection, and now I was being delivered to him like a package.” His wife wanted nothing to do with her – she could hear them arguing through the wall that first night. She can’t stay here! The next day, she was on a matatu back to Kisumu. Her mother, furious, put her straight back on another one before she’d even set her bag down. She had become a ping-pong ball, shuttled between people who didn’t want her.

She ended up at her grandparents’. “It was pure hell, Biko. Truly.” She called her mother every day. Mom, please come for me. I’m suffering. Her mother showed up one afternoon and found her walking back from the shamba, barefoot, a jembe on her shoulder. She went off on her parents. I don’t know how to till land myself. You will not make my daughter till land. That same day, Bosibori was back in Kisumu.

Rama

I saw a lot of men in our house over the time I lived with my mom,” Bosi says. “A lot – like maybe 300 men or so.” Men who came in cars and men who came on foot. Younger men, older men, rich men, poor men, loud men and mousy men. A whole taxonomy of men. Their one-roomed house in Railway Staff Quarters was a railroad that men passed through, heading towards the great search.

I know the man who infected my mother with HIV,” she says. “He is a known doctor in Kisumu, a family man.”

How do you know it was him?”

Because one night I heard them argue – he was a frequent customer – and my mother was hysterical, crying. She was saying, X, umenipa ukimwi na mia tano. Umenipa ukimwi na mia tano?  Five hundred shillings; that’s what her life cost him. The man shouted back, calling her a whore who had slept with many men, and that it could be any of those men. It was ugly to my ears, listening to that.” She says while bringing her hand to cover her left ear as if those loud voices are still ringing in her ear.

Then there was Rama.

I remember him distinctly.” Another frequent customer, a mix of Indian and African, younger than her mother. Maybe 28 to her mother’s late 30s.

Why does he stand out, this Rama?”

Because he was kind to me.” Suddenly, like rain on a hot day, tears spring to her eyes. She blinks and looks away. “I’m sorry – gosh, I’m sorry.” She starts crying. I let her.

She rummages through her purse and produces a pink chequered handkerchief. A fragile smile, trying very hard to be brave. Then a deep breath. “You know, I have done some work on myself, and I promised I wouldn’t cry when I met you. Look at me.”

It’s fine. Really.”

We sit in brief silence; the hubbub around us muted.

He would sometimes give me 100 bob for school,” she continues, steadying herself. “Or come during the day and cook for me. Help me with homework. I just didn’t understand why he was so kind to the child of a woman he paid for sex…I don’t get it…” She breaks down completely this time. The couple at the next table –  a hairy guy who looks like Artur Margaryan with a very tiny, bird-like girl not bigger than Bosi’s lemonade, wearing a crop top – turn to look. I give them a stare that sends them back to their food.

Am I embarrassing you?” she asks, through tears.

Hell no.”

Will you write that I cried?”

Yes, of course. And I’ll mention the pink handkerchief. I’ll say it’s a Kisii handkerchief.”

She laughs and blows her nose.

Why does Rama’s memory make you cry?”

Because kindness was very rare in my world.”

I lean in and write that phrase in my notebook. Maybe I will make it into my header, maybe I won’t. Either way, I love it. Because kindness was very rare in my world.

She spent as much time away from their house as she could. The house felt like a wound that wouldn’t close, its ugliness clinging to her like woodsmoke. Shame does that – it doesn’t wash off, it soaks in, it becomes your tissue, a gangrenous tissue. She and her girlfriends found refuge in churches that fed people. “We’d attend baptism and catechism classes because they fed participants.” She completed class eight with 378 marks, a disappointment for a girl everyone had marked as exceptional. Her mother continued her work. She continued leaving early to go sit in church, putting as much distance as she could between herself and that curtain.

Peter

One morning, a Sunday school teacher found her under the tree she had claimed as her own, sitting alone as she did every morning. He sat beside her. “I always see you here every morning. Is everything okay at home?”

So she told him. Everything.

He was so moved, he reached out and hugged her, and that hug – she has never forgotten it. “I don’t know how to describe it, Biko. It was the best hug anyone had ever given me. I have never been hugged by a man like that again. It was like being hugged by Jesus.”

He prayed over her, and she remembers his exact words: God, give me the strength to father her.

She starts weeping again. “God, this is not going well. This is not how a healed person should tell their story.”

“I think it’s exactly how a healed person should tell their story.”

Peter did more than pray for her. He gave her money when she needed it – and she needed it many times. He prayed for her consistently. And he told everyone in that church about her, this girl who needed a chance, until the right person heard. That person was Dorothy, who knew teacher Achieng, who worked for an NGO called Nyanza Initiative for Girls Education and Empowerment – NIGEE.

And just like that, following the invisible thread Peter had pulled, Bosibori was sponsored to go to high school in Nyanza, where she would become head girl, for she was bright.

Daniel

During school holidays, she continued her old habit – slipping out early, finding churches, looking for food and something that felt like peace.

At Jesus Celebration Center, where the cool kids went, and they served biscuits and juice, she met Laura. Laura came from a rich family, a single-father home. “The difference between a single mother home and a single father home,” Bosi says, “is that a single father home has a free vibe. Men are not very particular domestically as women are.” This allowed her to go for sleepovers, spend whole weeks there during holidays. Her mother was relieved – one less mouth.

Laura eventually told her father, Daniel, about Bosi. And her father embraced her like his own. He would buy her school uniforms, shopping, and gifts when he travelled. If he bought Laura a blue bag, he bought Bosibori the exact same blue bag. For a girl who had spent her childhood being surplus, being treated as an equal was its own kind of miracle. But then Daniel remarried, and the new wife arrived with a new world order. First, she fired the help, Eunice – because perhaps she was a student of Machiavelli’s teachings? “Also, Eunice used to bring men into the house.” I laugh. Oh Eunice. Eunice.

Then she turned her attention to Bosibori. And this girl who keeps hanging around – we know about her mother. She’s a bad influence. Bosi was also axed. The new wife was draining the swamp. Another door closing.

In form two, NIGEE ran out of funding, and she was staring at dropping out. She went to the school counsellor, Madam Otieno, with her fears. They had had a long relationship with Madam Otieno, who was conversant with her situation at home. Madam Otieno listened and said simply; Go to the bursar. Tell him I sent you. “So I go to the bursar, and I tell him I’ve been sent by Madam Otieno.

You won’t believe it, but he not only wrote off my debt, but I never paid a cent until I finished form four.”

“How?!”

“Because Madam Otieno and the bursar were having a thing.”

That makes me laugh so hard. “Damn! The powerful things women whisper in the ears of men.”

Then Kisumu County flattened the Railway Staff Quarters – about five years ago  – and her mother was forced to move to Obunga. The ghetto. To supplement the sex work, she started selling changaa, which meant more men, more noise. Except now Bosibori couldn’t escape to church. She had to stay and help serve these men. “Some of them were terrible,” she says. “They’d grope at you.” Her world, which had always been small, shrank further. “The ghetto is a completely different ecosystem. The boys and girls I used to run to church with are either dead or in Kamiti or Kodiaga maximum prison. The ghetto will swallow you.”

Her brother, who had escaped once, kept getting caught by the police in drinking dens. The same with her mother. She found herself at the station constantly, negotiating their release. “I had the OCPD’s number until recently, when I deleted it. I’d go to him crying, promising him sex to release my mother or brother.” She knew the currency was sex. She had always known. It was the only currency the house trades in. And the house always wins.

She scored a B-Plus in KCSE. Kenyatta University offered her a place to study Gender Studies and Community Development. Naturally, it was impossible – there was no money. Those doors were not open to people like her. She got a job selling Safaricom SIM cards, but it wasn’t enough to raise fees. “I was stuck.”

Then Mary happened. Her best friend, also heading to university, who refused to leave her behind, who went around raising 24,000 shillings from friends and well-wishers. “That’s a whole other story, Biko, what Mary did for me.” It is another story. But it ends with Bosibori on a bus to Nairobi, for the first time in her life, landing at Afya Center and heading to university.

It must have felt a little like those ships arriving in New York a century ago, the Irish standing on deck after weeks at sea, craning their necks for their first glimpse of the Statue of Liberty. For her, Afya Centre must have looked a little like the Statue of Liberty  – a sudden promise that the life behind you might not be the life ahead.

Timothy

Her money runs out in the first semester. She scrounges from an NGO that dries up after one semester, leans on church connections, patches together what she can. “I’m seriously struggling. It looks like I can’t proceed, and I’d be forced to go back to the ghetto. And it’s heartbreaking because I can’t imagine going back to my mother’s one-roomed house, to those men again.”

“Hold on, I will be right back,” I tell her and dash to see a man about a dog.

When I come back, I ask her playfully, “Have you been reading through my notebook, Bosi?”

She chuckles. “I wouldn’t even read your handwriting. You write in Greek.”

“Good. Where were we – yeah, you’re broke and at the end of your rope.”

One day, a boy with a physical disability sits next to her in a lecture and asks her to sign his attendance sheet – he has an interview to get to. They exchange numbers. Later, he calls to confirm she signed. She asks about the interview. He tells her it was for the Mastercard Foundation Scholars program. “I asked him, how do I apply? Can I apply? He said, when they next roll out, I will inform you.” Timothy gets into the program and moves to USIU. She watches his life change on WhatsApp status updates, the way you watch something beautiful from the other side of a window. She craved to move too, to get into this program of dreams.

When the next call comes out, she applies. “They only take students who haven’t gone to university, so I lied that I hadn’t. I was desperate.” Timothy coaches her beforehand. Just tell your story. Be real. “So I go in, and I tell my story to this panel, and I can’t stop crying. I hadn’t told anyone this story in detail before. It was very difficult and painful.” After the questions, a woman named Lynette – a director of some kind – leaned across the table and handed her a branded Mastercard Foundation pen. “Your life starts here,” she said. Bosibori broke down.

“The ink in that pen is over, but I still keep it.” Because it’s not a pen but a key that has unblocked an unimaginable life for her.

What the key unlocked: a room at USIU with her own door that she opened and closed as she pleased. For the first time in her life, she had control of who entered her space. Medical cover that allowed her to go for therapy. Four years of fees, paid. The stipend gave her brother half the money he needed to buy a bodaboda. It paid for a dermatologist who cleared a skin disease she had carried for years without money to treat. It moved her mother out of Obunga – still a single room, but no more ghetto, no more men. Her mother’s health was failing, and the sex work was behind her now. “She doesn’t have to deal with these men again,” Bosibori says, and her voice drops to something private. “I love her so much.” She starts crying again, and this time it doesn’t feel like grief. It feels like the relief of a child who has spent her whole life trying to save her mother.

Martin.

At USIU, she met Martin. Ugandan. Kind fellow. A man of faith, too. “He is the man who took my virginity,” she says, matter-of-factly.

“Perfect,” I say. “I wanted to ask about the impact of your childhood on your relationship with sex.”

“My attitude towards sex and men is not very good. I have seen men in their element – very important men and men who have nothing, all coming to our house for the same thing. It made me think men are weak. That they all succumb to sex regardless of their station in life. I hated men for a long time. How they came into our home and claimed my mother’s body.” She pauses. “But I have also experienced great kindness from men. Rama is proof that one person can be many things. You can pay a sex worker and still be a decent human being. Therapy helped me understand that. It helped me forgive these men, my father, the man who infected my mother with HIV, my mother, my brother.” She smiles. “I wish you could hear the first thirty seconds when my brother calls. He just praises me. Queen of queens. Leader of women.” She laughs. “Oh, my brother. I love him.”

“You were telling me about the impact of your childhood on intimacy.”

“Oh yes. I viewed sex as something dirty. Something illicit that dirty men engaged in. Something, a cruelty to the female body. And my sexual experience was very difficult because of that – all those things in my head when I was with my boyfriend. Therapy helps, and healing is a long process. But that’s not why we broke up.”

“Oh.”

“We broke up because he said I was too much; too confrontational. That he was tired of being everything to me – my father, my doctor, my therapist. I was checking his phone constantly. If I found messages from any woman I found suspicious, I called those women.” She shakes her head.

“You are mad.”

“I was.” A sad laugh. “I was very temperamental, and I drove him away. And it broke my heart because Martin was my first and only relationship, and a great one. A kind man. We had plans – marriage, children. He gave me a promise ring. He knew all about my past, and he still allowed me inside and gave me a family. I’d go to Uganda and spend a month with him and his people during holidays. I became a completely different person. I adopted the Ugandan culture of kneeling while serving and greeting men. I would have knelt while greeting you, Biko.”

“I’m truly disappointed in you.”

“Ha-ha. I made Martin fall out of love with me. But it’s okay. I finished university late last year, I’m waiting to graduate, and I already have a job. It’s not much but it covers my rent and supports my mother.”

She looks down at her half-full lemonade glass.

“I want to build my mother a home.”

“Of that,” I said, “I am certain.”

It only occurred to me later, as I reversed out of the parking lot after signing my book for her, that she hadn’t said a house.

**

Otherwise, if you’re in Nairobi, you never quite know where these rains will wash you to Mahi Mahiu. And what better way to drift downstream than with a book?

item.title: A Virus And Matoke Walk Into A Bar
item.description:
I have the flu.

It’s not that bad, but I’m a man, so it’s very bad.

My head hurts in ways that feel biblical. My throat was on fire, but has since negotiated a ceasefire. I am on ColdCap and hydration salts. I’m breathing through my mouth like a fish. I may take a drip later. A drip. With a needle and a bag. A nurse. Actually, a day nurse and a night nurse. Like the ColdCap.

I just came back from Kampala, which could easily be Addis Ababa, given the number of Ethiopians I encountered there. I also ate Luwombo  – that thing in the photo staring back at you. It’s a traditional Ugandan stew cooked in banana leaves, which means it arrives at your table looking like a gift from the earth itself. I had the fish in groundnut sauce. I had matoke. I had beans. I had chapati. [why not]. What I didn’t have was shame.

Then I didn’t wake up for 21 hours.

Please like and subscribe to my food channel.

I hope your souls are intact. Mine is horizontal.

I will be back next week.

[Sniff.]

Inshallah.

item.title: Babies Don’t Have Principles.
item.description:
Everybody is dead.

Grace is dead. John died. Polly. Oh, Aunt Pol also died. Arthur is dead. Arthur! Won’t you believe that? Of course you know Michael is dead, right? That rat. Lizzie also died. So did Alfie; gone with his lovely dreadlocks and his long secretive face full of the Bible. Little Ruby is dead.

Tommy Shelby is alive, though.

And he hates it.

We know this because he says things like, “All of us are dead, except the one who wants to be dead.” You’d say things like that too if everybody you knew was dead. Like him, you’d self exile in some lonesome massive property estate in the village. Which is exactly the kind of thing Tommy Shelby would do. Melancholy follows him.

He’s grief stricken and he’s haunted. I don’t think he eats much. When he sleeps he has nightmares of war, death and getting stuck in tunnels, stabbing another man with a knife. I don’t want to say he is tortured because that would be akin to saying amoeba is shapeless.

The Blitz is ongoing in the midlands. This is 1940 or thereabouts. The German Luftwaffe are dropping bombs after bombs on the heads of the British, mostly in Birmingham and Coventry. It’s astonishing. War. We see a bunch of women celebrating a birthday in an arms factory and before the birthday girl can blow out a candle, a German bomb drops over her head. Dead with held breath.

We know that Birmingham is Tommy’s hood but Tommy isn’t there and Tommy doesn’t care. Who is there is Tommy’s illegitimate son and he’s a thug because he’s a rotten apple that didn’t fall too far from a cursed tree. But he isn’t even a good thug, but we will come to that later.

For now we are trapped with Tommy in this remote rural property. It’s cold, winter of some sorts. The trees are dead. The sky is dead. Together with the birds. Everything is dead. And it’s beautiful, this desperation of life. He takes long walks in the dreary cold landscape, through the trees that look like ghouls. But he is Tommy Shelby and he makes solitude and torture look sexy. He is out there, alone, with his rifle shooting pheasants even nobody can claim to have ever seen Tommy Shelby actually eat. We have seen plates in front of him. We have seen family meals happening. And food being served. But we have never seen Tommy bring food to his kisser. We have seen him smoke. We have seen him pour whisky. And his favourite pastime – stare.

When he isn’t out there brooding in that dead nothingness, he’s out standing on graves. He stands on Grace Shelby’s grave, the middle of his face sunken deep, holding all the grief and sorrow a face could ever collect. You remember Grace, don’t you? Even though it’s hard to keep track of all of the women he loved.

Grace was a spy. Undercover. Waiting at Tommy’s bar, The Garrison. Seducing Tommy. Reporting Tommy to the authorities. She is eventually discovered, and she flees to America where she marries someone else. Then she comes back to England and tells Tommy she is pregnant with his child. Of course Tommy loves her because Tommy loves complicated. They marry in season three and she dies in Season Three. Took an assassin’s bullet meant for Tommy. The Italians – the Changrettas – had already dealt Tommy the Black Hand. [Luca was my favourite].

Yes, that Grace.

She is buried out in the grim remote estate where Tommy is locked up with his ghosts. He stands over her grave. He also stands over little Ruby’s grave. His daughter. Ruby was small. Soft-voiced. She believed in things children believe in – songs, whispers, shadows. Then she fell ill. Quickly. Tuberculosis. But she also had strange visions, the Romani beliefs of a curse. She died quickly, too quickly for a man like Tommy Shelby to understand, let alone control.

He stands over her grave as long as a man should stand over his daughter’s grave. Her grave is there. Small. Complicated. Death got there before life could find its voice. And Tommy places a red scarf on it.

So that’s where we find Tommy, in this blighted place.

He’s out there with Johnny Dogs. You remember him. Still as loyal as a dog. Still there, gingerly stepping around Tommy’s foul moods, his demons, the weather inside him. Johnny Dogs isn’t even family. Which, in this world, might be the point. Because in Tommy Shelby’s world, loyalty is often strongest where blood is absent. He gets things done. And Tommy trusts him.

Johnny Dogs.

If you hate spoilers, if you haven’t watched Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man, then stop reading right here. Go smoke on the balcony and stare yonder, keeping with the theme here. Or just chew gum.

Tommy, sequestered out there in the fog, is writing a book. Imagine that, gave up his revolver for the pen. On a typewriter, in this case. He’s out there banging copy about his life when a woman – a Gypsy woman – comes calling. Claims to carry a message from the dead. From Duke’s mother. Duke is his son, the one wrecking things up in Birmingham. That he should go save his son. Of course Tommy doesn’t shoot the messenger, he sleeps with the messenger. Can’t blame the man; he’s out there alone dealing with many ghosts, probably the only female he had seen in a while. Also, she’s sexy, with tattoos against her pale white skin, her small little bones, her black clothes.

While we are in bed we discover that Arthur died in a road accident, and Tommy doesn’t want to stay with this memory because he was involved. Before we can get over the fact that Arthur is dead, Ada, Tommy’s sister, arrives. [Not on the same day, come on.] Ada is now an MP. Ada is a lady. Elegant and composed. She shows up driving a lovely 1930s-type Bentley; low-slung, rounded, a little like a well-bred insect.

And she tells Tommy that his son Duke is causing a ruckus back in Birmingham. He already lost Ruby from TB, couldn’t save her, now his son needed saving and he wasn’t trying. So he leaves for Birmingham to save his son who is about to take fake currency that the Germans are about to dish out in a financial warfare that is meant to bring the economy of Britain to its knees.

Guess who Duke is in this movie?

No, guess.

Barry Keoghan!

I know.

He’s amazing, isn’t he? A bit psychotic, isn’t he? The quintessential villain. I absolutely loved him in the Banshees of Inisherin which is a movie you need to watch if you haven’t. If only for the dialogue. The storyline is quirky and dark. Two men fighting over a donkey. And a friendship. What a beautiful film.

He is also in Dunkirk, which is a war movie. And I love all war movies. I like when men die by gunshot, bayonet or an ambush. All Quiet on the Western Front? A movie like that. Barry isn’t in that movie, though. But he is also in The Killing of a Sacred Deer, a dark, dark, disturbing film. Barry is properly unsettling there. I’m also told he is in Batman. I haven’t watched Batman. I’m not 12. I can’t stand those comic/marvel movies where characters wear capes and fly. And they possess perfect jawlines and blue eyes. And they save other people with blue eyes from burning buildings. Hero worship!

Can’t stand ’em.

Barry is Duke. And Duke is out of order, as a Peaky Blinder should. He says things like, “accidents of blood do not concern me.” He is taking money from the enemy, Germans, at a time of war, a treacherous and treasonous act. Even I, who don’t mind the brand of villainy of Germans really, shook my head and thought, No, Barry, we don’t take money from the Germans during war!

Tommy rides a horse through the streets. Tommy lights cigarettes. He pours a drink. Tommy stares with his wounded eyes, all the deaths he has endured and caused drawn on his face. Tommy kills the villain, even though he is the greatest villain.

And because the villain has to die…

Tommy dies.

***

So? What great thing – documentary, movie, series – have you watched lately?

item.title: Who The Hell Is Thomas?
item.description:
You are from Ndindiruku, a place in Kirinyaga that only people from Kirinyaga know. It sounds far, but it’s only two hours from Nairobi. You could cycle to the city from there. Or, if you have really strong arms, hang from the back of a truck bringing rice to town. You did neither. You came to the University of Nairobi, which you didn’t graduate from. Money problems. But also, books – reading gave you constant migraines. “No, really,” you told people. “If I read any book, my head hurts so bad.”

You are allergic to education.

Which isn’t a bad thing if you have talents. And you do. You are good at buying and selling. Enterprise. So you start downtown – a printing and photocopy place, subletting a small space next to a hotel that sells tea and mandazi. It thrives. It thrives so much that people tell you to move further uptown, towards Kenyatta Avenue, where people do more photocopying. So you open a second shop near Nyayo House and leave someone else from Ndindiruku – your cousin, Macharia – to run the one downtown. Macharia will later steal from you and disappear to Mombasa. When you find out, you call his mother, your aunt, and say something like “neki?” I’m not Kikuyu. I’m just telling this story.

But before Macharia steals your money, you make quite a bit from both shops. Enough that when the car-hailing business arrives on your shores, you are among the first to get into it, while people with education are still asking: but how does that work? You know exactly how it works; it works if you work hard and jump in immediately. You get Wairimu – another relative from Ndindiruku, who studied accounting at KCA and speaks well and thinks fast – to manage the shop near Nyayo House. Then you start driving an Uber.

And the whole time you drive your Uber, you never meet Njoro wa Uber. Which you find peculiar, right?

You do well enough that when Macharia’s theft finally lands, it doesn’t create a financial dent so much as a sharp stab of betrayal. You sell the printing business and put the money towards a second Uber car. Two Ubers now. Still no Njoro wa Uber.

In between all this, you meet a girl and marry her quickly. Who she is and what she likes isn’t important to this story, so don’t think about her too much – in fact, forget her. But because we don’t want to be accused of erasing the women in stories the way the Bible does, she is called Faith. Everybody called her Fei. There. Happy?

Two Ubers. A thriving printing shop that Wairimu runs with a firm hand. A wife. A small flat on Naivasha Road, before Naivasha Road became the melee it is now. You buy small pieces of land all over because it is in your bloodline – you are from Kirinyaga, you speak fluent Land. You work hard, but not too hard to miss beers and nyama choma at a joint in Kawangware on random days, Mondays sometimes, the odd Tuesday.

Things are really looking up until one day a man forgets his phone in your Uber.

When you think about that day, you think: but why did he have to use my cab?

What happened was this. After Covid nearly crippled everyone – including you – and you went back to your businesses leaner and more careful, a man forgot his iPhone 15 Plus under the passenger seat. Your car wash guy, Fuls – short for Wafula – found it and brought it to you, where you sat in the shade, drinking a soda and eating mukimo. The phone already had a few missed calls. You set it aside and went about your day.

He called while you were dropping a client off at Imara Daima, stuck in a backup at the entrance to the estate. A man’s voice. He said he’d used your Uber that morning, been dropped at Upperhill, must have left the phone behind. You remembered him. Short. Jacket. Brown shoes. He’d only uttered two words the entire trip: here is fine. OK, three words. Then he was gone.

“Yes, I found it under the seat,” you told him

“Where are you?”

“Imara Daima.”

“OK. Can you send a rider to the Java in Hurlingham? Leave it with the manager. Tell her it’s for Thomas.”

You said you would. But before you’d even dropped the current client, another ride request came in – Pangani – and then another, and another, and another. You forgot about the phone and Thomas entirely. He called again after 6pm, sounding irritated. “You didn’t send the phone. I’m here in Java.”

You were parked near a petrol station in Kikuyu, having just dropped someone at PCEA Kikuyu Hospital. You were eating roasted maize. You said, Shit. You’d forgotten. You promised to send it first thing in the morning. He asked if you could leave it with the security guy at Transnational Plaza instead. You said you weren’t sure when you’d be in town, but if you got a ride heading that way, you’d sort it. He wasn’t too amused. He said he’d call you in the morning, find out where you were, and come collect it himself.

In the morning, the phone – sitting in your glove compartment – is dead. Thomas doesn’t call.

Not that day. Not the day after. Not the day after that.

The man simply never calls you again.

You don’t know what to do with the phone. Sell it? But you are not that kind of person. You are the son of peasant rice farmers from Ndindiruku. Your mother is a respected, active member of the ACK church. Your father is an honest man. He owns three pairs of shoes. Apart from Macharia, you don’t know of any thieves in the family. So you leave the phone at home, in a drawer, and wait for Thomas to call. You forget all about it. You do your Uber business. Still, no sign of Njoro wa Uber.

Three weeks later, your wife calls while you’re on the Expressway, having picked up a client from JKIA. The sun has just set. The billboards are lit. Your fuel gauge has been in the yellow for some time, and you keep calculating what happens if you stall on the Expressway – you’ve heard they penalise heavily for towing, and you cannot afford that right now. So you are already distracted when she calls. She’d taken her mother to Kijabe Hospital for tests earlier in the day, so you assume she’s calling to update you.

“There are people here looking for you,” she says.

“What people?”

“Three of them. They say they are with the DCI.”

Because your first instinct is that these are thugs – because why would the DCI come looking for you – you tell her: “Don’t let them in the house.”

“They are already in the house!” she cries. “What do you mean, don’t let them in? What does the DCI want with you?”

“I don’t know,” you say, and then you hear a voice in the background: acha tuongee na yeye. There’s the sound of the phone changing hands, and then a woman’s voice  – calm, almost bored – says: “Inspector Jennifer hapa.” You are surprised it’s a woman. In your mind, DCI is full of men with guns. She tells you they need to speak with you. Where are you? You say you’re on the Expressway, dropping a client in Westlands. She says: come home after. Immediately.

“What is this about?” you ask.

“We are waiting for you here,” she says, and leaves it at that.

You drop the client. You fuel up on the way home. An hour later, you pull up to find a dark-tinted Prado parked outside the apartment with two men and a woman inside. The men don’t look like DCI except for the jackets and the way they hold eye contact a beat too long. Inspector Jennifer introduces her colleagues. She has the face of someone who works in a bank. Jeans. Sneakers. Well-kept nails. She asks if you know someone called Thomas X.

You say no – and you mean it, because you have forgotten everything about Thomas from three weeks ago, and besides, you are scared. You have never had to deal with police before. The two men are watching you, and when you say you don’t know Thomas, they exchange a look that makes your stomach tighten.

Inspector Jennifer says, “You’ve never interacted with Thomas X?”

“Never,” you say, looking from her to the men as if appealing to them.

She says: “You don’t know him. But you have his phone.”

“Phone? What ph-” And there it is. The coin drops. You remember the client and the iPhone in the drawer at home. Now you look like a liar. And how did they even…

“Get us the phone,” she says. Not a question.

One of the men accompanies you inside. You notice he removes his shoes at the door when you do, and you find this so bizarre, and so unexpectedly human, that you almost say something. You go to the bedroom, open the drawer, and hand him the phone. Like in the movies, he doesn’t touch it – he produces a small polythene bag, you drop it in, and he zips it shut.

They tell you they need to bring you in for questioning. You ask why. They say it’s related to the phone. You ask more questions. They answer none of them. Your wife is near tears. You are near tears. Your mother-in-law, who was diagnosed with stage two breast cancer just that afternoon at Kijabe, asks the officers what this is about – why are you taking her son-in-law, this honest man? The man tells her not to worry, it’s routine questioning. Before they lead you out, your wife presses ten thousand shillings into your hand, because at this stage, you both still believe this is the kind of thing that ten thousand shillings can make go away.

They don’t handcuff you.

You sit in the back of the Prado. It smells of stale cigarettes. They don’t address you. They talk among themselves – office things, unrelated to you entirely. Someone mentions a market fire. Their voices are ordinary. Normal. They sound like people on their way home from work, not people ferrying a man who doesn’t know why he’s been taken. One of them had asked, back at the house, whether you had any weapons, and when you said no he hissed: are you lying to us? But that was the only edge. Since then, nothing. No aggression. No warmth. Just the motorway and the radio and these ordinary voices.

They don’t take you to DCI headquarters. They take you to a house off Ngong Road, behind Toi Market – compound gate, overgrown grass, a naked bulb burning outside. It has the feeling of a place that is used but not lived in. Inside, more men. Maybe four, moving from room to room. They pay you no attention. There is almost no furniture. The curtains are cheap. You are shown into a room with two chairs and a desk, and left there. It’s exactly like the movies. The people who collected you don’t come in. Instead, a heavy-set older man enters in a short-sleeved shirt. He doesn’t introduce himself. He says only that he is with the Anti-Terrorism Police Unit.

Your mouth goes dry. Your hands begin to tremble.

He opens his file. He doesn’t look at you. Then he says:

“I suppose you know that the owner of that phone is dead.” He says. I suppose? I suppose? God!

Your vision blurs for a second. You might have made a sound; an anguished cry. You look at a wall and think: what the fck! What the fck! You know, in that moment, that you are in serious trouble. He sits across from you, calm, unhurried, eyes on his file, while you quietly fall apart.

“I want you to tell me how you know Thomas.”

You tell him everything. The whole truth and nothing but the truth. You wish your voice were steady. It is not. It is high and trembling and fast, and he never once interrupts you. In fact, he wears a bored look, like how you would listen to a child tell you about monsters.

**
