item.title: How A Goat Makes Sausages
item.description:
I was invited to see how Nyashinski makes his sausages. 

Over at HomeBoyz Entertainment studios at Galana Road. Ian invited me. Ian is his Creative Director. We did a project once before, where I interviewed Nyashinski for a Johnny Walker project a few years ago. The interview ran so long that by the time I stumbled out of The Stanley, Kimathi Street had gone eerie, quiet and apocalyptic. Like everyone had either fled the city or been eaten by a strange monster.

Here is how I know Ian, for context, because to understand the spectacle, you have to understand the men who design it.

Ian grew up in Kisumu. His mother was a tailor, who spent days bent over her Singer machine. So the soundtrack of his entire childhood is the cha-cha-cha of needle through cloth. Pieces of clothes falling on the floor. His mother made all their school uniforms, sometimes introducing a flash of Ankara print at the collar or cuffs, something subtle enough to almost pass, and the teachers would call him out – that is not the official uniform, Ian – but the other students thought he was fresh and cool.

So he fell in love with clothes young. He could also draw. He could draw pretty much anything. His mom bought him a massive drawing pad, and he filled it page by page with imagination. In school, he began drawing illustrations in the margins of textbooks because “they were too wordy, they needed to be illustrated.” The first time he heard the word “sketch,” his teacher was scolding him for having drawn on the textbook: why do you keep sketching on the textbooks? So everybody started calling him Sketch.

He was very good at writing and drawing and one day – after high school – he came to Nairobi for a funeral and he never went back. He worked for Story Moja – that’s where we first met – where he wrote and illustrated tens of children’s books and a couple of his own. He then co-founded a men’s apparel brand, Dapper Monkey, because clothes won’t let the man rest. This was while art directing for an advertising agency, before finally starting his own company that he named – no one’s surprise – Sketch Experience Ltd.

We became good friends when he would come up against me in the Kenya Blog Awards, the creative writing category, and for four consecutive years, I’d beat his skinny ass. He wrote a brilliant blog called Dear Doris, a collection of love letters to Doris, a light plus-size woman with tiny feet. Every two weeks, he’d post a letter to Doris, something mushy and glowing and vulnerable.

Through his girlfriend, now his wife, he found his way to Nyashinski. Now he designs album covers, concert posters, and social media visuals. But that’s the small stuff, the visible tip. What he really does is build the world the music lives in. He designs the stage – the physical architecture of it – the lighting rigs, the choreography of light, the geometry of what an audience sees when they look up. He put it simply when I asked him what he really does: “Nyashinski is in charge of everything you hear. I am in charge of everything you see.”

And this is how I ended up in that studio, watching The Goat make sausages.

I don’t know what I expected but what I walked into was some sort of movement. There were over a hundred people milling around the stage, engaged in one thing or the other. A large choir was just coming off the stage as I arrived, still breathing hard, making way for a wave of dancers coming on. And they were all young; the average age being 21. The place throbbed with youth and energy.

There were tens of people managing sound, cameramen, dancers and theatre. Mugambi Nthiga, of Too Early For Birds, directed the actors. Wambui Thimba was managing costumes. Fakii, Nyashinski’s manager, sat at the edge watching. Cameramen tracked positions. Sound engineers touched knobs on their machines, headphones pressed to their ears, listening to frequencies only whales would appreciate. Everything was moving, and yet everything had a logic to it, the way a busy kitchen has a logic that looks like chaos from outside the door.

I went to say hello to Nyashinski. He was taking a break up a small flight of stairs, seated alone at a table. It felt like climbing up to see a king – not by design but because he needed to burrow away to recenter himself for the next set. He crushed his cigarette and stood when I approached, reaching for his mask – he couldn’t afford a cold, not this week. We hugged. He was gracious. Later, when I was talking to a few of the dancers, they said, “he knows everybody here by name.”

Later, I watched him rehearse the last few sets. There are like seven sets, a whole production of music and theatre. Every movement accounted for on the stage. Nothing by chance. And they do it again and again and again, daily for a month before the show until it’s tweaked to within an inch of perfection. There were two dancers I spoke to, friends who grew up in Dandora, who said they were saved by dance. That being there, dancing for Shin, was their crowning moment. There is one particular dancer I spoke to, Juliana, petite, the size of a rolled ball of wool, who did this dance up a silk rope that dangled from the ceiling. She flirts with gravity.

There was song and dance and theatre. People came on and left the stage in perfect synchrony. Everybody seemed to know exactly what they were doing, but better still, they enjoyed it. The dancers, I noticed, all smiled when they moved. That changes everything, doesn’t it? It’s like talking to someone on the phone and hearing the smile in their voice.

Later, Shin walked up and asked what I thought. Not that my opinion carried much weight. I said, genuinely, that it felt spiritual. It was the only word that came to mind, watching it all unfold.

He nodded. Then nodded again. He said, “That is a high compliment.”

I told him, “Only because this is high art.”

I honestly didn’t imagine this much goes into a show. That the light guy rigs a galaxy of blinking bulbs. That the sound guy shows up sober at the very least. That the choreographer gathers half a dozen bodies that cannot afford to miss a beat. Not this whole production.

I grew up watching Kiini Macho on TV, mouth open. Magic, I thought, was pulling a rabbit out of a hat. Burning your hat while it sat on your head.

But magic is work. Magic is dance. Magic is lyrics and language. Magic is waking up early to do the same thing you did yesterday. Only better. Doing it when you don’t feel like it. When you’d rather be in bed watching Bridgerton. Magic is many people, aligned in one belief, insisting on getting it right.

And it’s a beauty to watch.

So go watch it. https://nyashinski.co.ke/ 

***

item.description:
I didn’t like what I wrote. Mostly because I’m feeling out of it. Do you feel that sometimes; a listlessness, some apathy. Days you wish you were a smoker, so that you sit on the balcony, burning through cigarettes, staring at nothing. 

Anyway, I rewrote it after a few hours. And it still felt odd. The sentences heaping over one another, as if scrambling for the door.

Then yesterday I woke up early, eager to get to the bottom of it. Sat at the computer. Read it. And the more I read, the more it felt like something I wouldn’t write.

So I canned it.

This is the female version of when women wake up and say they feel fat. And it doesn’t matter what you tell them. And they hate their clothes. It’s a tide that comes and goes.

item.title: Who The Hell Is Thomas? Part 2
item.description:
You are not a killer. You are not shady. You are from Ndindiruku. Your mother sings in the local ACK church. Your father is an honest man. You were raised by peasants – honest people, God-fearing. You have one wife. You drive an Uber.  You shouldn’t be sitting in an unmarked house off Ngong Road, talking to someone from the anti-terrorism unit. There is no universe where the law is interested in you. 

“I swear I don’t know who Thomas is,” you keep telling this man. And he keeps asking you the same questions, only dressed differently each time. You tell him the story of how you met Thomas so many times, and it doesn’t change. Because it’s the truth. When he shows you three photos of three different men, you don’t know who Thomas is because you are a driver, the client sits at the back, you barely look at them unless they are annoying, or they can’t stop talking, or they refuse to pay. 

The man leaves the room, leaving you alone in this bare space with a table, two chairs, no window, and a naked bulb humming faintly above you. It’s so quiet you can hear your heartbeat. Loud. Treacherous. He comes back with another man. Younger. Slim. A hat pulled low. The slim one stands behind him.

The man sits. No files this time. He folds his hands on the table, as if to conclude this conversation. Or rather, interrogation. 

“You aren’t telling us the entire truth.” He declares, and when you try to protest, he raises a hand – like a traffic cop stopping a reckless turn.

“We don’t pick people randomly,” he says. “For us to come to your house and find that phone, this isn’t guesswork. We investigate. Thoroughly. And those investigations have led us to you. This is no coincidence, I would like you to know that.”

You open your mouth.

He cuts you off.

“I understand that you’re tired. Your memory isn’t very good right now. Get some rest. Tomorrow morning, we will try again. OK?”

“But – ” 

“My colleague will show you where to sleep. Make sure you get some rest.”

Slim leads you to a room at the back. There’s a bed. Neatly made. Military neat. He takes your shoes. Your belt. Locks the door.

You stare at the silence. You can’t sleep. You can’t think straight. You lie on top of the bed, staring at the ceiling, your mind running in circles. You think of those films – men in the wrong place at the wrong time who disappear into systems that don’t explain themselves. Men who never went back home. Innocent men, like you. You think of your wife. Your mother. Will they believe you or the government? They found a dead man’s phone in your house. It’s terrifying. 

You must have drifted off just before dawn because the door swings open almost immediately after sleep finds you. A very tall man stands there. Not Slim. A face as hard as a court bench. A face that has never known a smile.  He hands you a small toothbrush and an even smaller toothpaste and directs you to a small sink outside a small toilet. Then leads you back to the room you were in the previous day. There is a different man now. A fat fellow. Small nose. Darting eyes. He smiles too much. You fear him immediately.

He makes small talk. Then asks the exact same questions you have been asked since this saga started. Only this time, smiling. A slow, patient, unsettling smile. If lizards could smile…It goes on for an hour. At some point, you ask to use the toilet.

“Number one or number two?” he asks brightly.

“Number one.”

The toilet is at the end of the hallway. No door.

You are later served tea. Bread. An orange. You can’t bring yourself to peel the orange, so you ignore it.  When you ask to call your wife, they say you will. Your wife has ulcers. Her mother has cancer. You imagine her moving from station to station, looking for you. Her ulcers flaring. Her mother worried sick, praying for you. You spend most of the day in your room, seated on the bed. 

That night, Slim comes for you. You are put into a car with windows so dark they swallow the outside world. There’s a barrier between you and the driver. You can’t see ahead. The car reverses, then moves forward. It lurches on a rough road. You can hear the sound of gravel. Then tarmac.  You drive for about an hour. It’s cold when you arrive. Proper cold. Limuru cold. Tigoni cold. High fences. Dark sky.

The men aren’t unkind. But they aren’t anything else either. They hardly look at you, but you can tell they are very aware of you.  When you ask what’s happening, one says, “Usijali bro. Hii mambo itakamilishwa.” The new house is a maisonette. Better than the last place. There’s carpet. Sofas. But nothing on the walls. No life. No warmth.

“You drink coffee?” a new man asks.

You say yes.

He brings it in a white mug. Sits with you. Drinks his. And suddenly it feels like two men having coffee.

He asks about your life. Where you grew up. Your businesses. How much you make. What you do with your money. What you do when you’re bored. He asks what your wife does. How frequently you send money home. How much. Who else do you send money to? How often you operate cash. How much. Where did you meet Thomas? Do you know Andrew? What about Ahmed? Have you been to a mosque before? How did you raise money to buy the second Uber? 

You find yourself answering. Because he is good at this art of conversation. He isn’t threatening. And that frightens you more than anything. You get the nerve to ask him about Thomas. He tells you Thomas was a serious criminal. Terrorism. Money laundering. An enemy of the state.

“I didn’t kill him,” you say.

He shrugs. “We’re not interested in whether you killed him. We’re interested in whether you worked with him.” You tell him you barely knew Thomas. Didn’t know him from Adam. Or Eve. 

He asks suddenly, “Have you worked with Somalis?”

“No,” you say immediately.

He just looks at you. Patiently. Waiting for you to recall because he seems to know the right answer, and ‘no’ isn’t it. Then you remember – a few years back. A Somali client. Small job. T-shirts. Posters. That kind of thing. You don’t recall the small jobs. 

“What was on the posters?” he asks.

“I don’t know,” you say. “They were in Somali.”

He nods. Sips his coffee.

You ask what they said.

“Nothing much,” he says. “But they ended up in Somalia. With people who are… not good.”

You swear you didn’t know. Not the client. Not those people.

“I know,” he says.

You are exhausted. You want a shower. You want your phone. You want to call your wife. He tells you you can’t access your phone until you are cleared. You ask him if you’ll go home. He looks at you, almost amused.

“Of course. What do you think we are? Have we treated you badly? Have we denied you anything?”

You want to say: You’ve denied me my freedom. But he is kind. Or appears kind. And you don’t want to break whatever fragile thing this is. So you nod. You even thank him. You tell him about your wife. How fragile she is. Could he call her? “You’ll be home soon.” He says. 

They take your shoes again. You are shown into another room. Two beds. Ensuite. A towel. Soap. And somehow that reassures you. Because why would they let you shower if they planned to kill you? You shower. Hot water. It feels like a renewal. A blessing.  You feel human again. You lie down and fall asleep instantly.

When you wake, someone is standing over you. He hands over your shoes. Your belt. He’s leaning against the door, scrolling through his phone as you wear your shoes and loop your belt.  Outside, it’s still dark. Early morning dark. Panic rises up your chest. Is this it? Will they take you to a forest and shoot you in the head? 

The car again. Another hour. Then the car stops. The door opens. You step out. You recognise your flat. They hand you your phone. The man says nothing to you. He simply gets back into the car, and they drive off. You stand there. Not moving. Not believing it. You half expect the car to return. For the men to take you away. Freedom is unbelievable. You look up at the flats, darkened windows. Up there in one of the houses, your wife is sleeping, or she started up worried sick. 

You can’t move. Something inside you has shifted. Your hands start to tremble. Then you begin to sob. You hold the wall with two hands and sob uncontrollably. You feel relieved and angry, grateful and powerless. You feel like something powerful and unjust happened to you, but you can’t put your finger on it. 

**

item.title: Old Shoes
item.description:
I saw a man carry a massive baguette in Amsterdam. He wore a beard and baggy pants and looked like he was going home. At that moment, the baguette didn’t look like food; it looked like a weapon. I saw an old woman drag a trash bin out in Uithoorn, in the southern part of the Netherlands. The bin rattled over the pavement like it was protesting her.

We got onto trains many times, and nobody once asked to see our tickets. I was told by my host that here, you are expected to do the right thing. One morning, I wore my running shoes and stepped outside. It was cold for me -maybe six degrees – sharp, unfriendly weather. I ran further south, following paths, passing trees and fences and small canals, not knowing where I’d end up, or if I’d get lost.

Women cycled past with children strapped behind them, pink-cheeked, small helmets bobbing. I wondered what thoughts sat in those small heads.

I got lost. Which is what I secretly like – the thrill of finding my way back. I become alive that way. Alert. I also tend to run more when I’m lost.

After three days of walking, my lower back started acting up again. So we went into the World Trade Centre in Amsterdam and found a physiotherapist. I didn’t have to remove my clothes. He ran some machine over my thighs, the back of my thighs, my back. It made a drilling sound.

He asked where I was from, and I told him Kenya. “Ahh, Kenya! My girlfriend is from Lesotho.” As if we walk to Lesotho often to buy bread. 

He took a needle and pricked me four times – twice on my back and twice on my thighs – to “relieve pressure.” I yelped. He asked if I had been to Lesotho. I said yes. I told him I went to Maseru once, in the middle of a harsh winter. I saw a lot of sheep.

“Did you ski on their mountains?” he asked.

I winced at that Caucasian thought. No, I didn’t ski! 

“You should have,” he said. “I did. Quite the experience.”

He told me about his father, who was a doctor. He told me he has been a physiotherapist since he was 25.

“And how old are you?” I asked.

“Sixty-two.” He said. “That was my son who ushered you in. We work together. He studied sports medicine. He is 32.”

I said, “You look amazing.”

He looked amazing.

“And my girlfriend is 47.”

“Good for you!” I said.

When he was done, he retrieved his phone. “Let me show you her photo, in case you think I’m making all this up.”

I laughed. Yes, most people make things like that up for giggles.

He scrolled and found what was clearly the best photo. She looked all right. A bit thin. I nodded appreciatively. “Elegant. Very elegant.”

“She’s very petite,” he said. “This size.” He indicated something closer to a mini-fridge.

“You like petite girls?”

“Yes,” he chuckled and shrugged as if he just can’t help it with them, pint-sized babes.

He walked me out, and when I fetched my card to pay, he said, “That is free, for my African brother.” Saved me a ton of money. 

I wish I caught his name.

We took the canal tour. A very touristy thing to do. The last time I did this tour, it was just the beginning of summer, and a drunk tourist almost fell in the canal. I don’t know why I remember that more than anything else. This time, nobody tried to tip over. The guide made everybody laugh – an ageing man with a wizened, tired voice, like it had seen too much water. We drifted past old houses leaning into each other as he told their stories, which were also the stories of the city and its people. I’m very much into such things.

I saw some contemporary art at Moco museum and was reminded how good the white man is at curating a simple experience.

In the evening, the Dutch rushed home in long lines of bicycles, wheels whispering over the road, scarves fluttering behind them, to sit in yellow-lit, curtainless homes and make dinner. Later, we smoked weed in a coffee house, which is what they call places where people smoke weed. On the train back home, I felt disoriented. I leaned on the window and watched things pass. It felt like someone had occupied my head and was quietly moving furniture around, careful not to knock anything over.

It’s not for me. Weed. And all that furniture movement.

Then a train out of Copenhagen, sliding south through flat farmland and grey sky, until Sweden appeared – quietly, the way modest countries do. Kristianstad. A small town. The buildings stood there like they had nothing left to prove – old, symmetrical, quietly unbothered. Frederik’s Church rose out of the city, large and imposing, with that calm religious poise. Inside, people shuffled in, lowered their voices, and looked up in awe. I like cathedrals. They are like whales. They remind me of my place in the pecking order. 

Outside, life moved efficiently. Bicycles again. Clean streets. Order. Everything working the way it should. Almost suspiciously so. It felt like The Truman Show.

To get a good cup of coffee, you have to sell your body at a street corner. It’s expensive. A cup goes for over a thousand bob. [Thanks, Kendi, for being a fantastic hostess]. 

Then a train to Sweden. A small town called Kristianstad to the south. I love small towns. They feel like a long foreplay. Our host took us to dinner at her mum’s, in a provincial, charming village called Mjönäs, about 40 minutes away. Population: 200, give or take a dog and a sheep. Their house looked like something from a storybook we read in primary schools. The countryside was quiet, devoid of humans. The roads empty, so much that each time a car drove by, I had to turn to look and almost point and say, “a car!” 

After dinner – salmon, clean and honest – we took a walk to the nearby lake. The wind came at us eagerly. We hunched into it, hands buried in our pockets.  The next day, we took a train for an hour to Lund, a charming university town. Everything felt arranged but not stiff, like an old place with great bones. Bicycles leaned lazily against centuries-old walls, students spilling out of cafés with academic cheek. Some sat in bars, drinking beers. Others sprawled across green patches, on their bellies, legs up, reading books. Like a university brochure.  The streets were narrow, as if leading you by the hand. There was a calm intelligence in the air. Even the light felt considered, falling gently on cobblestones and shoulders, as if it had been doing this for years and saw no reason to change.

Inside Lund Cathedral is something that defies imagination. Consider a cathedral built 900 years ago, an architectural wonder. Thick Romanesque walls, squat towers. The stone, pale and worn into itself. Inside, the arches are heavy and deliberate, curving low, carrying the weight of centuries. I descended into the crypt, the pillars feel almost human – short, stubborn, each one carved differently. Spooky too.  There’s a figure there gripping a column, refusing to let go. Like a bat. But not a bat. Like I said, spooky. It’s dim down there, the air colder, light streaming from the windows above in long, sharp pillars.

Upstairs, an old astronomical clock marks time with quiet theatre, reminding you that this place has been measuring days long before you arrived, and will continue long after you leave. Like I said earlier, a whale. 

Upstairs again, Lady lit a candle for her dad, and I lit a candle for my mum.

One time, my mom came to visit me in high school and left me with her shoes. I have carried those shoes with me ever since. I remember that afternoon. We sat under a tree overlooking the rugby pitch, students and parents scattered under other trees. She sat with her legs stretched out in front of her, like a woman in a market. Her shoes were off. 

They were simple leather shoes. Worn, but not unsightly. The same ones she had worn to drop me off in Form One – her shoes for church or anything that mattered. She couldn’t afford the luxury of buying another pair because she was paying school fees for all of us. And it broke my heart to look at them, because they carried more than they seemed to: love, sacrifice.

I was never one to ask her for anything, for fear of adding to her troubles. So I went without a tie, proper socks, shirts, and a sweater – until she noticed and made a noise about it. Then she died when I was 35. And when I think of her – her life – I think of her shoes.

They were love, yes, but also sacrifice. And sacrifice often means going without.

It unsettles me that her life became all about raising children. I don’t know what she loved. Maybe she loved sunrises. Or the sound of waves. Maybe she would have loved to ride a loud motorcycle. Or to kiss someone else who wasn’t my father in a foreign city. Or to wear a short dress and hold a cigarette in her mouth, even if she wasn’t going to light it. Or to see France. Or ride a horse. Or be alone, away for the weekend, from the rigmarole of motherhood. She never did any of those things. She just raised children.

Nobody’s life should be only about raising children. 

Isn’t that sad?

To walk in those old shoes. Because you have children. Not to be able to do much else in your life?

I travel because I want to see as much of the world as I can afford. To meet people. To learn how they live. To see the shape of clouds in a foreign land. How the rain falls. I want to live in a village in Senegal one day, even though I don’t speak French beyond pourquoi – mostly because Fally Ipupa sings it in Travelling Love.

When I think of my hour of death, I don’t want to carry the regret of things I didn’t do. And certainly not because I had children.

The night before I left Kenya, we sat in the living room for a small family meeting. I handed authority to Tamms and told them to live in peace and harmony. I told them I’d be gone for a few weeks. Kim thought it was too long. Maybe even selfish. 

One day, I want them to remember how I lived. That no matter what happened, they woke up and found me at my desk. That I worked to my bone. That I did what I said I would do for them. That I followed through. But that I also packed my things and left – sometimes with them, sometimes without them.

Maybe that will teach them how to live.

Because we have a saying in Luo, Kama iluokorie ok itwoe.

Ask a luo to translate. 

***

item.title: Hallo, You
item.description:
Hello from the edge of the world – or what feels like it.

The edge being Norway. Asker, specifically, which is twenty minutes from Oslo by train and approximately 7,000 kilometres from my balcony in Nairobi. What has happened out here since we last spoke? Not awfully much. I went to the IKEA museum in n Älmhult, Sweden. There I learnt what I have always known; nothing comes easy. 

Yesterday we drove four hours from a small southern town called Grimstad – I did some running there, on hills, with the sea watching below – to catch a ferry into Lysefjord to see the famous fjords. Sunny day, beautiful day. One of the most awe-striking things I have ever stood in front of. 

Otherwise, the sun sets around ten in the evening and rises by four in the morning. My tropical body is now feeling it.  I’m tired in the good, honest way. A week or so left of this cold, beautiful, light-soaked continent and then I am coming home. I hear Kenya is underwater. Stay dry.

Speak soon. 

Yours, somewhere in the north

item.title: Europe
item.description:
“I can’t run because I have big boobs.”

“But you don’t run with your boobs.”

“It’s hard to run when your boobs are hitting your face.”

“Please allow me to sit next to that analogy a little longer.”

“You wouldn’t know anything about that. You are a man.”

“I know men with big boobs who run.”

“Ha-ha. There is no man alive with boobs bigger than mine.”

That’s me chatting with this girl on social media who DM’d me after seeing one of my running stats. She asked why I love running. I told her I don’t love running. I love the feeling I get after running, so I’m chasing that feeling. Plus, running keeps me alert in the mind and fit in the body. Running itself is a slog. Anyway, that’s how the conversation veered into boob avenue.

“I think you need a proper sports bra.”

“I have tried.”

“And?”

“And I still can’t find one that holds them together when I run.”

“Maybe the problem is the sports bra, not the boobs.”

“It’s the boobs, trust me. Have you seen any Olympians with big boobs?”

I quickly went on ChatGPT and asked: Are there any known Olympians with big boobs? Female, not male.

“Serena Williams,” I wrote triumphantly. “She had big boobs.”

“They aren’t that big. I don’t think there are many runners with big boobs.”

“Would you do away with them in order to run?”

“I would do away with them now, not just to run but to live.”

“Now? When were you crazy about them?”

“When I was younger and stupid. Mostly because men were crazy about them.”

“You thought you were your boobs.”

“Ha-ha, sort of.”

“Did they stop going crazy about them?”

“What, the men? No, I stopped seeing the value.”

“Well. You could reduce them. I know a guy called Dr Tilman Stasch, an acquaintance. He’s over at Riverside Drive, fancy clinic and all. Check him out. He takes care of boobs and things.”

“Oh yeah. But also it’s scary, I’m not very sure I want to get done with them.”

“You could also just stick to chess.”

Anyway, somewhere between conversations about Olympic breasts and reduction surgery, I started thinking about Europe and the things I loved – and occasionally disliked – about it.

You can run and cycle

Because my boobs aren’t big, I travel with running shoes.

Running is the quickest way to see a city before it introduces itself properly. You discover which neighbourhoods smell faintly of money and which ones smell like old water and cigarettes. You get lost. Which is the whole point.

Europe is built for people in motion. Runners. Cyclists. People in suspiciously expensive tights gliding past canals at seven in the morning, looking emotionally stable. I ran in all those cities, but Amsterdam stayed with me the most. That city seems permanently half-submerged. You are either running over water, alongside water, towards water or away from it. Sometimes all four at once. Oyunga lives in a very quaint, lovely town south of the city. Yesterday morning, somewhere in an estate outside Amsterdam, I ran over a canal so cinematic I stopped my watch and leaned over the rail to look at the water and the estate below.

And the cold – God, the cold was perfect for running. I like weather that makes exercise feel mildly punitive. Cold enough for gloves. Cold enough to feel virtuous and engaged. 

Everything is on time

I have always felt that lateness is a form of disrespect. Not only for your own time, but the other person’s time. It’s a f*k you. It’s incongruous to the normal nature of relations. 

Nothing irritates me more than arriving for a 6 pm play only for someone to stroll onto the stage at 6:32 and announce that “we are waiting for a few more people.” As though the rest of us who arrived on time are throw pillows arranged around the venue for ambience.

Europe was deeply comforting in this regard.

Trains and trams arrived exactly when they said they would. Doors closed without apology. Nobody begged the driver to “just wait for one guy.” Time moved with or without your emotional readiness. And because everyone seemed to understand this arrangement, there was very little drama around it. No theatrical excuses involving traffic, weather, or the pesky “I’m five minutes away” when someone is still looking for their car keys at home.

Punctuality is not really about clocks. It’s trust and respect. It’s about an entire society agreeing that your time matters as much as theirs.

I found that deeply erotic. Like someone tickling my inner sole with a feather. 

…uhm, you know what I mean. ​

Landscape

This isn’t a Europe thing. This is a life thing.

Landscapes are God’s own art gallery. 

We mostly took trains between countries because trains force you to earn a landscape slowly. Flying tells you nothing except mankind’s determination. But trains – trains let a country unfold at human speed. Trains are the foreplay of a country. 

You begin to notice the lay of the land. How hills rise gently into forests before collapsing into lakes. The colour of skies. The temperament of light. The shape of houses, which is really the shape of lives. You can tell, just by looking, where people retreat to, what they fear, how much privacy they require from one another. I noticed that many European homes don’t have fences the way ours do. No towering walls and imposing gates. It sent me down a rabbit hole about the origins of that difference, which eventually led me, naturally, to colonialism.

When you travel by train, you watch big towns loosen gradually into small towns. Apartment blocks giving way to lonely farmhouses. Industrial greys softening into impossible greens. Church spires appear suddenly like old ideas.

Landscapes reveal people eventually. Their ambitions and anxieties. Their relationship with beauty. Even their relationship with silence.

It’s easy – and honestly a bit lazy – to say rural Europe eventually starts looking the same. That’s usually the precise moment to start paying closer attention.

Pastries.

Everywhere you look: pastries.

Everywhere you look: pastries.

And they look back at you.

Seductive little carbs displayed behind glass like the girls in Amsterdam’s Red Light District. Honestly, Europe is just one giant Red Light District for bread. Bread is everywhere. Cakes. Cinnamon buns. Pastries with names that sound like minor Scandinavian diseases. And croissants. Dear God, croissants. Did I tell you about my love affair with croissants that only come second to chapos?

But the bread – the bread was extraordinary.

In Grimstad, our host served us this dense brown bread packed with seeds and addiction. I still think about that loaf fondly. Which is probably how you know you are getting older; when your memories become emotionally attached to good bread.

Coffee.

I understand why someone might consider commercial sex work in Scandinavia. One has to afford coffee somehow. Everything there is obscenely expensive. At first, your body rejects Scandinavian prices the way a body rejects a transplanted organ. In Copenhagen, two mochas and two pastries set us back about 3,400 bob. You gulp when you receive a message notification after you have run the card. 

One afternoon in Norrmalm, north of the King’s Palace in Stockholm, we bought a single 500ml bottle of water from a street vendor for roughly 900 shillings. Nine hundred bob for water. At Oslo Central Station, two burgers and a drink at Burger King (for f*ksake!) came to nearly four thousand shillings. Burger King.

Eventually, you learn survival tactics. Buy water from supermarket chains. Avoid tourist traps. Eat strategically. Forget fancy dinners unless you are a politician, in the tender business, or moving narcotics professionally.

Nobody says hello.

And when you do say hello, people react like you are about to ask for a loan.

People mostly mind their own business. Maybe it’s the weather. Maybe it’s the price of croissants. There’s very little unnecessary interaction. No eye contact on trains. Headphones. Faces arranged in polite neutrality. If someone smiles, it’s often the restrained kind that doesn’t quite reach the eyes. Their smiles are like their sun. It looks warm outside until you step out and realise how cold it actually is.

Even many black people on the streets rarely looked at me. Almost like they are afraid to acknowledge their blackness. Still, there were moments. One big black guy working in a mall waved at me and boomed out a cheerful hello that felt almost African in volume. In Oslo, a Kenyan man holding hands with his white babe spotted the small Kenyan flag on my jacket and immediately asked, “Niaje, uko sawa?” And in a Thai restaurant in Stockholm, a man pushing a pram with two children walked over to our table and struck up a conversation. “I looked at her,” he said, nodding at Lady, “and she reminded me of my sisters. That’s how I knew you guys are Kenyan.”

Otherwise, warmth is not something you casually expect from strangers there. Starting conversations on trains feels almost illicit. 

The Airbnb 

Stay with friends wherever you can.

In Gamla Stan, the Old Town of Stockholm, we stayed in an overpriced Airbnb near the King’s Palace that was roughly the size of a Weaver bird’s nest. To be fair, Gamla Stan is painfully touristy, all cobblestones and beautiful people dragging luggage over ancient streets. But the room was so tiny I started giggling the moment we walked in and simply couldn’t stop. It was like playing kalongolongo.

Oddly, the bathroom was spacious, beautiful and tastefully done. I briefly considered sleeping in there because the actual room was so small I spent the night with my legs sticking out into the corridor while other tourists stepped over them politely on their way to their rooms at night. Which, to be fair, felt very European. 

Polite?

Are Europeans polite or do they just mind their own business? Is it passive aggression? I couldn’t tell. I once sat in a flight to Kisumu on a Saturday, and this was the one time I had bought a newspaper in ages, and I was there reading it like an adult. The only ‘problem’ was I wasn’t the only one reading it, my seatmate, someone I never met in my life, was also reading it. It was irritating, yes, because his head was tilted into my damn newspaper, but in hindsight, I find it warm. That someone could shamelessly read your newspaper with you in a plane so much that you give him the magazine insert to read. I shudder to think of the same thing happening in Europe. Do you know, I learnt, it is considered rude to sit next to someone in a train or bus in Oslo when there is a free seat nearby?

So there you are, just two Kenyans, sharing a newspaper. Isn’t that humanity? 

Marriage.

I’m looking to interview three men and three women in happy marriages that were not always happy. And y’all who have been married for only five years don’t count, so please sit down. 

Kindly ping me on bikozulu@gmail.com 

Otherwise, have you been well?

item.title: Cat Person
item.description:
Biko said he’s fatigued. Imagine that travelling to see cathedrals can make one fatigued. It’s pure nonsense. Anyway, he will be here next week. In the meantime, Eddie is holding things together here this week. 

And he got a cat. 

By Eddy Ashioya 

I got a cat. It’s a black and white cat, with glassy green eyes, vacant of any emotion, but would still make you feel things. She’s called ‘Lady’, and when people inadvertently ask why, I say, “I am hoping she grows up to be one.” Ha! Ha! They reply, right before they roll their eyes. I don’t care. They don’t know her like I do.

This is not my first cat, however. That would be Moscow, a gingerbread male cat with the attitude of a Primadonna and the looks of one. It was supposed to be a temporary matter: C – had rescued Moscow from the streets (surprise) and she needed someone to stay with him overnight, “Just one night!”, she said. Moscow was what? Two weeks old? So I said fine, because what else would I have said? Two weeks turned into seven months, and by this time I had developed a reputation as a cat dad (cad?), and I liked it known that rescuing cats was a calling, divine providence, koso koso na kadhalika. 

But my pursuit of happiness was insidious: the girls who gave it up when they heard my carenting stories. That Moscow boy served me well. He died after he fell off a friend’s balcony, where I had left him, during one of my restless man trips, the original sin. I felt terrible the day Moscow died, a drab Saturday evening, but my friend, B -, was devastated – I think he had developed a parasocial relationship with Moscow, like how one feels they know a celebrity or a news anchor cause they see them on TV every day.

Lady inherited most of Moscow’s things – the bed, the collar, the man. I’ve never been a cat person, not really. Many a time I have sauntered into meetings or interviews with Lady’s fur hanging on my pants, and I only discover this when one of the subjects, usually some middle-aged man, starts sneezing, because they are allergic to cat fur. Imagine that. What grown man is allergic to cat fur?

We never kept cats as pets in Shirere, Kakamega, where I grew up. My earliest interactions with a cat was in Mombasa, where we had been warned specifically not to talk or pet the cats, because they could be really not cats. That was a scary moment for me, and I grew up believing in paka jini, and I would avert my gaze from the TV whenever Jeff Koinange was on, because legend had it that Jeff Koinange’s hair was curly and dark because alikuwa amerambwa na paka jini. In those days, Jeff Koinange was a mythical creature; he seemed to have been whispered into existence, passed on from mouth to mouth, living on the tongues of newscasters and lubricated by the saliva of kids who would imitate him. Of course, I grew up and met Jeff Koinange, and I indeed confirmed that no Venus hair relaxer could achieve what a paka jini can.

When you grow up in the village, animals are purveyors of superstition. A dog was not just a dog; they were the spiritual watchmen of our houses. Believe me, don’t believe me, we had this dog that was kidnapped by those mari mari people, taken all the way to Majengo in Vihiga County; and for a while, two months hivi we thought he had died. So imagine our collective shock when the dog walked back in, bruised and battered, but still battling. The negroe had walked from Majengo to Shirere and was back to take his rightful place in our compound. From that time on, we called him ‘Survivor.’

My father loved Survivor. He would never go to the farm without Survivor, and his radio, pitched to 101.9 Metro FM – the House of Reggae. My father, Peter Tosh, named after his favourite reggae musician, Peter Tosh aka the Steppin’ Razor, loved reggae. He’d never miss any show by DJ Stano and Papa Lefty and Jeff Mwangemi, HSC on Mother Radio. Everyone called him Tosh; they feared him, respected his dash, his temper, the way his Bata safari boots always seemed to know where to step.

During the school holidays, my brother Johnny and I would accompany him to the farm sometimes, watch as he spared Survivor some meat from his plate, doing it with such tenderness, Survivor of course lapping it all up, and I was a little jealous I guess, and maybe Johnny was, too, that nothing in life could mean so much to our father as some survivor beast, and when Survivor caught a rabbit, or bit an intruder, it had the power to make him happy in a way we guessed we never could. But the reggae music will persist, Burning Spear or Gregory Isaacs or Joseph “Culture” Hill negotiating and warning the white man that we will no longer be slaves. Dad liked that shit. He was not a man to take any shit from anyone, and he expected his sons to do the same, and he would use those songs as teachable moments, lowering the volume so he can inject, while stroking his ashy goatee, which suggested the fire of deeply held knowledge. He called them the ‘reggae prophets’, people who had a firm grasp of how big and awful the world could be. “The music is in the message, the message is in the music…” Peter Tosh being Peter Tosh, I thought. Deep down, where my boys don’t know me, this is still the warmest memory I carry of my father; sure to be passed on in the gene pool when I become a father myself.  

My father’s mother, my grandmother, Kukhu, was the original animal matriarch. She kept everything that could be kept: chicken, ducks, goats, cows, cats. If there was enough space, and a Great White Shark to be tamed, she would have kept that too. She taught me how to milk the cows, inadvertently, and perhaps inevitably turning me into a boob guy. Early Sunday mornings, she would lead me to the cowshed, show me how to press the udder, how to apply the brakes of self-restraint, how to be firm while being gentle, qualities that have served me well while dealing with the other two-legged gender. Kukhu would be humming Angela Chibalonza songs, or Rose Muhando songs, and in the background, on West FM, I would hear the radio play Bahati Bukuku’s song, which could take the whole day, just one song.

And then Kukhu fell sick, and I could see her wasting away, but she would still let the girl behind her eyes come out, still asking me to milk with her. There was this one cow she loved, Regina, that was the name Kukhu gave that cow, a black Friesian with the biggest udders known to man. At that time my father had lost his job, no, that’s not correct, he had quit his job, because some Indian boss had accused him of orchestrating a fire, and he had beat up that Indian, also not correct, he had driven his safari boots so up his ass the Indian could not forget what shoe size my father wore (size 10, America), the way a strong man might do a lesser man, because my father doesn’t take shit from anyone.

Kukhu’s final act was to sanction my father to sell Regina, so I could go to school. She gave up what she loved most for whom deserved her love least. And then she shut her eyes and closed her heart to the world. It was a painful moment. My mind drifts to Moscow and Kukhu often when Lady starts petting me, like she is doing now, at 3.49 AM, as I type away, Nairobi still jerking itself awake. There is a larger sadness at play here, the sadness of attachment and loss, and the way the world wreaks its changes, whether we’re ready for them or not. How life, or a story, could end abruptly, like this.

item.title: Letters in the Dirt
item.description:
It’s a wretched thing when men grieve. When they hurt. Especially men of my generation, who were taught that hurt is a room you lock from the inside and never mention again.

Oh, this is my generation.

I’m writing this in traffic over the Nyali Bridge. Twenty minutes ago, at the breakfast table, one of the photographers I’m on assignment with asked how old I am – he is early 20s – and I said “48.” He lowered his fork to the plate and stopped chewing. Looked at me like I’d said something tragic. I don’t think that was a compliment. So yes. This is my generation. The one that swallowed things.

Halake, you know him. My friend from Juba. This man always texts me at odd hours – always past 2 am. Always. Never during the day, when the world is loud and watching. Only at night, when the armour comes off a little. This morning I woke up to his message. He said this is the week his daughter died. He’d written something about her. Could I run it? But only if it’s not a bother. Only if it’s not too much trouble. It’s not much, he said. Only if it fits the blog. Then several deleted messages followed – which I suppose weren’t nudes, because that would be awkward and cheap, seeing as we haven’t even had dinner yet.

But I know what those deleted messages were. They were a man trying to say I am not okay and pulling back, trying to form a language that doesn’t expose his wounds. Typing and erasing. Erasing and typing. The oldest dance of men in pain.

I know what this is. I have grieved before. I know the face of it. I know the particular mask it wears on men who are not supposed to fall apart. He is out there in Juba, in his small air-conditioned prefab, thinking about his dead daughter, with nobody to sit beside him in it – because he is Borana, and he is a chief in his village, and strength is expected of him the way rain is expected of clouds. So he writes about her. About Rufoh. Because that is the only way he can keep her somewhere permanent. And sharing this wounded part of himself, with strangers on a blog, at 2 am, is the only way he knows to ask for peace.

Thankfully, he also writes well.

So here.

***

Halake

I am the man by the wallpaper. Always.

In meetings, I mean.

Not by choice. Sometimes the room chooses for you.

You arrive two minutes late because the driver could not find parking, because the Land Cruiser was boxed in by another Land Cruiser, because humanitarianism, for all its noble intentions, has never solved parking.

You enter, and all the seats are taken. So you stand by the wall, near the second door, the one nobody uses because the handle has been loose since the days of the previous Country Director, and you pretend this was your plan all along.

After some years, it becomes your plan.

The wall is not a bad place to stand. From there, you can watch people become themselves. The man from Logistics removes his glasses when he wants sympathy. The donor from Amsterdam uncaps her pen only when someone says “funding gap.” Programme says “last mile” with the confidence of a person who has never sat in black cotton soil watching a truck sink slowly like a bad political promise.

Someone says, “Let’s circle back.”

We circle back.

The circle is large. It has per diem. And barbecue at the close of the meeting.

Other men know how to sit at the table. They have the wrists for watches. They shake hands from the shoulder. They say, “How was the flight?” and mean it for almost three seconds. They have airport-lounge warmth. They know where to stand in group photos. They have opinions about red wine and refinancing.

I have opinions about leaks.

Mine starts above the fridge at 2:13 a.m. during the rains and lands in a steel bowl with the punctuality of a retired math teacher.

The United Nations pays me anyway. So, all is well.

They gave me a blue UN badge, a laptop, a walkie-talkie, a per diem, and a white Land Cruiser with “OCHA” letters on the doors. A car that makes small boys stop playing football and stare, because maybe you are bringing food, maybe medicine, perhaps a Habasha man with sunglasses who will ask their mother where the borehole is.

My title is “humanitarian affairs analyst.”

It is a long title. Long titles are useful. They give shame somewhere to sit.

What I mostly do is visit places where people are hungry, dying, write down the starvation and death in haunting, unforgettable English, and send it to people in rooms where the coffee arrives fresh in porcelain.

The report says: “caseloads remain elevated.”

The child says nothing. The child always says nothing.

The child weighs less than the sentence that flew to Geneva.

Last Tuesday, in Bentiu, a fifteen-year-old girl walked into a feeding centre with a two-month-old boy tied to her chest in a green cloth.

The roof was tin and furious. A jilted sun. It threw the heat back at us.

Women stood along one wall with ration cards folded in their fists. Children sat in the dust with the patience of people who had queued before they learnt breastmilk. One boy pushed the torn lid of a cooking-oil jerrycan along the ground like a car. He had made a road with his toe and was driving carefully through it.

A goat put its head through the doorway. A woman told it to leave. The goat thought about this, then left with the dignity of a Kenyan civil servant.

Faith was at the weighing table. Faith is Kenyan, from Eldoret. She has the posture of a woman who has seen men cry from the flu and still asked them, kindly, to move so the next patient can sit. Her phone plays Sauti Sol softly, as if Bien is also on the UN payroll, assigned to motivate.

The girl stood before her. Her right sandal had split near the toe. Not completely. It had failed in that Kenyan way, where a thing has died but continues reporting to work. Her dress had a tear near the hip, tied into a small knot. She held the baby with one hand and used the other to pull the green cloth higher over his back.

Now and then, her thumb disappeared beneath the cloth to find his neck.

Not stroking.

Checking for life.

She did not look at me. You notice these things when you wear a UN badge. People look at you. They look at the badge, the shoes, the car key, the radio, and the logo on the door outside. They arrange their needs into the shape they think you can understand.

This kid did not recalibrate around UN definitions.

Faith clicked her pen. “Mother’s name?” The girl answered in Nuer. Faith wrote it down. Nyalat. “Age?” The girl answered. Faith looked at her, then at the baby. “Fifteen,” Faith said to me.

Nyalat shifted the baby higher. The cloth had loosened. She tucked it behind his head without looking, her fingers quick and practised. One nail was broken close to the skin.

Faith motioned for the child. For half a second, Nyalat did not move. Then she untied him.

The baby came out of the green cloth as if the cloth had been his body, and this was only what remained. He was asleep. His mouth hung open slightly. His skin had that thin, careful look of paper held up to light. One fist lay closed on his chest, holding nothing.

Faith placed him in the sling. The scale hung from a rusted hook in the roof beam.

A hook is an ugly thing to hang a child from, even when everyone agrees it is for his own good.

For one breath, his whole body floated there, wrapped and silent, while the women in the queue watched the needle.

Outside, the Land Cruiser coughed. Inside, nobody moved.

“Moderate,” Faith said. Then she leaned closer. “Hm.”

You do not want a nurse to say hm.

“Possibly tipping.”

Tipping. One of those aid-sector words that combs its hair before entering a room. Tipping sounds like a chair leaning backward. It does not sound like a baby arriving at the edge of his own body.

Nyalat held out her arms. Faith was still unhooking the sling when the girl reached in and took him back. Not rudely. Not gratefully. Quickly. Like a woman rescuing a pot from the fire just before the bottom burns.

“What is his name?” I asked. Faith translated.

Nyalat looked down. The baby made a small movement with his mouth. She touched his lower lip with her thumb.

“Buom,” she said.

“Iron,” Faith said.

Nyalat heard Faith repeat it and said the name again, this time to the child. “Buom.” As if correcting the room.

The word sat down among us and refused to apologise.

There was no place for it on the form. The form had boxes for age, weight, oedema, referral, and follow-up. It did not have a box for a girl in a torn dress giving famine a child and saying, Not this one. It did not have a box for a mother whose own arm was thinner than the clipboard, naming her son after something that survives fire.

When she said iron, my daughter, Rufoh, stepped into that small Bentiu room.

Not with wind. Not with lights flickering. Nothing with colour. Grief is not always a movie. Sometimes it is a word in another language that opens a door you nailed shut years ago.

Her name was Rufoh. She died in May 2011, in a small children’s hospital in Muthaiga. She was three years, four months, and eleven days old.

I have tried, over the years, not to remember the eleven days. The eleven days have remained committed.

She had a dimple on the left. It arrived before the laugh, like a messenger sent ahead. She called me Da-da-da. Nobody else has ever made my name sound like it had been invented in a hurry by joy.

Rufoh had a stuffed giraffe called Mr Tall, though by then Mr Tall’s neck had collapsed from duty. She believed the moon followed our car home from town. “See?” she would say from the back seat. “It is coming.”

We buried her in Isiolo. Four months later, I bought a one-way KQ ticket to Juba.

Leyla came with me to the airport. She wore a blue sweater. I remember this because grief edits strangely. It deletes whole weeks and leaves you with buttons, shoelaces, and the sound of a spoon inside a cup.

At the counter, the woman weighed my bag. “Nineteen kilos,” she said. “You are fine.”

Leyla looked away.

Fine.

At home, Mr Tall lay under our bed. He had been there since Rufoh’s burial, on his side, one felt eye facing the wall. Neither Leyla nor I could touch him. We swept around him. Imagine that. Two grown people defeated by a dummy giraffe.

Nairobi had become a city of ambushes. A child laughing near the frozen-food aisle. A pink hair clip on the floor of a pharmacy. The moon over Waiyaki Way, fat and innocent, following other people’s cars.

South Sudan had never heard Rufoh’s laugh. That is why I left.

Its dust had not entered her shoes. Its roads had not learnt her voice. Its rooms did not know to keep a corner empty for her.

When colleagues asked, I said the work mattered. It did. But under that, lower down, where men keep the things that embarrass them, I was looking for my daughter’s dimple in the faces of other people’s children.

Faith did not know this. Nyalat did not know this. Buom slept through it.

Outside, the Land Cruiser idled like a large white bear with no shame.

Three weeks before Bentiu, I drove to Isiolo to see my mother. Kameh.

She opened the door before I knocked. “Halake.” My name left her mouth carrying food, complaint, blessing, and a small audit of my absence.

She is small now. Not weak. Folded. Like a leso put away carefully because it has done enough public work. Her hands were dry and warm. The hands of a woman who has washed children, slapped sense, planted things, counted coins in darkness, and continued.

I told her about Nyalat. The broken sandal. Buom in the green cloth. Faith saying moderate, then tipping. About the name. Iron.

The kitchen went quiet.

My mother set her cup down. In Borana, she said something English cannot carry without spilling. But it meant this, close enough:

A mother who names her hungry child Iron has already saved him once. Do not bring her pity. Bring your hands.

Then she said, “Rufoh would have been eighteen this year.”

There it was.

No warning.

No parade.

Just my daughter’s name entering the kitchen and taking a seat.

“Yes,” I said. “She would have.”

She reached across the table and held my face. Her palms smelled of smoke and soap. For fifteen years, she had never asked why I went to South Sudan. Never said running.

“I see what you are doing,” she said. “I have seen it.”

I closed my eyes.

“Come home when you can.”

Not come home now. Not come home and be repaired. When you can.

A few nights after I returned to Juba, I called her. The line was bad. Our voices arrived in pieces. She told me her knee was troubling her, then in the same breath said she had walked to the gate to see which fruit the neem tree had dropped and could be saved.

My mother believes everything deserves examination before being declared useless.

Fruit.

Children.

Husbands.

Governments.

Knees.

“Rest,” I said.

“Hayye,” she said.

That hayye contained her full medical opinion of my advice.

We laughed.

The line cracked.

For a while, there was only breath and distance.

“Mama,” I said.

“Mmm.”

“You taught me letters in the dirt.”

Static moved between us.

“I taught myself,” she said.

“And me.”

A pause.

“And you,” she said.

Then, after another pause, “And whoever you teach next.”

The line died soon after.

I stayed on the steps of my prefab with the phone in my hand.

I thought of Nyalat’s thumb checking her son’s neck under the green cloth.

I thought of Buom hanging in the sling, asleep while strangers watched a needle decide the colour of his hunger.

I thought of the teacher from Sennar, his good shoes ruined by the road, standing beside a hot UN truck and asking about rain for sorghum he did not have.

I thought of my mother on the kitchen floor in Kinna, chalk between her fingers, approaching the alphabet as if it might bite.

And then, of course, I thought of Rufoh.

I always get there.

She would have been eighteen. Maybe she would have had Leyla’s laugh and my forehead, poor girl. Maybe she would have become one of those daughters who look at their fathers with deep affection and mild disappointment, the way Kenyans look at public institutions. Maybe she would have asked why I kept going to places she could not visit.

Why do you go there, Da.da.da?

I have answered ambassadors. I have answered donors. I have answered men in pale shirts who ask whether the crisis is worsening or simply complex. I have answered panels, clusters, briefings, calls with bad networks, and emails beginning with Many thanks.

I do not know how I would have answered her.

The dust at my feet was the colour of old copper.

I bent down.

With my finger, I wrote a K.

Then an R.

The wind came almost immediately, rude as ever.

It blurred the stem of the K first.

Then it entered the curve of the R.

Grain by grain, it took the letters apart.

I watched until they were almost gone.

Then I leaned forward and wrote them again.

item.title: Guy From Tamale
item.description:
She liked him immediately because he looked like his dog. And she likes dogs. Throughout her childhood, until she went off to high school, they had six German shepherds and four Rottweilers. Her neighbours had dogs. Men who like dogs understand a language that isn’t spoken, she says. “They just know.” She says.

I don’t know what that means either.

The man – like the dog – was bearded. She likes bearded men. Men who occasionally spit. Who pee against fences when necessary. Who open bottles with their teeth if the opener is taking too long. Or forget they have toothpicks in their mouths, so they drive around with that, reverse parking with the toothpick dangling. Man. She swiped right.

They started talking about dogs. She told him dogs loved her. All manner of dogs. She believed she was a dog, or that a dog lived inside her, or that she had been a dog in another life, or would return as one. He sent a lot of love emojis in response.

The dog in his profile photo was an Otterhound. Rare breed. Fewer than 1,500 remaining in the world, he told her. It wasn’t his dog – he was once a pet walker in the UK, moonlighting at a care agency while he schooled. The dog belonged to a strange old man who he suspected had money but wore old clothes and pointed with his walking cane when he talked. Kwesi had grown up with dogs, too. He was from Tamale, in Ghana, though he thought he looked Nigerian – wide face, body structured face, half of it beard, smoker’s lips.

“You ever been?” he asked.

“No.” She laughed. What would she be doing in Tamale?

His mother had been a diplomat but had since gone back home. He liked it here. Kenya had what he called “a fusion of people and things” that he found addictive. There was always something happening. He seemed open and chatty, and wonderful. 

So that night, she sent him her number.

The second day, she woke up to flirtatious messages on WhatsApp. He had sent a photo of himself shirtless, seated on a bed, curling a dumbbell. Muscles didn’t get her hot. “Actually, I find very muscular men stupid,” she said. “Because all you seem to do is tend to your muscles, not your brain.” The masculinity she preferred lived in character, not circumference. “If I were to pick a man from a police identification parade, it would be the wiry one. The one with hair on him. The one standing with his weight on his left leg.” 

Like a doomed ship listing to one side.

“Blocky fellows don’t excite me. But he was a dog guy, and he was interesting.”

“And from Tamale,” I added. “Which sounds like the Kitale of Ghana.”

The third day, a Thursday, he invited her over. Kileleshwa, Githunguri Road. A few friends, some drinks, come through. “This was disappointing. A bit presumptuous and not my idea of a first date.” She admits. “But I went because I liked his energy and I had nothing to do.”

He offered to send an Uber. She declined. You don’t want men knowing where you live. She wore a black bodysuit, cream-tailored trousers, and barely-there heels. She ran expensive cinnamon beige lipstick over her lips and walked through a plume of Kayali Vanilla 28.

The elevator opened onto a floor with an old plastic dustbin outside the door. He opened it wearing a white vest and a wide grin. Music spilled around him – some thudding afro fusion – and behind him, voices. Male voices. Inside, on leather sofas, sat two men. They turned to look at her the way men turn to look when they have been expecting a delivery that has finally arrived. 

“You felt like pepperoni pizza,” I said. 

“Thick crust,” she added, and we laughed because she is on the thick side of things. 

The bigger one of the men was the size of a commercial fridge, with small beady eyes that didn’t know how to rest. The other one had a thick gold chain around his neck and the quiet, unsettling stillness of an animal that hadn’t been vaccinated. The air was dense and heavy with the unknown. 

Neither of them stood up like men do in the movies when a lady walks into the room.

She wondered if they were from Tamale.

The coffee table told its own story – rolling paper, weed seeds, old newspaper, phones that didn’t match the number of men in the room, and one white sock soiled at the heel that made her want to throw up in her palms. Kwesi said their names like he was listing pets. Then pointed at the one with the gold chain to move.

She looked at the leather sofa before she sat. She had grown up with a cruel aunt who never let her sit on the leather sofa, even as her cousins lounged freely on it. She had associated leather sofas with subjugation, oppression and old cows. She sat on the edge of it anyway, purse on her lap, and told herself she wasn’t going to be there long.

“I wasn’t going to eat anything or drink anything apart from water. This guy had a vest on while I was wearing my most expensive perfume. He could have been a turnboy dressed like that. Or a drug dealer.”

She dropped a pin to Fifi.

“Fifi is your pal.”

“My sister – who is also my pal. We are only two of us – if I die, it will be upon her to give birth, to show that we were ever here.”

Kwesi, who had small, hairy legs because he clearly and consistently ignored leg day, offered her something to drink that wasn’t Hennessy. It was some tacky-looking brandy that he said was high-end. “I have been around men enough to know that if a man has to tell you something is expensive, it probably isn’t.” So she asked for water. He seemed hurt by that, like she had refused his handshake. From the corner of her eye, the fridge turned to look at her.

“Were you scared?”

“Not yet. I was just wary at this point. But fear was coming.”

The boys played PlayStation, passing a blunt between them, while Kwesi sat close enough to her that she couldn’t read her WhatsApp without him reading it with her. Close enough that she could smell the hair on his legs. No food was offered. At some point, a fourth man arrived – tall, sinewy hands, a bony knee that stuck out when he sat. The boys made fun of him in their local language. He looked at her and said “hello” in a booming voice, as if volume was its own form of introduction. Now there were four of them.

Kwesi, who had been only half paying attention to her since she declined the brandy, put his hand on her upper knee and said, “Do you want to go to the bedroom?”

She laughed. Because it was a joke, right?

“No, I don’t think so.”

He stared at her with a smile that was sharp and kind in equal measure, which is the most dangerous kind of smile. One of the thin ones heard the exchange, glanced away from the screen, and made a sound in his throat that wasn’t quite a chuckle and wasn’t quite a grunt but lived in the uncomfortable space between the two.

Then Kwesi turned back to the TV and said nothing. For ten full minutes, he simply ignored her, as if she had already served whatever purpose she had been invited here for and the remaining details were administrative.

“I sat there knowing I had to leave, but not knowing how. Look, I’m a very forthright person. I’m brave and bold because that’s what you become when your parents die early, and you have nobody but yourself and your sister, and the world doesn’t owe you anything. You force yourself into rooms, or you leave them. But I couldn’t leave this one. It’s almost like I owed these men my time. My company.”

She looked around the room and wondered what she was doing there. The room had reduced her, she felt, by a factor of 12.

She told him she needed to leave. “Let you boys do your ball thing.”

“You should have said, let you all do your balls thing,” I said. “Seeing as it was a sausage fest.”

She snorted and raised one finger. Oh yeah, that’s so bad it’s good.

Kwesi said. “That’s why I wanted us to go to the bedroom.”

“Come on,” she told him. “I’m not going to your bedroom. But let me leave you guys to hang out. You and I can do a proper date next time.” She lied. 

“This is not a proper date?”

“This is a date with me, you, and your pals.”

“So why did you come?” he snapped. And she felt fear arrive, finally, the way it had been threatening to all evening. “And these are not my pals. They are my brothers.”

She looked at them. They were as related as rocks are to rabbits. She said, “Anyway,” and moved to stand. Kwesi reached out and pressed her back down by the hand. Not violently. But deliberately. The way you close a door that a pesky wind keeps trying to blow open.

“I was stunned. The act felt violent even though it wasn’t completely forceful. I looked at his hand on mine, hoping that would convey the message that he had crossed a line. But it occurred to me that there is never a line with men like Kwesi. That they were accustomed to taking things that didn’t belong to them. That being manly, to them, was taking. Dominating. And I wasn’t going to become part of that.”

He didn’t let go. Instead, he said, quietly, “You can’t leave now.”

Which could mean anything. It could mean the moment wasn’t right, that she simply had to wait a little longer. Or it could mean the time for leaving had already passed, long ago, and the gates had since closed.

She had grown up with dogs. Aggressive ones. Almost rabid ones. She had been bitten once by a dog she had misread, underestimated, and she had learned. The first thing she learned was that you never show a dog fear. The moment you do, the dynamic shifts. You become the smaller dog. And small dogs get killed.

So she stood up.

The clicking of the PlayStation controllers stopped. All four of them turned to look at her, the way dogs turn when their master hasn’t yet given the word, but everyone understands it’s coming. One of the thin ones reached the door before she did and stood against it. Kwesi was right behind her. The other two had swivelled on the sofa, watching. Her heart was going fast, but you wouldn’t have known it from looking at her.

She stepped away from the door and addressed Kwesi directly. Not the one blocking it, because that’s just a smaller dog waiting for word from the big dog. 

“You have to look barking dogs in the eye,” she told me. “Don’t avert your eyes. Don’t show hesitation. Don’t show fear even when you are ready to pee on yourself – and I was. I didn’t want to get raped or killed. I wanted to live. To meet a man who would make me a wife. To bring forth children, I would name after my mother or my father. To continue the legacy of my family. So I asked Kwesi, calmly, if he had a problem with me leaving. Are you keeping me in this house against my will? My voice wasn’t frantic or desperate. It wasn’t menacing either. With a dog, you raise your voice. With weak men like these, you strengthen it. They don’t know how to handle that energy.”

“Are you holding me in this house against my will?” she asked him. “Is this what is happening here?”

Kwesi looked around as if addressing a crowd. “Who is holding you against your will? I’m not. But you can’t just stand up and leave. It’s rude. It’s against my cultural norm.”

“I’m not part of your culture,” she said. “And in my culture, nobody stops a woman from leaving when she wants to leave.”

A brief silence.

“What culture is that?” one of the boys asked from the sofa.

I laughed when she told me that. Yeah, you can’t give a speech about your culture without telling us what culture it is.

“A civilised one,” she said. “I’m sure your culture respects free will. I’m sure what’s happening here at this door isn’t something your culture is proud of.” Then she stopped. Because saying less is saying more. Silence is words. And you have to know when to push and when to go quiet. She went quiet. She wanted to live. She wanted to go to her sister’s house and cry.

From the sofa, the one who had asked about culture leaned back and said, flatly, “Let that bitch go.” He didn’t even look up. “I told you we needed to call our usuals.”

Nobody moved for a moment.

She held Kwesi’s stare. The one at the door raised his blunt to his lips. The only sound was the faint crackle of seeds in the weed burning. Then Kwesi said, “Why are Kenyan babes so difficult?” He motioned the one at the door aside. Then he opened it for her himself and insisted on walking her to the lift.

As they waited at the lift, he said reconciliatorily, “I’m sorry about today. I didn’t think my brothers would be around. Can we do this again?”

“Your brother called me a bitch,” she said as the lift arrived. Inside, once the door closed, she realised she had been holding her breath. And her hands started trembling badly as she tried to find her phone to call an Uber, and when the doors opened, she ran out and sat on the ledge of a flowerbed until she stopped trembling.
