item.title: What Kind Of A Spa Doesn’t Have Candles?
item.description:
Not many people can claim to have finished a marathon and then gone straight to a brothel.

I can.

But brothel aside, I’m sure you are dying to hear how the city marathon went first. How they handed out 500ml bottles of water. Five hundred millilitres! That’s not hydration; that’s waterboarding. Running with one felt like carrying a jerrican. Most runners took two dutiful sips and then flung the bottle onto the road. Soon stretches of the route looked less like a city marathon and more like a regatta, the bottles bobbing behind us like buoys. Then there were the water points. Not only were they spaced so far apart that at one stage it felt easier to divert to Nairobi River and drink directly from the source, there wasn’t a single ORS station on the route. Just water. Which is fine if you’re watering houseplants. 

And then came the most annoying part of all.

Towards the final five kilometres of the half marathon, the toughest part, we suddenly merged with runners from the 10K and 5K races. Hundreds of them. They poured in from the side of the road and spread across the expressway like tourists at a viewpoint. Some stopping abruptly to take selfies. Others drifted from one side of the road to the other to greet friends. The closer we got to the finish, the thicker the crowd became until the final stretch felt less like a race and more like leaving a concert.  When I crossed the finish line and checked my watch, it wasn’t exactly 21 kilometres. So after joining another throng to collect my medal, (which my body had figured we were done) I had to jog around a bit, topping up the missing metres.

When I finished the marathon, I knew I was finished with the City Marathon.

I finished strong at 2:36. My pacesetter was my friend Martha, an ardent runner, hiker, adventurer and – lastly – a mother. Because these days you can’t just be one thing. You can’t simply be an auditor. You also have to be a foodie. Or belong to the Tulip Lovers Society, a group where people who love tulips meet to discuss their tulips. It’s like Toastmasters, but for tulips.

She dropped me home and I limped up the staircase, whereupon Kim opened the door and asked, “You finished?” as if he hadn’t expected me to. I went to my bedroom and lay on the cold floor for a few minutes before taking a long shower.

On the street where I live there is a spa I only recently noticed. I should mention that I live in a fairly decent neighbourhood because this detail will become important shortly.

Anyway, one day I said to Lady, “Did you know there’s a spa down the road?”

“That spa has always been there,” she said.

So one morning towards the end of last week, I walked over. A security guard opened the gate. The reception was clean. It looked like a salon designed by someone whose favourite colour was purple. There was nobody at the reception desk – it was just after 8:30 am – so I wandered farther into the common area. It’s one of those old houses converted into a business.

“Hello?” I shouted.

I was tempted to add, “Anybody home?” like they do in horror movies, but that felt excessive. Especially after a marathon. 

A petite young woman with long eyelashes emerged from one of the rooms.

“Sorry,” she said with an apologetic smile. “We were just cleaning up.”

Back at the reception, I asked a few questions. I was particularly keen to know if they offered deep-tissue massage.

“We do better,” she said. “Thai deep massage. Good for people who go to the gym.”

I wasn’t exactly sure of what Thai massage was, but I told her that’s what I wanted. But not today. “On Sunday,” I said. “I’m running the marathon, and I’ll need it afterwards.”

“Can I book for 3 pm, then?”

“No, that’s not necessary,” she said. “You can just walk in.”

“But what if there isn’t an available slot?”

She smiled her Marilyn Monroe smile and said, “Then we’ll create a slot for you. Don’t worry.”

The place looked clean enough. You don’t want to go to a spa and come back with something unexpected, like a skin disease.

On Sunday, I run the marathon, and at 3 pm I’m back.

There’s a new girl at the reception. Pretty. Quite young. Twenty-six, perhaps. She has makeup on – her cheeks are flushed. 

“How was the marathon?” she asks enthusiastically.

“It was good,” I say. “How do you know I ran it?”

“I heard you speaking to my colleague the last time you were here.”

Oh. I didn’t see anyone else the last time I was here. 

Right.

I wonder where her colleague is.

Maybe she’s visiting a friend who is having a baby shower, it being a Sunday afternoon. Or maybe she’s at home watching television, her hair unrecognisable, hidden under a bonnet. 

She sits me at the reception.

I ask for water, and she disappears inside, returning shortly with a bottle. She doesn’t bring it on a tray and a glass or anything. Just a bottle of water. 

She leaves me studying their menu of treatments, which has diagrams. I like diagrams. I also like restaurants with photos on their menus. Because what the hell is Boeuf Bourguignon? I need to see what it looks like. Nobody should waste ten minutes of their life studying a menu and trying to figure out what they’re ordering. Or worse, Googling menu items. Food should arrive before the dissertation.

One of the diagrams shows a fellow seated while somebody steps on his back and pulls both his arms behind him. I want that one too. I want to be pulled pork. 

It’s quiet.

Like a spa should be.

Like a tomb.

And you know how a health facility smells like disinfectant and formaldehyde? This place smells like nothing. 

She returns and says, “Please follow me.”

We were warned our whole lives never to follow strange girls up staircases, but I follow her up a winding staircase to a floor lined with rooms. Each room – I can see from the open doorway – has a massage bed neatly made, complete with stones and those decorative petals that spas seem contractually obligated to scatter everywhere.

She settles me into one of the rooms. There are two beds inside.

“I want your strongest,” I tell her. “The strongest you have.”

She says. “You could get two hands if you want.”

“Two hands?” I ask, turning to look at her. I had been staring at the stream of light escaping through a gap in the curtains.

“Yeah. Like two girls,” she says.

“No,” I say. “One girl is sufficient. One strong one.”

She smiles.

“Enjoy your treatment.”

Then she slips out of the room.

I look around. First, I open the bathroom door and peek inside. You never know who is hiding in these bathrooms. Or there could be a secret door leading to a dimly lit room where two men sit at a desk, smoking and playing cards.

Satisfied that nobody is, I take one of the two seats in the room and wait.

To pass the time, I take photos of the massage bed. The lighting is strange. Very blue. Psychedelic blue. Like I’m underwater. No, not underwater. Underwater is dark and unsettling. More like the bottom of a swimming pool.

Then the door opens.

A lady walks in. She’s dark and voluptuous. The first thing I notice – and perhaps this has something to do with the voluptuousness – is that she’s wearing very tiny cotton shorts. 

As in, tiny.

Shorts. Cotton. 

Like those that female volleyballers wear. 

I remember thinking, What kind of spa is th—

But before the thought can complete itself, she says, “Hi! Did I interrupt something?”

“No, no,” I say, suddenly feeling guilty. “I was just taking photos. You know, of…”

“Of yourself?” she asks, turning from the console with an amused raise of an eyebrow.

“No. Of course not. We don’t do that here,” I say.

“I like that,” she says, nodding. “A gentleman.”

That statement, in hindsight, should have told me everything I needed to know about that place. That and the lack of a tray. And, of course, her lack of a uniform. I don’t want to come here and pretend that I’m a pious SDA boy, but I swear, by this time I just felt, this is a bit lax, but hey. Besides, I just ran a marathon, cut me some slack. 

“My name is Poppy,” she says.

I actually laugh.

“I don’t suppose that’s your real name.”

“It is,” she says, deadpan.

“Your name is Poppy? It’s on your ID?”

“Yes.”

“Isn’t that a flower?”

“I am a flower,” she says, turning away.

I can tell from the back of her head that she’s smiling.

She moves the two tables apart and brings over one of those thin camping mattresses, which she tosses between them before covering it with a white sheet and white towels.

“So you run marathons?” she says, making conversation as she sets up. Half marathons,I tell her.

“Never ran a marathon in my life,” I say.

She looks at me appraisingly and says, “Well, you’re young. You have time.”

No masseuse has ever spoken to me like that. Ever. I want to say I’m 48 but why look at a gift horse in the mouth?

And if this were a pious movie, this is the point where I would excuse myself and run out of the room. But this is not a movie. This is a story about a man who ran a marathon and then went to a brothel.

Which, admittedly, sounds a bit like a movie.

After she’s done arranging the beds, she says, “So? Ready?”

“Wait,” I say. “Aren’t you going to give me that form people fill in before a treatment? You know, the one with questions about underlying conditions, previous surgeries, whether you’re pregnant, and which areas you’d like worked on?” Actually, now that I write this, I feel stupid. I feel green behind the ears. Like I just landed from the village, fresh off the bus. 

Do you have areas you’d like me to focus on?” she asks, ignoring my foolish question. She probably thinks, What does this idiot think this is? The orthopaedic wing of Aga Khan Hospital? 

“Yeah. My left foot is sore and my right shoulder.” I tell her. “My lower back could use some stretching too.”

She’s folding towels now. Then she asks if I’m ready.

Of course I’m not ready.

Where is the disposable underwear?

“Don’t you guys provide those ugly underwears?” I ask.

She laughs.

“Oh.”

Then she leaves the room and returns with one.

I told Lady later, “Then she just stands there and waits.” She doesn’t say, ‘I’ll give you a moment. Take your time.’ She just stands there! It is increasingly apparent that one of us has done this before.

I’m feeling a bit shy now. She’s made me shy, and I resent that she’s made me shy. I feel like a schoolboy who hasn’t finished his homework. Who has the famous dog that eats homeworks. But, at the same time, I’m also intrigued by how things are unfolding. I’m not entirely sure what the hell is going on. I’m fairly certain this is not standard operating procedure, yet I’m enjoying our little banter. She’s smart and articulate and has surprising bursts of wit. It’s also the longest conversation I’ve ever had with a masseuse.

I know it’s hard to believe, but not once did it occur to me that I was in a brothel.

Not once.

Look, so they didn’t bring the water on a tray. Since when did a tray become probable cause? Do you want water or do you want a tray? I wasn’t about to split hairs over crockery. 

Anyway, I swallow my pride, blink first and walk into the bathroom to change.

When I come back, she’s fiddling with the stereo, a small contraption with a flash disk plugged into it. It looks like one of those 80s stereos. 

“Any particular music you want?” she asks, her back turned to me.

Uhm, shouldn’t they be playing spa music?

“I don’t know,” I say. “Play what you want.”

“You won’t enjoy what I like.”

“What do you like?” I ask.

“I listen to many things. What do you like?”

“Well,” I say, shifting from one foot to the other. I feel silly standing there in those ugly disposable underwear, my clothes bundled in my hands. It feels mildly scandalous. I can feel a breeze through my jewels, which is strange because I don’t think the window is open. Oh, I forgot to mention that there are no candles either. 

“I like rhumba, for one.”

“Oh, look at that!” she says excitedly. “I like rhumba too.”

“Really?”

“Yeah.”

“How old are you?”

“I’m 23.”

I want to say, No way , you’re 23, lady. You must be, like, late 20s.

But it’s rude to say such things to a lady. A lady’s age is her business and God’s. Besides, I already look ridiculous standing there in my balloon-like underwear.

Soon a Luo tune fills the room. It’s Ajawa. I’m not particularly well acquainted with Ajawa yet.

“You know Elisha Toto,” she asks. I tell her no. 

“But that’s not rhumba,” I say after listening for a bit. “That’s Ajawa.”

I lay face-down on the floor and she commences her sorcery. 

“So how does a 23-year-old know about rhumba?” I ask when she starts twisting me and pulling me. 

“My dad is Kikuyu,” she holds my knee up and bends it, “but my mum is Luo.”

How did they meet? Twist, bend. What kind of a guy is your dad? Pull! And your mom? Is she feisty like luo babes? Bend toes; crack. Are you fiesty? (“Yes, you will save me as Bitch Boss Poppy,”) OK. Can you speak luo? 

“Of course,” she says.

“I’nya kanye? To tij rwayo ji ni to ichako nade, yawa?” I ask.

She bursts out laughing.

“Dala mara en Kisumu,” she says.

I groan. From the pain of her Luo. 

“Don’t ever speak Luo in that accent again.”

She was generally very good at whatever it is that Thai massage is supposed to do. My only complaint was that she was a little careless with my left knee. I also had to ask her to ease up on the back-stepping. She was strong considering she was only 62 kgs. [Yeah, I asked]. We talk throughout the session, the most I’ve ever spoken during a treatment. Normally, I sleep. The deep tissue massage was very decent too. But not the best. Maybe her strengths lie, uhm, elsewhere. 

The gold medal for deep tissue, however, still belongs to a masseuse in Diani. After the triathlon, Amani Maranga, the self-appointed Mayor of Diani, referred me to her. The spa itself wasn’t much to write home about – the room had a rattling fan and all the charm of a government waiting room – but the lady was five-star.

“You are a bit of an idiot,” Lady told me later, “That was a brothel. The signs were there.” 

Maybe.

Regardless, not many people can claim to have finished a marathon and then gone straight to a brothel.

item.title: Martin Luther Of Grass
item.description:
Men were trying to take over their ancestral land. 

What men? 

Just some men, he said. 

I pictured them with burning torches, prowling at night. Or just one man, standing in the middle of a small overgrown farm, doing nothing. The grass up to his hips. A wide-brimmed hat casting a shadow over his features. A small thicket nearby with a stream where a hyena had been spotted once. If there are hyenas in Navakholo, Kakamega.

So he had to dash to the village. To sort out this little wrinkle.

Right. Of course. A show of might.

You know, before it gets messy. He said. And messy here is always people cutting each other up with machetes, and then we will have to read about it in the newspaper, and I will say casually, “Oh, that’s Ken’s family.” I have never seen anybody I know on TV, someone who is in trouble with the law and is seen in a hoodie and a mask and handcuffs, getting out of a police cruiser to face the law, avoiding the cameras and being called ‘the accused.’ 

Anyway, I told him, you just have to find someone who will hold fort when you are gone. He said his brother will do it. I didn’t know he had a brother, I said. The brother travelled to the village. I saw him a couple of times on the CCTV. Once, when he was struggling to open the gate because the gate had a latching system that needed getting used to. He was stooped over, skinny, like Ken, his spine long and elaborate against the light work shirt he had on. The second time, when he was raking the leaves off the grass in the morning. He was standing there, back to the camera, opposite the kitchen garden that nobody wants to grow vegetables on, holding the rake with both hands. He seemed to be so deep in thought. I could almost hear him think. He just stood there for a minute or so, before he resumed the raking. 

Before Ken left, I called him and asked him if Ken had properly oriented him on what to do. I asked him to walk me through it quickly. He said, The grass has to be watered daily. The sand on the beach has to be raked, the debris vomited by the shore retrieved and disposed of. His outside bathroom and toilet cleaned daily. If anything attempts to grow on the parking, it has to be plucked by hand. Hedges trimmed, when necessary. 

Good. Good. Good man.   

And don’t forget to feed the cats, I said. Or to lock the door to where the pigeons live at night. And don’t cut any branch of a tree without my express permission. Or any tree, for that matter. Prune off the dead branches. And don’t let anyone inside the compound unless I tell you to. No strange men lurking about there. There is not going to be anyone showing up to say, Biko sent me to pick the lawnmower. I will not be sending anybody to pick anything. 

Then I let him be. 

A week later, I called Ken and asked him when he intended to travel back. He started talking weird. Mumbling. Saying things like, “nitakuambia, nikiwa tayari. Bado nashughulikia mambo hapo, unajua tu mambo ya shamba.” I said, Uhm, I get it, but you didn’t take indefinite leave, you can’t just say you will tell me. Nothing works like that. You have a job. He said, “sasa sina la kufanya.” He made it look like he was there to actively scare away those people trying to take their land. That his mere presence, his intimidating height and wide shoulders, is a deterrent enough for land grabbers. Never mind that he’s a skinny, tall, man with very sombre sunken features. He would look like Adrien Brody if he were black and acting like a shamba-boy, minus that hawkish nose. 

I was mighty irritated. I asked him what he thinks I should do now, just wait until I get word from him that his land is now secured? Land issues take years to resolve. You want me to wait a year for you to get back to work? That doesn’t sound like a Leave to me, more like a Left. I could hear him shrug over the phone. He said, “Sasa hivi ndio kulivyo.” Like he has given a news roundup on a Swahili channel. Well, I have a solid rule never to beg. Or to grovel. So I asked him, “Ken sisi sio watato, sisi ni watu wazima na kama hutaki kazi tena, sema. Hakuna haja ya hadithi. Unataka kurudi kazi ama umechoka?” 

“Sasa ni hivo tu nimesema.” He said. 

I wanted to laugh at how blunt he was. But I was also taken aback. So I said, Sawa bas. And that was it. I hated to see him go. I truly hated to see him go. He has been my best. We have been very peaceful. He was a very hard worker, very committed. He put his scrawny back into it. He mowed, he trimmed, he watered. The place was always immaculate. I never had to complain about the state of the grass. Or the plants. He never drank alcohol. We never disagreed about anything. Things were great. Until they weren’t. And when things ended, it was abrupt and brutal, which seemed violent to me. I don’t like long drawn out things. If things are going to end, let them end now, today, this hour, so that we don’t have to deal with it tomorrow morning, or early next month. We cut it here, and we all move on with our lives. I prefer such endings, but this one staggered me a bit. It left me confused. Because I thought he was happy and I was happy. I thought he was just going to shoo away some land grabbers and go back to my grass, my tree and my cats. 

So it felt like a bit of a breakup. 

So I had to call Duncan, the man who landscaped my place eight years ago and who has brought all the shamba-boys I have worked with. I told him the story, and he said, “Did you guys fight over something?” I told him we didn’t. The last time we had a tiff, he had cut off my rose bushes and overtrimmed the hedge of the fence. But that was a year ago. We were cool. I pay him on time. I supported him each time he had a funeral. Or wanted to change the roof to his mother’s house. I even buy him unga every month, because ugali is his love language. 

Strange, Duncan said. 

That his love language is ugali? 

No, that he just quit. 

So he called Ken up and asked what the hell happened. Was this man a terrible guy? Were you not happy with your pay? Ken insisted that we were fine, but he just wanted to sort out the shamba thing. 

So Duncan travelled to the village to sort that out. He met Ken’s brother, who he reported was a good shamba-boy, as a gun is good for painting. He works with tons of gardeners; he identified one who he says used to work for an Indian guy in Muthaiga. Good with his hands, he said. Family man. But he moved back home to Kakamega and has been looking for a job. Does he drink alcohol? I asked. Apparently, he used to. But he stopped. Not sure he still does anymore. We could try him out, he suggested. He’s called Godfrey. I said, sawa, not that I had a lineup of them beating down my door. So now I have a new sheriff in the village. I haven’t met him. I haven’t seen him on the CCTV. But we speak on the phone. He also writes me texts in English. And he says things like, “I did a postmortem of that section of the grass.” Which made me happy. When people speak like that. It’s a bit mad. I like that madness. 

This is my what, sixth shamba-boy in eight years? My mum used to say, if you see a home where they keep changing the house-helps, the Helps are not the problem, the owners of the house are. 

She was right. I’m the problem. I hold firmly a three-strike rule. If I speak about one thing three times, I’m done. I’d rather recite poetry to sheep. I’m impatient. I can’t understand why someone can’t just water grass daily and trim a hedge and prune and take care of flowers. I’m not asking you to work the whole day in the heat. Just wake up at 6 am and work until midday. Then you can sleep under a tree. Or listen to the radio. Half-ass folk, drive me up the wall. Mediocrity.

I intend to travel to the village and meet this fellow. The first day, we will just get to know each other. Where did you work before? Did you enjoy it? See that section, try not to trim it a lot. There is manure in the store, did you see it? Use it on struggling plants, like that one. Plants are like humans, like you, when they are struggling, you will always tell, but only when you pay attention. You said, you have three children, how is the one in high school doing? Is she a good girl or is she being a teenager? This solar pump works best when you turn on this knob this way. What did you say the wife does? How is that going? Kwani how many wives you got? 

Just banter, to get to know who he is. 

The next day I will wake up and watch him work while I work from my laptop. I will take notes. We will then sit under a tree around noon and talk. I will have printed photos of the place from when it was nothing but scrubland and wandering cattle. I will show him and enjoy his expression. They always marvel at the transformation. Then I will launch into my favourite monologue. This monologue is best delivered on day two, by the way. Not immediately. You don’t want to sound like a cult leader on the first day. I normally tell them: this isn’t really a job. It’s a dream. My dream. And I’m inviting you into it. And if you accept to be part of my dream, I expect commitment. I would very much like us to part ways as friends, I tell them. But I won’t be completely heartbroken if we part ways as enemies. Not ideal, obviously. But what do you do?

I enjoy giving that speech. Eight hours on the road to the village gives a man plenty of time to rehearse his own mythology. I’m intoxicated by it. I keep finding new ways to tell it, mostly for my own amusement. I feel like Martin Luther, but for Mbita. The Martin Luther of grass. Because the truth is, I’m selling them something they particularly don’t give two shits about. Screw my grass, and while at it, my pigeons too. 

But the grass means something to me. The trees mean something to me. Every flower bed, every hedge, every cat skulking around the compound means something to me. To them, it’s work. Honest work, hopefully. But work nonetheless.

And why shouldn’t it be?

Godfrey’s dream [my new guy] is not my dream. Ken’s dream wasn’t my dream. So normally, before the speech, I have to have identified their dream, something they care about greatly and then be invested in it too. That’s how you try to get through to a man with a hoe. Mostly, their dreams are what we all dream about; for our children to be healthy and happy and for them to get an education. So normally it’s school fees. A new roof for mom’s house. A motorcycle. A better house for mum.

And if they show commitment to your dream, you show commitment to theirs. You invest in their dream, the way they have invested in yours. That way, the arrangement becomes something more than employment. It becomes a quiet exchange of dreams.

But it doesn’t always go that way. Human beings are complex. They want different things at different times. What they wanted yesterday isn’t necessarily what they want today. So they change. Or you change.

I’m learning to accept that.

So Ken leaving wasn’t entirely surprising. I just thought we had a good thing going. He was very good at his job. My best, really. And I’ve been through the whole gamut: drunkards, lazy-bums, mediocres, petty thieves and assorted madmen. It teaches you something. And at the same time, it teaches you nothing.

The sun still rises, and it still sets. In between, very little should ever be taken too seriously to give you palpitations.

***

item.title: A Casino Without Free Drinks
item.description:
You are 68, and your children are busy.

They aren’t children anymore, of course. The world has had its way with them. It has given them mortgages and blood pressure, WhatsApp groups called Parents of Grade Three Blue and calendars that require planning lunch three Thursdays in advance. They are in their thirties now, perhaps older. They have become people.

But they remain your children.

You could be living in Nanyuki, in the stone house you once sketched on the back of a receipt while in the bar waiting for your late-comer friends. A house that was meant to face the mountain, where Ngai – the supreme God – lives. A house where you imagined taking tea on cold mornings, watching the peak emerge from the clouds like an old magic trick.

Instead, some enterprising idiots put up apartments. You know the type. Beige ugly monstrosity, with names like Mountain View Residency that successfully block the mountain view they are named after. Or maybe you moved to Kitale because Nairobi had become too loud, too hurried, too inward-seeking. You wanted to hear birds again. To grow things. To stand in gumboots after rain and discuss soil with your neighbour. 

Or perhaps you live in Narok, tucked beneath a hill that throws a long shadow over the house every evening. Cows. Sheep. A tractor that you thought you’d drive but haven’t, because that romance only lived in your heart. Maybe you bought acres and acres of land in Laikipia, God’s own land. Because you drove a big plane for a living and you wanted to live on a flat land, a ranch, where you could read your important books and drive your big car out in the mountain ranges for a higher dose of silence. 

Or maybe you never left Nairobi.

Maybe Nairobi never left you.

Maybe you live on the twelfth floor of a fully paid-up apartment in a Chinese-built high-rise, sharing lifts with young people with truly strange trousers and hairstyles that appear to have been done during a power outage. You watch them with a sinking feeling and wonder if this is how your father felt looking at you. Life, as it turned out, never became what you imagined. This isn’t fully what you expected of growing old. But you are learning to love even the bad parts. 

The children don’t call.

They don’t call because calling is out of fashion. Everything is out of fashion. Technology – for instance – is unrecognisable. Sometimes you feel like a man who stepped out briefly to buy milk and returned to find the entire house renovated. The kitchen doesn’t have a door anymore. Sometimes, in the morning, while holding a cup of tea, you look down at your hands and get a small shock. Those can’t possibly be your hands. Yet there they are. Wrinkled. Veined. An old man’s hands.

The strange thing about ageing is that it mostly happens on the outside. Inside, you don’t feel particularly old. Inside, you are still young, making plans. Still postponing things. Your thoughts never quite caught up with your body. But your hands have. They remind you of your father. Your father is dead. So is your mother. Most of your uncles and aunts have gone too. Your generation is standing at the front of the queue now.

The children prefer sending video messages. 

They installed some strange app on your phone. Everybody uses it now. For the life of you, you can’t figure it out. Whenever they send messages there, you never see them until they have to ping you. Not ping exactly- how you wish people could still poke each other like they did on Facebook. It’s something far stranger. Suddenly, their faces pop up on your screen and say, “Dad, you have a message!”

Only it isn’t really their faces.

It’s AI. An approximation of their faces. A digital version of your children reminding you that your actual children are trying to reach you. Anyhow, you still insist on typing your replies. You cling onto what you know, what you knew. They laugh at you. 

You are probably divorced.

Or perhaps you’re in your third and final marriage. The second one was a wrecking ball. You were 58. She was twenty-seven. Neither of you understood half of what the other was saying. Your daughter was horrified. “She’s my age, Dad!” She screeched. Actually, revolted is the word she used.

Or maybe you are still married to the same woman you married all those years ago. She is no longer the woman of your youth. Then again, you are no longer the man of hers. She hates Kitale, the weather and the sound of cows, so she stayed behind in the city where you raised your children. You suspect the children see her more often than they see you. They certainly seem to know more about their lives. 

Seldomly, she will call and say something like “Jabari is getting baptised in two weeks. Do you think you can make it?” You will pause. “Who is Jabari?” And there will be a very long, dead silence on the line, which will remind you that Jabari is probably one of your grandchildren. Why the hell can’t they just name children normally, like Paul and Grace? What’s with this Jabari, Tayari nonsense, you will mumble after you hang up. 

Your memory -like your knees – won’t be what it once was. You will call one child by the other’s name. Sometimes you will call your grandson by your son’s name and your son by your favourite cow’s name. You won’t remember all the grandchildren’s names. Even if “all” only turns out to be two.

You will walk into a room and forget why you went there. You will miss appointments despite having enough AI assistants, digital reminders and predictive technology. You will mix up places and dates. A story that happened in 1998 will suddenly have occurred in 2017. Somebody you met in Kisumu will mysteriously relocate to Eldoret halfway through the telling. Why let facts get in the way of a good story, you will argue. You will spend more time than you care to admit staring at screens. The phone. The television.

Radio, especially, will be strange.

There will be no presenters trapped in studios discussing traffic on Mombasa Road. No spirited debates about the topic of the day. You will talk to the radio, for a change. You will say, “Good morning, 107 FM. What’s the weather looking like today in Uvombo, Kilifi, where I am?” The radio will immediately tell you.

“Good. Looks like I’ll be able to go for a walk later. Now play me a mix. I’m feeling melancholic today. Something that reminds me of childhood. You can give me a bit of commentary between songs, but keep it brief. I tend to fall asleep when you talk too much.” I suspect that radio – like cockroaches, will never die. It will only know you intimately. It will know which songs remind you of your mother. Which songs remind you of the girl who got away. (Toni Braxton, in my case. Sniff). It will know the sound of your nostalgia. Radio will play back your life. 

Or maybe you became a new father again. It happens. You met a woman 30 years younger than you and, against the advice of common sense, your adult children, several close friends, your radio, you fell in love. Then she moved in. Then she got pregnant. Now, as you approach seventy, you find yourself packing lunch boxes and attending school concerts and asking bookshop attendants where you can find pencil sharpeners. Life, it seems, has an excellent sense of humour. 

The child is seven.

You are sixty-eight.

Everything is stressful.

The mother is too young for you. She wakes up with ideas. She wants to hike mountains and travel to strange countries and sleep in tents and ‘chase sunsets’ and discover herself. You would like to discover a comfortable chair. Your back hurts. You can’t get a hardon.  You have become one of those fathers you used to see at swimming galas and school plays. The fathers you quietly mistook for grandfathers. To mean, you have become a cliché. But the worst type; an expensive cliché.

The child is steadily eating into the savings you had carefully put aside for this chapter of life. The chapter that was supposed to involve quiet mornings, long walks and maybe a tomato garden. Instead, you are bending over school shoes at Bata. The truth, which you would never say out loud, is that connecting with the child hasn’t come naturally. Fatherhood at thirty-eight and fatherhood at sixty-eight are entirely different countries. You couldn’t get down on the floor to crawl after her. You couldn’t kneel beside the bathtub. You couldn’t spend twenty minutes folded into impossible positions assembling brightly coloured toys. When she was little, and you took her for walks, she would suddenly bolt towards something, pulling you with her as she ran, you would feel a small stab of panic, not because she might fall. Because you might.

You have nothing in common with your new wife. Sometimes you watch her lips move, but you could never hear a sound coming out of it. Also, maybe because your hearing isn’t what it used to be. Your adult children are mortified. They believe you have made a spectacle of yourself. A cautionary tale. Whenever they raise the subject, you become defensive. “This is my life,” you tell them. “Go live yours.” Late at night, when the house is quiet and everybody is asleep, you lie awake staring at the ceiling. And for a moment, in the privacy of your own thoughts, you are completely bewildered by how you ended up here.

Or maybe you were a very busy father. Out before sunrise. Home after dark. Always on your way somewhere. Sleeping in on Sundays. Waking up to the family gone to church, or to visit Auntie Gertrude. And when you had free time, you would be out golfing with your friends with big beards. Or drinking in a bar. You were providing, after all.  You paid fees. You paid rent. You paid for birthdays and uniforms, and family holidays. Maybe you didn’t attend many of the school’s events. Or when you did, and when your child looked up, you were looking down on the phone. Checking emails that felt very important at that time, something that couldn’t wait. And when you looked up from your phone, your daughter was 17. 

Or maybe you were a complete asshole to their mother. The ordinary kind. You corrected her in front of the children. You spoke over her. You dismissed her concerns before she’d finished expressing them. When she scraped the car reversing, you asked, “Weren’t you using your head?” You thanked waiters more often than you thanked her. You were polite to strangers and impatient with her. Sometimes, after you told her something hurtful, your son would find her in the kitchen, fighting back tears. You were an asshole toward her for so long one day she decided to be an asshole towards you too. 

And you didn’t realise the resentment that had built in your home until they started slamming doors, and then they became teenagers, and they started drinking and doing drugs and leaving you notes next to your car keys reading, “Dad, you are toxic. Do better.” And you made a dismissive sound and went off to golf. 

Now you are 78. If you’re lucky, they show up on your birthday. Or once a year, they bring the grandchildren over. The grandchildren tear through the house, touching things they shouldn’t, asking questions you don’t have answers to. Then, just as quickly, they disappear into screens.

You sit in the living room with your children. You ask how work is going. They give you a quick summary. Then silence. For people with so much history between you somehow you have little to tell each other. Then they go find their mother in the kitchen, and you hear them all chatter and laugh. It’s so strange that they are the same children who had nothing to tell you moments ago. You sit there listening to it from the next room, how effortlessly they speak to each other. How quickly they have become themselves. And for a moment, it feels as though there are two families in the house. The one in the kitchen. And the one sitting alone in the living room.

You tell yourself it doesn’t bother you.

Or maybe you had loads of money, and you threw money at parenting. You thought children were puzzles to be solved by Mpesa.  Whenever they needed your attention, you distracted them with money. Whenever they needed guidance, you paid someone to guide them. You mistook provision for presence, and they grew up believing that inconvenience was a thing other people experienced. That rules were for people with fewer options and that consequences were negotiable.

Consequently, they never learned to wait for things. Never learned that disappointment was survivable. That nobody is on a machine in the ICU because they were disappointed. They never learned that the world owed them nothing. When teachers complained, you blamed the teachers. When they got into trouble, you blamed the system. When they failed, you lowered the bar. When they succeeded, you raised the allowance.

Now they are adults. They treat waiters badly. They never arrive on time. They are rude to people who can’t help them and charming to people who can. The sort of people who drive on the wrong side of the road and flash their headlights at you as if you are the inconvenience. The sort of people who never hear the word “no” because they learned very early that somebody would eventually say “yes.”

Psychopaths wearing expensive cologne.  

Now you are old, lonely and sickly. Occasionally, you end up in a private hospital room, staring out the window and wondering where all the years went. The children come to visit. But you can never quite shake the suspicion that every time they find you still breathing, they experience a brief moment of either surprise or disappointment. Because they can’t wait for you to croak so that they can inherit what is owed to them. Every time they find you still breathing, they seem mildly inconvenienced.

I know what you are thinking, come on Bikozulu, it’s not that bad. Actually, it is. But let’s say you were a wonderful father. Maybe you did everything right. Or as right as anyone can. You attended school events. You sat through those dreadful talentless music recitals. You listened to long, boring stories about classmates you would never meet. You paid fees. Paid for trips. Offered guidance when asked and sometimes when it wasn’t. Maybe you even introduced them to faith. You taught them kindness. Humility. Gratitude. Tried to teach them how to move through the world without becoming an asshole.

And yet somehow they arrived at adulthood carrying none of the lessons you packed for the journey. They became entitled. Proud. Greedy. Self-absorbed. You look at them sometimes and struggle to recognise yourself in them.

One evening, sitting on the verandah in Kitale as the light drains slowly from the fields, you turn to their mother and ask:

“What the hell happened, Suzie?”

And she doesn’t answer.

Not because she doesn’t know.

But because after all those years, she has arrived at the same conclusion you have: Children are the longest gamble of your life.

You place your bets early.

Then you wait. 

Fatherhood is like a casino. Without free drinks. 

Happy Father’s Day, gentlemen.

item.title: The Walker At Jaffrey’s
item.description:
“Why was Mum screaming at you?”

The little one asks as he drops them at school. He’s the caesarean one. Six years ago he almost didn’t make it, things went pear-shaped very quickly, and they had to cut him out frantically. He has thick hair, cheeks still full of baby fat. He looks like his mother.

“She wasn’t screaming at me,” he says.

“But she was.” A pause. “Are you in trouble?”

He looks up to find the boy’s eyes in the rear-view mirror.

“A little. Just a little trouble.”

They drove briefly in silence. 

“You have to tell her sorry.”

“I will, darling.”

He calls his sons darling. Or sweetheart. 

He drives with one hand. Traffic’s a sloth. At the Ngong Road roundabout, a policeman halts his lane even though the light is green. It feels familiar. His life has been sitting at a green light for over a year. And there is nothing to do but wait. Waiting is harder when the light is green, and it’s your turn to move but you can’t. When other cars peel away in other directions, motorbikes squeeze through gaps, life rearranges itself around you while you remain exactly where you are. It’s dilapidating. He feels like he is crumbling, like a condemned house that has stood empty too long, with dirty windows and a sagging roof. 

Outside the school, his eldest comes to the window. Eight years old. A normal delivery, this one. More like him in temperament; hates confrontations. Nice, lovely eyebrows and small lips, like plums.

“Who are we?”

It’s the same question he asks them each morning he drops them off.

“We are kind,” they answer.

The little one is already looking over his shoulder, having spotted a friend.

He kisses the back of the older boy’s hand. Then he kisses the younger one’s even smaller hand. A very papal gesture. 

They walk away holding hands.

He watches until they disappear into the river of children with colourful bags on their backs. Soon they are no longer his boys, just two more children among children, swallowed by the morning, each one loved by someone, each one carrying the whole weight of someone’s worry.

He drives to Jaffery Sports Club, where the early walkers are already doing their slow laps around the track. He doesn’t come here to keep fit. He comes on the days his wife is working from home. It buys him two quiet hours before he has to return to the complex domesticity that his life has suddenly become, where the quiet between them has weight, and knives.

There is something about walking in circles. The repetition steadies him. Makes him feel part of a community, even if nobody knows his name. Or his story. He likes that everyone here is moving in the same direction. That for an hour or two, complete strangers become companions without ever exchanging names. They overtake one another, nod occasionally, occupy the same small geography and then disappear into their separate lives. It is a kind of community, held together only by routine. He sees faces he sees here every week. He nods at the elderly man with a saggy face who probably had a stroke a few years ago from how one side of his body droops. There is the plus-size lady who breathes hard, like a lorry up a hill. They smile at each other. The guy with a cane. The two middle aged men who are always talking. Lately the place has filled with influencer types, barely dressed against the morning cold, stomachs out, arses out, phones recording, performing health for strangers. He walks for two hours with Kendrick Lamar’s Mr. Morale & the Big Steppers in his ears.

He thinks about how a man arrives here. About the jobs that never called him back. The friends who never do either. His siblings, who seem to have quietly stepped away, leaving him alone at the helm of this heavy ship. His phone has gone quiet. His head hasn’t. He hadn’t realised how noisy his life was until it went deathly quiet. Now the world, it seems, doesn’t need him. The things that he imagined would grind to a halt without his attention are moving on.

He thinks of his wife. Rather the wife before she’d become a stranger. The woman who once drove across town with flowers after he’d broken his leg in a rugby match. The funny one. The one who was always fixing problems – a trait that has quietly turned her gaze on him. She now looks at him the way she looks at broken things. His parents still think she’s the best thing that ever happened to him.

These days he catches himself imagining another life. A smaller house. Shared custody. Seeing his boys when the court says he can. Cooking for them. Putting them to bed. Starting over as somebody’s divorced father. He wonders what his parents would say, whose side they’d quietly take. His siblings. Their friends. What stories she would tell his boys about him when he wasn’t there to defend himself.

None of it scares him as much as it should.

He thinks about that life that awaits him. He is willing to begin again on a mattress. Just a bare mattress. He doesn’t even need a pillow. He will bunch his clothes up and place them under his head.

Later he buys a coffee and sits on a bench beside the track, his headphones resting around his neck. The coffee is hot, so he cradles it between his palms and watches people walk by. The regulars. The serious runners, glancing at their watches every few minutes. The retirees walking three abreast, mumbling their conversations. The pair of women in hijab, talking fast and walking not so fast. The corporate girl taking a work call on her AirPods, saying, “Let’s align before we take this to ExCo…” People whose mornings already belong firmly to something.

He wonders if ‘unlucky’ is a real thing, or if people simply call it that when they can’t make sense of their lives. He wonders if this is how failure arrives. He wonders if any of this is his fault. Whether he should have stayed longer at his last job. Taken a pay cut. Learned another skill sooner. Forty-one suddenly feels older than it did when he was employed. He wonders if 41 is too old to start over in the rat race.

Artificial intelligence has shaken up everything. His wife thinks he should go back to school and do an MBA. What the f*k would that solve? He bets if he stuck his foot out on the track an MBA degree holder would trip over it. She also thinks he should start a business instead of just “moping around.” Her vocabulary has increasingly gotten barbed. As if entrepreneurship were a switch one simply flipped. As if, in some people, lives the instinct to buy and sell.

He drops the empty cup into a bin. Back in the car, he looks at his phone. Exactly as he left it. No missed calls. No messages. Nothing except the endless chatter in his old school WhatsApp group. His phone is not any more different from a bar soap you leave in the bathroom after you have showered. It drizzled last night. The bonnet is still dirty, tiny islands of rainwater sitting in the dust.

He doesn’t want to go home. Because it’s not home anymore. It’s a place his children live. Where his clothes are.

But there is simply nowhere else to go.

He drives slowly, waving other cars into his lane. Takes the longer route. Watches apartment blocks in construction, climbing into the sky. Watches people crossing roads. Passengers clinging to the backs of bodas. People with some place to be, with things to do. When he finally gets home, he stays in the car for a bit to catch his breath. He looks around the empty parking lots. All dads are out working. He listens to the radio. He looks up to the balcony of his house on the second floor and feels himself getting tired at what awaits. 

He knows how this will go. He will find her seated at her desk in the spare room, her back to the door. She won’t turn around when he opens the door. He will not attempt small talk but rather jump straight into an apology even though he doesn’t believe he’s done anything wrong. He will say he’s sorry about this morning. She will not take his apology with the grace the bible expects of her. She will swivel in her chair, like the boss she is, and address him like a child. When he once asked her not to address him like a child, she had said, “You’re forty-one. I shouldn’t have to.” She uses that voice now. He will let her talk at him. He will take it.

Because one day he will leave.

***

I saw this gentleman at Jaffery Sports Club the other morning. Actually, this was the third time I’d seen him. He always looked slightly bewildered, as though he’d walked into the wrong chapter of his life. I wondered what burdens he was carrying. Then I stopped wondering. And wrote him one.

item.title: This Is Not Home
item.description:
I do these one-on-one writing mentorships every so often, mostly with people who live in the diaspora, which is its own kind of solitary confinement. You are away from home, and also from the language home speaks in, and also, often, from anyone who might read a paragraph of yours and say, yes, that’s it, keep going. So sometimes I become that person. It’s not a program. There’s no certificate. It’s just two people and a shared document and a lot of “cut this” and “no, leave that” or “ I didn’t feel this one,” or “I skipped some paragraphs, what were you trying to say?” Mostly on WhatsApp and virtual calls. 

One of these mentees is Armella Gahimbare, writing from somewhere across the Atlantic. She sent me something that I enjoyed. It starts at a wedding, and then it goes dark. Dark enough to want a torch. But I could be biased, so I thought I’d share it here, see what it catches. 

Well, here’s Armella.

***

BY ARMELLA GAHIMBARE

I didn’t wear a bra for most of 2020.

I let everything loose. I embraced slow mornings and lazy stretches on my carpet, got to know a part of me that surprised me – the artsy, hippie side who made bread from scratch, played piano, watched her plants grow. I learned that I did not crave social interaction, and that relating from a distance was another skill I had.

When the world finally resumed, and we were back to socializing, I struggled. I made excuses to get out of invitations. I had spent so much time with myself it turned out I liked my own company, and I wanted to preserve that.

Now all that feels far. I have an event to attend, and I feel genuinely excited to get all dolled up. My bottles are lined up on the bathroom vanity like little soldiers ready to march. A bit of this, a bit of that. A spray of scent here and there. Then I pour myself into the black dress that has been waiting on the hanger all day, the fabric silky and soft on my skin. Leaning into the mirror, I apply my favorite rouge, step back, and smile, pleased with the results.

Heels on. Purse in hand. I head out.

The car is waiting. I get into the back seat.

“Ma’am, seatbelt.”

I grab the belt and fasten it carefully, making sure not to crease my dress.

“Prakash?”

“Yes, Ma’am.”

“You can call me Armella.” This must be the third time I’ve asked him this.

“Yes, Ma’am.”

I met Prakash last week. I was looking for someone to drive me out of town for Ella’s gusaba irembo, and when I sat in his Uber a few days ago, his car felt comfortable. So I asked if he could drive me to and from Quebec City on Friday.

“Now?”

“No, next Friday.”

“Ma’am, me only here.”

“What is your name again?”

“Prakash.”

“Prakash, I am asking that you be my driver next Friday. You take me to an event, wait for me, and bring me back the same day.”

“How much?”

“You tell me.”

He gave me a number, then asked for the address to confirm the distance.

“Wedding?”

“Pardon?”

“You go for wedding?”

“Yes, well – it’s some sort of pre-wedding party.”

Prakash seemed worried I was going to dance through the night while he sat outside in the cold waiting for me, so we agreed on a wait time.

“We have a deal then. Pick up at 3pm on Friday. If you change your mind, let me know at least a day before so I can figure out a plan B.”

He rocked his head side to side in agreement and promised to be there. I thanked him and opened the door to step out.

“Ma’am, sorry, English no good.”

“Same for me. We’ll get along just fine.”

His head swings again as he smiles.

Prakash is now speeding on the highway. He’s put in extra effort to clean the car – there’s a box of Kleenex in the back, bottled water, and the whole thing smells of fresh lime. This is one of my favorite things, going for long rides without having to sit behind the wheel. Here in the back I can daydream and watch the scenery speed by. Soon the landscape changes to lush open fields.

Prakash points to the fields.

“Same to my home.”

“Where is home?”

“Sri Lanka.”

I had assumed he was from India, because of the head swinging when he agrees to something.

“The whole country is this lush?”

“Sorry?”

“Your country is green like this, everywhere?”

“The village more. My grandfather, all life, growing food. Live very long.”

“How old is your grandfather?”

“Ninety, plus more. My grandfather’s eyes green always, and strong. Because whole life, lives like this.” He points again to the fields.

“Did you live with your grandfather?”

“No. I was in the city. City no good, very hard.”

I can picture his grandfather standing in the fields.

“What language do you speak back home?”

“Tamil. World’s oldest language!” He says it proudly.

Prakash is quiet for the rest of the drive, probably thinking about his country and his grandfather.

When we arrive at the venue, it’s empty. No one is there. I stand in the lobby waiting. My aunt arrives a few minutes later, looking upset and tired, like she hasn’t slept in days.

“Is your back acting up again, Tata? You don’t look too well.”

“My back is as is,” she responds dismissively.

It dawns on me – she’s uneasy about the event.

“Why don’t we go sit in the car while we wait for everyone to arrive?”

Without waiting for her response, I lead her to the door. We walk slowly back to the car. Prakash unlocks it and leaves us inside. As soon as we sit, she bursts into tears. I hand her a tissue, grateful to Prakash for his thoughtfulness.

“Of all the men in this world, she had to choose those people. Why?”

I know the question isn’t mine to answer, so I keep quiet.

“Ella is so naive. She thinks she knows them. Those people are not like us. A bunch of barbaric killers.”

She’s shaking her head, sobbing. I’m not sure what to do.

“His mother is a hypocrite. She calls every day, saying she wants to check on me.” She snorts, her lips pursed with disdain.

“That’s nice of her,” I say, without thinking.

“Nice? I have other in-laws. None of them does this. And you know why?” Her voice is dangerously escalating. I press the button to close the windows the rest of the way up. “Because none of them has anything to prove. They are good people. Not criminals! My daughter is marrying criminals.”

As if she’s just remembered this, she starts sobbing all over again, her face in her hands. This time I hold her. How is she still reacting this way? As though she’s hearing the news for the first time.

“Tata, you’ve known this for a while now. And you’ve met Ella’s boyfriend many times. I’m sure you’ve had time to get to know him and his family.”

“Did we not know the people who killed our families? Were they not our neighbors? Did our kids not play together? It doesn’t matter how they present. They are not to be trusted.”

I lean back in my seat, discouraged. We’re silent for a while.

“Tata, have you considered that maybe they didn’t take part in the massacre? They could be innocent.”

“Do you believe that?”

I pause. There are high chances that at least one of their relatives fell into some category of it – the ones who planned, the ones who killed, the ones who pointed to where the victims were hiding, or the ones who simply did nothing to stop it.

My aunt is still waiting for an answer. I can feel her pointed look.

“Tata, I don’t know what I believe,” I whisper carefully. “What can we do?”

She shrugs, picks more tissue, blows her nose loudly. Cars have started arriving. The parking lot is filling up.

“We should go back in.” I help her arrange her hair, and she takes a few sips of water. Getting out of the car isn’t an easy process – her back dictates that she ease out of her seat slowly. I hold her hand so she can stand on both feet.

As we walk back, I turn to her.

“Tata, not once have you complimented my outfit.”

I stand before her and twirl. She smiles, for the first time.

“You look beautiful.”

“Just beautiful?”

“You look stunning. Uratwenga izuba rikaka…”

“You never know – today I might meet my husband. Aren’t you the one always saying I need to get married?”

She grabs both my shoulders firmly, looks me straight in the eye. “Don’t you dare.”

I laugh. She releases me, and I walk her back into the hall.

When the guests arrive, ladies in traditional outfits line up at the entrance to receive the woven baskets. My aunt is seated at the table across from ours, her face arranged in a mask of pleasantness.

A thud sounds as Ella’s uncle, Yohani, taps the microphone before speaking, welcoming everyone into the traditional theatrics – saying we were having our own little celebration and have just seen a group of strangers walk in, and since we’re generous people by nature, we’re pleased to welcome them. This little masquerade is meant to go on for at least an hour before anyone gets to an agreement. Usually entertaining, especially with a skilled speaker.

But the man speaking for our future in-laws is too eager. He shoots up from his chair, grabs the mic, and asks for the favor right there and then. He does something else we don’t do -forces a bottle of wine into Yohani’s hands. I can see Yohani’s disappointment; he was prepared to go on and on, and this is anti-climactic. He tries to slow things down, invite the man to sit, relax, have a drink.

I look at my aunt. She’s offended by the wine – I can hear her thinking, so tacky, no decorum at all.

Their speaker doesn’t rest. He’s a man on a mission, back on his feet, brandishing another bottle. Says he won’t rest until he has an answer. It’s like watching bad sex with someone who won’t listen to feedback and take his time. An awkward chuckle ripples through the guests on our side.

Yohani is forced into a corner – he doesn’t even get to sit between speeches, as is usually done. The man holds his hand and begs for an immediate answer. What’s meant to be a smooth dance now looks like coercion. Yohani gives in and says yes. The groom’s side stands to clap and ululate. Their speaker looks relieved, a little surprised, and brings out yet another bottle of the exact same wine.

My aunt has a forced smile, like she’s sitting on needles.

Food is served. I text Prakash and ask him to come eat. He refuses. No thank you, Ma’am.

Ella comes out to greet the guests, in a long strapless emerald gown, her hair in a high chignon. She looks lovely. Her mother-in-law hands her a gift and dances with her. People are hugging, taking pictures, dancing.

I pick up my purse, ready to make an exit. Someone taps my shoulder. I turn to see a man in a suit.

“I’ve been waiting all evening to ask your name. I’m Max.” He extends his hand.

Before I can respond, someone pulls my arm. My aunt. For someone with back issues, she has a lot of strength.

“I need to borrow her for a moment. She’ll be right back,” she tells him.

I give Max an apologetic smile and follow my aunt.

“Tata, that could have been my husband,” I tease. She’s not amused. We chat a bit and hug goodbye. I congratulate Ella and leave.

Outside, the air is crisp. I text Prakash to pull the car around. Max shows up beside me, asks if I was planning to disappear without telling him my name. Thankfully, the car arrives. I smile nervously, walk away without a word, feeling terrible about it.

In the car, I finally drop my shoulders, relieved to be done with the day.

“Wedding good, Ma’am?”

“Armella.”

“Sorry?”

“Call me Armella.” The irony isn’t lost on me – I was asked my name tonight and refused to give it. Now here I am, asking Prakash to use mine, and he won’t.

“I am sorry, Ma’am.”

“It’s fine. The wedding was exhausting.”

“Sorry?”

“Wedding no good, Prakash.”

“Ah, sorry, Ma’am.”

As we ease back onto the road, memories of my childhood flash back.

The bed shook, and the windows clinked so loud my eyes shot open. My heart raced. I rolled off the bed, crawled to my brother’s, grabbed his arms, and dragged him to the floor. The room was pitch black. He groaned, protesting in his sleep, but when he realized he was on the floor, he understood, and started crawling behind me to the door.

The first blow was followed by others. Still on my knees, I reached for the handle. We crawled into the corridor, and I shut the door carefully behind us. My sister and other relatives joined us in the dark hallway, sitting on the floor.

My eyes adjusted, and I could make out everyone’s face. I grabbed my siblings’ hands and pulled them close. Seconds later, my parents’ door flew open. Papa ordered, calmly, “Stay away from the windows, and don’t be in the same room.” Then he walked outside, as he always did.

We knew it was the right thing to do, but we never followed his instruction to spread out. My siblings and I had agreed: if we died, we would die together. None of us would be left behind alone. We’d have these conversations whispering in the dark hallway, our backs against the wall, arms interlocked, sitting on the cold tiles.

In those moments I asked myself, is this the night we die? What would it feel like? I hoped it would be quick, that we wouldn’t suffer. My mind went down the rabbit hole of every atrocious scenario.

The explosions differed. Some made a strident whistle before landing. We believed, without knowing where the idea came from or if it was even true, that if you heard the whistle, the bomb had already passed you and would land somewhere else. Massive relief. It was the ones you didn’t hear coming that you feared – the ones that might land on your own house.

Every time one of us dozed off, something went off, and sleep became impossible. After a while someone would start the rosary and others would join. I never did, but the sound of voices humming together in repetition was calming. I didn’t understand how God operated. Was he listening, or away somewhere on vacation? If he was listening, why didn’t he intervene? A lot of prayers were said every night. People who, not long ago, had been living their own lives in their own homes, were now here with nothing but the clothes on their backs. Some relatives were still missing. We waited. Maybe they’d come. Maybe they were still alive. Maybe not. We didn’t talk about the missing. There was nothing to say.

Despite it all, there was a lot of laughter at home. The next morning, we’d recount the funny incidents of the night before.

Muco, my cousin, had panicked and tried to squeeze under the bed instead of coming to the hallway, but her chest was too big and she got stuck – couldn’t get further in, couldn’t get back out. She showed us the whole thing, over and over. We hollered.

One afternoon, my cousin Ntwari showed up from boarding school. He and his classmates had run for kilometers, nonstop, while others chased them with machetes. Those chasing eventually gave up, but he kept running anyway, as far as he could get. The ones who couldn’t run fast, mostly girls, were caught and butchered in the street like animals. He said there was no bigger motivator to run than hearing people being struck and screaming behind you. It was gruesome.

Once we knew Ntwari was physically fine, the cousins made fun of him – called him Muvuduka. Any time there was an errand to run, they’d say, send Muvuduka, he’ll be back in no time as long as someone’s chasing him.

My aunt Schola would paint the picture of her neighbors pillaging her home and farm, threatening to kill her, then burning the house down in front of her.

“They showed up at my house, all of them, machetes and hoes in hand, women and men.”

“What is going on?” she’d asked.

“Leave your house now and go. If you don’t, we’ll kill you. We’re burning it down anyway.”

When she told the story, she’d describe the funniest features of the people threatening to kill her. The ringleader, Gikona, had no front teeth – and though the situation was grave, the scene was undeniably comic. He’d stepped forward waving his machete, eyes wild, but missing his front teeth, so his attempt at menace came out as a wet, whistling hiss.

Aunt Schola had just finished building that house. Less than a year earlier she’d called all her neighbors to celebrate it – the very same ones now standing in her yard with machetes had come, drunk the alcohol, danced, congratulated her. The same people who borrowed her seeds and salt for years. Now threatening to kill her.

“They kept chasing me away, and I stood there unable to move as they burned down my home. They had this crazy look, like they were possessed.”

After a night in the hallway, we’d get ready for school in the morning like nothing had happened. Some days were ville morte – roads closed, everyone home. Other days we were told not to drink the water, that it might be contaminated. People would be shot, disappear, or turn up dead in the streets. Classmates reported windows blown out, bullets lodged in their walls.

I remember writing my final high school exams with bombs going off and helicopters circling the city – hundreds of us hunched over our papers in a big hall, writing frantically, somehow still believing we had a future. I guess we all assumed that if we kept doing what we were supposed to do, our world would right itself again.

“Ma’am?”

I was startled. I must have fallen asleep.

“You are home.”

“This is not home, Prakash.”

“Sorry?”

“My home is Burundi.”

***

item.title: Talking Of Broken Limbs
item.description:
When my cousin Steve died a few years ago, they discovered they had bought a coffin that was too short.

Steve was 6’4″. A very tall fellow. So tall that he instinctively ducked under doorways even when there was no danger of banging his head. Imagine doing that every day. Before long, you start looking slightly stooped. He also moved in slow motion, like somebody had turned his life down to three-quarter speed.

The coffin was a standard size. At least in Nyahururu, where he lived and worked, it was. When they wheeled him out and tried to fit him inside, the mortuary attendant must have said either, “This fellow is too tall,” or, “This coffin is too short.” I wasn’t there. I heard all this from my other cousin, who is also called Steve. Yes, we can get quite imaginative with names. Steve was there when all this was happening. Both Steves were, actually, but only one was participating.

Anyway, they took the coffin back to the coffin maker. They found him at his workshop having madondo and chapati, surrounded by a small army of coffins, the place smelling of fresh paint and turpentine. He looked up when they walked in.

“Look,” they said, “this coffin is too short.”

“What do you mean, too short?”

“The deceased can’t fit.”

“Kwani how tall is he?”

“Taller than your coffin.”

He shook his head.

“My coffin isn’t short,” he said. “Your fellow is too tall.”

He couldn’t simply extend the coffin. It would become another coffin altogether. It would ruin his handiwork. And it would cost more money. Besides, he had other deadlines. (See what I did there? Ho-ho-ho)

So back they went to the mortuary.

The mortician wore one of those dust coats that had once been white but had long given up trying to stay white. In the breast pocket sat a phone that he kept pulling out and frowning at deathly. He told the living Steve, “You should leave. I might have to do something you don’t want to be here for. I’ll make him fit.”

He had the languid air of a man who’d just woken from an afternoon nap.

“What are you going to do?” Steve cried.

“Do you want him to fit in the coffin or not?”

So Steve left.

When he came back, Steve was in the coffin.

He thinks the mortician broke Steve’s legs.

Sometimes, when people ask me to tell them something interesting, this is the story I tell them. 

***

Talking of broken limbs.

I once walked into a lift and found this handsome little girl with her arm in a cast. She was with her mother, standing in the corner the way children stand in lifts, pressed right against the wall, almost hiding behind their mothers. Because strange men walk into lifts, smile at them and say, “Hi. Gosh, what happened to your arm?” That strange man, in this case, was me.

She looked up at her mum, checking if it was OK to speak to strangers because, you know, stranger danger and all that.

The mother smiled at her. A silent code that said, He seems harmless. He hasn’t acted like a sociopath. Yet.

“I broke it,” she said in a small voice.

“Where? How?”

“In school,” she said. “I fell.”

“Sorry! Does it hurt?”

She shook her little head.

“Does it itch inside?”

Another shake.

Her cast was grimy. Like sometimes she used it to clean the chimney. Or crack walnuts and lobsters with it. Or let birds perch on it on sunny afternoons. It was also covered in little smiley stickers and messages from friends. She was probably a celebrity in school because of that cast. Maybe she’d even swung it at a bully or two. It was a busy cast. A lived-in cast. I found it oddly charming, how dirty it was, how it carried the fingerprints of a child’s life. I bet if you asked her to tell you the story of her life, she’d hold out her cast and say, “It’s all here.”

I asked if I could sign it too.

She looked at her mother, who nodded.

She held it out. I found a small patch of white that hadn’t yet been claimed and wrote something on it.

She was chuffed.

But not nearly as much as I was.

Sometimes I still wonder about that little girl.

Still on this lovely subject of broken bones.

One time I was having a meeting at 254 Racquet Club when I saw this fellow hobbling past in one of those fancy casts they put on feet these days. The modern plastic ones that look like they belong on a spacecraft. I think they’re called Air Walkers. He also had a cane. He leaned on it as he dragged that doomed foot behind him.

I found myself thinking, He’s exaggerating that walk. He wants sympathy.

Then I heard myself say it out loud.

“He’s exaggerating that walk. He wants sympathy.”

The two ladies I was meeting looked at the poor fellow, then looked back at me as if I’d just admitted to kicking puppies for sport.

I said, “Most people with canes exaggerate their walk. In their heads they’re Ed Dumani from Gangs of London. Or Captain Jack Sparrow.”

Silence.

“That’s what I’d do if I had a cast and a cane,” I ploughed on, inspired by the stunned silence, nothing to lose. “I’d convince myself I was some sort of villain. I’d imagine the cane could shoot someone. Or stab someone. Or, in a pinch, turn into an umbrella.”

“Like James Bond?” one lady said sarcastically, but I could tell she was warming up to the idea. 

“Did that guy also want to break his leg to gain sympathy?” the other one asked. The more serious one. 

“No,” I said. “He’s just a glass-half-full kind of fellow.”

“So are you saying you wish you’d break your leg,” she asked, “just so you could walk around with a cane and gain sympathy?”

“Yes,” I said. “But only if the cane looked expensive.”

***

How the hell did that tragic BMW climb those stairs in Mbagathi Way? Who studied physics here?

***

Tamms is off to university in a month’s time. I can’t believe it. And because I can’t believe it, I tell anyone I meet, whenever they ask how I’m doing, hoping to register this fact in their own great disbelief. “Wait, what? Didn’t you start writing about her when she was born the other day?”

Then, because nobody likes carrying that realisation alone, it turns back on them. “Oh my God, I’m old,” they gasp. And because nobody wants to grow old by themselves either, they toss the hot ball straight back at me. “We are old!”

It’s tremendous, the effect of time.

***

One December, four or five years ago, this fellow invited me to Samburu, his home. He’s Rendille. How many Rendille people do you know? There are only 96,313 of them in Kenya on the last count. Nairobi probably has more boda bodas than that.

He wanted to show me how his people lived. So he picked me up on the morning of December 26. The previous night, Christmas, I’d been in my brother’s backyard eating like a Roman general and drinking copious amounts of whisky to celebrate the birth of Jesus. I was spectacularly hungover. I slept through most of the journey until he nudged me awake as we swept past the iconic Mount Ololokwe.

I remember that trip because every day we disappeared into the wilderness with this fellow. One night we slept in an abandoned house that belonged to a Catholic priest who had fallen ill and moved to Nairobi. The nights felt enchanted. The sky, strewn with what looked like a trillion stars, resembled a sheet of black metal that someone with mad hair had peppered it with bullet holes while screaming into the night. Animals howled in the darkness. We drank whisky neat from teacups that we had rinsed with bottled water because the taps in this abandoned house were dry. On another day, as the day gasped its last and the light drained into an outrageous yellow, we stood at Malaso and watched the Kirisia Hills suddenly fall away into the vast Suguta Valley, exposing the immense belly of the Rift Valley. Some days we ate meat and bread, like men wandering through the Book of Psalms. Drove through the Chalbi Desert. Tossed bottles of water to the willowy figures of lone Samburu herders floating beneath an enormous blue blazing sky. We were driving a Toyota Fortuner, a vehicle I’ve come to respect because it isn’t really a car. It’s a wild animal with number plates.

He had a gun on him, this guy. I didn’t see it, and he didn’t tell me, but one time we were stopped by these badass anti-poaching, anti-terrorism, anti-everything fellows with small mean eyes and tight wry faces lugging automatic weaponry, and he quickly produced a permit before they could ask him a question. I don’t suppose that permit was his marriage certificate. They studied it, peered into the back seat, then waved us through. Anyway, later I asked him casually what would happen if we ambled upon the dreaded Pokots. And he said simply, “then it would be all over. They will rob us and kill us or rob us and leave us.” I wanted to ask him, “So why the hell did you carry the toy gun?” but I was a great guest. 

Anyway, on day three he pulled to the side of the road, yanked up the handbrake and said, “I want to show you something.” 

It was hot and dusty. The trees looked arthritic against the skyline. When we stepped out of the air-conditioned car, the heat caught me by the throat. Somewhere in the distance a cowbell echoed, lonely and beautiful, as he walked around the car.

We headed towards a great herd of cattle. The closer we got, the more I heard it.

A sound.

Not singing. Not quite chanting.

A deep, guttural sound, as though the earth itself was groaning under some ancient sorrow. It was primal and unsettling, violent yet strangely melodic. It felt like something inside me had begun to bleed- but not enough to kill me.

We trudged on in silence, our shoes crunching over the hard, baked earth. The sound grew louder, thicker. I realised, then, that I had never truly understood the expression the hairs on the back of my neck stood up. Mine rose, one by one, as if the sound carried its own electricity. Its current. 

Then I saw it.

The sound was rising from a hole in the ground.

Inside it were scores of boys, stripped bare, disappearing into the earth, passing buckets of water from hand to hand in a human chain. 

They were all naked. Every single one of them.

Now listen, I come from Nyanza. I’m used to seeing grown men bathe naked along the shores of the lake and river banks. There’s no novelty left for me there. But these were young morans. Waif-thin, all elbows and shoulders, these shoulders – sharp as coat hangers – that shifted beneath taut skin as they passed each bucket from the abyss of that well. Humming. Chanting. Grunting. Not in rhythm, but in something older than rhythm. A symphony. A beatific choir of chaos. A moaning language only the earth seemed to understand.

It was exactly how the earth would sound if you cut it deeply open.

“The famous Singing Well,” he said, almost proudly. “Not the ones tourists gather around.”

That sound has never really left me.

Sometimes it comes back to me. I’ll be sitting at my desk and hear it. Or stopped in traffic. Or halfway through a run. And then I stop whatever I’m doing and think, somewhere beneath the noise of ordinary life, those boys are still passing buckets in the dark, still singing the earth awake.

***
