item.title: Cats
item.description:
My kitchen window faces my next-door neighbour’s kitchen window. I live on the top floor, which also gives me a view into the kitchen of the lady who lives on the third floor. Sometimes, at night, I see her standing over a pot, stirring dinner with a wooden spoon. She’s a white young lady with a very friendly mixed-race son of about six who always shouts hello to me when I come out of the car. His bike is always propped against the wall at the bottom of the stairwell. A bike and a scooter. It gives the block a very vulnerable feel to know that a child lives there. He’s the only child in the building apart from my son. But Kim is turning 13, so he no longer identifies as a child. At 13, they think they are grown. 

My next-door neighbours are a young Indian couple; maybe in their early to mid 30s. The husband is skinny and bearded. The wife is skinny and, importantly, unbearded. A handsome young couple. They love plants. I know this because a few months ago they travelled and left the stairway landing crowded with beautiful potted flowers, presumably under someone’s watering custody. The husband is also deeply in love with his white BMW, which he is forever tinkering with in the parking lot. It is kept in the sort of condition usually reserved for museum pieces and firstborn daughters. He strikes me as the kind of fellow with an elaborate hair-care routine each morning. One day I’ll ask him about it. About the hair, yes, but also how a man comes to pour so much affection into a machine.

Some mornings, while making coffee, I glance up and get startled to find their cat sitting on the windowsill, staring directly at me. Black and white. The BMW of cats. The first time it happened I actually staggered backwards and said, “Whoa there.”

Now I simply stop what I’m doing and stare back.

We can spend embarrassingly long moments like that. Just two mammals silently curious about each other. Because I’m sure the cat wonders about me as much as I wonder about it. It looks like a cat with health insurance. And a chip. Apart from the chip on her shoulder.

Sometimes weeks pass without seeing her, and I wonder what became of her. I linger at the window too long waiting for her to appear, like a lover on a tryst looking into the mist hoping to see a figure emerge. During those long periods of time, I’m often tempted to ring their bell and ask, “Is the cat all right? Did she travel to Jaipur?”

Then one morning she’s back. Belly white. Expression unchanged. Staring.

One day I waved. She never waved back. There is a disdain she stared back at me with that mortified me. I never attempted it again. I respect myself. 

Speaking of cats. And people who become oddly invested in things.

A young lady in her twenties – as she introduced herself in an email- wrote to me a few weeks ago. She said she’d only just discovered this blog and couldn’t believe it had existed for sixteen years (since she was five!), so she has been going down a rabbit hole of old stories.

She’s an aspiring writer. She also wondered whether people “older than 29” – because it’s unimaginable that people older than 29 are roaming the earth – experience the same thing she’d been experiencing.

Her name is Melinda.

Here’s what she wrote.

***

It’s 2:30 AM. I ought to be asleep. I have an eight-hour drive at 6:30 AM. But I’m listening to a song. “I can’t make you love me,” by Bonnie Raitt. The song didn’t just pop up on my playlist. No. I went on Google and typed “Songs to listen to when you like someone who doesn’t like you.” Because once again, I like a boy who doesn’t like me.   

He’s called Leshan. He’s a mid-level marketing associate at a Pharmaceutical Company. I am an entry-level marketing associate at the same Company. He’s been there for four years. I joined the Company about four weeks ago. 

We first met at my job interview. I was seated in the lobby, panicking hard because I really wanted the job. I was lost in thought, trying to recollect the names of the directors of the Company, in case I was asked about them, when a gruff voice asked, ‘Melinda?’ 

I said yes. 

“We’re ready for you. This way.” He said as he opened the door. 

I looked at him, looked at the open door and wrung my hands as my breathing intensified. He whispered, ‘You look good. And they like you; that’s why they called you. You’ll do well.”    

Somehow, those words calmed me down, as he intended. And that was the beginning of my problems. Because when I finally got the job, and we interacted again, I felt indebted, I was biased, and his great looks didn’t help.  He was about 5’6, with broad shoulders and a body that knew its way around the gym. He had short hair with a taper fade on the sides. He had a symmetrical face, which was covered in a rich caramel complexion. His lips had a pink hue. Below them was a luscious goatee that made me forget my plans of experimenting with girls, if you know what I mean.         

We spoke again during orientation. “Melinda! Hi! Looking good as always. And didn’t I tell you you’ll do well?” He declared, not caring that he was in a room full of people who could hear him. “Welcome to the team! I can’t wait to work with you!” 

And that’s exactly what we did; work together. A lot. A lot more than we should have. He would place me in his team for assignments, tag me along during meetings, introduce me to clients as his senior, and on occasion, we would go on work trips, just me and him. Work trips that he planned and could have gone with anyone else. But no, he chose to go with me. 

We didn’t just work together; we spent a lot of time together doing things unrelated to work, like taking walks and watching movies. We had chats about our career ambitions, our desire to get more education, our love for reading, debates about whether the Obamas were overrated, his love for cooking, my love for eating, his dog, my farming ambitions, his hair, my height, society and how it treats women…and so much more. Talking to him was both intellectually rejuvenating and plain fun. Just the way I like it. I also liked how he showed up for his friends, how we shared religious beliefs and how he was quick to take responsibility when he was wrong.    

In my second week at the Company, he took me for lunch at a café near the Office. On our way there, he plucked a flower from a nearby concrete planter and handed it to me. I made a light moment out of it when he did. But when I went to my house, I created a mini-museum for it on my work desk. I would see it every time I was on my laptop, which was all the time I was at home and not in my bed, dreaming about what he and I would be.      

While we were at lunch, we discovered that I knew someone who knew someone who could help us get a client he had been tracking down for a while, and I offered to help. He was so thrilled, he threatened to propose. We laughed it off. But I stayed wondering, what if he did? Would it be so bad? After all, he was my type of guy; ambitious, kind, interesting, interested, and the cherry on top, he was good-looking!  

This last part is crucial because the universe rarely rewards me with a man whose face I like. I’m one of those girls who like a man’s personality over superficial physical attributes. Of course, it would be nice to be with someone with both. But I rarely find such. Well, except for ASAP Rocky, who got into a relationship with Rihanna before he could meet me. Lucky Rihanna!       

With ASAP Rocky off the market, I have mostly been attracting two types of guys: one whose personality I like but whose face I can’t look at twice, or one whose face I could look at forever but whose personality I abhor. The guys I have dated so far have struck a not-so-perfect balance. Meaning, I liked their personality, and even though I didn’t like their faces so much, I could tolerate it. That’s why Leshan was different to me. He had both looks and personality!! And what did that make him? My potential lover.    

After that lunch, I called my girlfriend and narrated how the impossible had finally happened. But because we had functioning brains, we noted that even though Leshan and I had interacted for two weeks, he had yet to officially ask me out on a date. So we gave him one more week to ask me out, before we labelled the interaction another failed ‘talking stage.’  

The third week came and went. Leshan didn’t ask me out. I began getting worried. But I was still hopeful. It’s what you do when you think you’ve found the guy who’s the closest thing to perfection- and Asap Rocky, of course.  The tides would eventually turn at 3:47 PM on Wednesday of the fourth week. I was on my way to consult Leshan on a crucial assignment. 

As I was walking towards his cubicle, which was very far from my cubicle, I overheard him and his mates discussing their preferences in a lover. One said he can’t date a girl who is too educated because they’re proud, the other said she can’t date someone younger than her even by an hour, and another likes them petite with a pretty face. It was finally Leshan’s turn. He said he likes them thick, light-skinned, and they must be from his community.  

Good people, I am petite, dark-skinned, and 41 tribes away from his community. He is Maasai, I’m Luhya. So, Leshan described everything that I’m not and might never be.        

My heart shattered. In fact, I got sick. I suffered from Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. The same sickness H.E. Rigathi Gachagua had during his impeachment hearing (allegedly, of course). The sickness happens when the muscles in your heart become weak. And who can blame those muscles? They were preparing to beat for someone. But they suddenly realise that the someone isn’t going to dance to their beat. That is a weakening realisation.     

And weak is what I became. I didn’t even go back to my cubicle. I ordered a cab and tried to rush home. I needed to scream into my pillow and cry in the shower. But the traffic in Nairobi doesn’t care about heartbreaks. The day you are in a rush is the day a truck hits a boda boda, and the boda boda brigade decides that everyone else must feel their wrath. They rule the road for an hour before the police finally arrive to contain the situation. You’re stuck on the road, wondering if the day can get worse.  

And it does. Because my pain grew impatient. It demanded to be felt and expressed, urgently. So, uncontrollable wails let themselves out of me in that cab. Tears, mucus, screaming into my handkerchief, throwing fists in the air, stomping my feet on the floor, asking, ‘Lord, why me?’ The whole shebang. 

The poor cab driver politely asked me if I had been bereaved, which made me wail more profoundly.  Blame my behaviour on Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, not me. I’m a sober person; my heart is the problem. It never learns not to beat for a guy who hasn’t asked me out on a date. No matter how much I like him, or how many times we hang out, or even if he’s the closest thing I could get to ASAP Rocky!    

But does the heart listen? Does it care? No! Because today is Friday, and since that fateful Wednesday, I have barely eaten. Which is a first because I never lose my appetite, even when I’m sick. I didn’t lose it when I went through actual breakups with people I actually dated. But this man managed to get in the way of me and food? Wow! He’s truly different, even in how he’s breaking me.

As I toss and turn in bed for the umpteenth time because I can’t get any sleep, I call my girlfriend and wonder aloud, “Are we sure I can’t make him love me if I tried? Not even if I turned into a light-skinned, thick girl? How much does bleaching cost? What did Vera Sidika do that I can’t? Also, love compromises, right? Maybe he can compromise the tribe requirement, don’t you think?” My girlfriend tells me gently, “Melinda, you know the answer.” 

Of course I do. But I hate it. And I don’t want to accept it. How do I even begin? I will be seeing him at work, five days a week, sometimes more. We are in the same team! He’s my senior! I must consult him EVERY WORKING DAY! Even his name is nice! Why couldn’t he be called Brian, or Tom, or Tim, like other men? It’s easy to get over a Brian! But no, let’s deal with ‘Leshan’!  Leshan, the mid-level marketing associate, who looked forward to working with me.  Leshan won’t take my heart, but he is taking away my sleep. At 2:30 AM. When I’m supposed to be resting, because I have an eight-hour drive at 6:30 AM. Yet I can’t make him love me. How is this fair?   

**

P.S. Nothing makes you write better than living a life. But you can live the richest, strangest, most scandalously interesting life and still sit in front of a blank page wondering where the hell to begin.

item.title: Small Hands
item.description:
She crushes her last cigarette underfoot and walks up the ramp leading to the hospital’s side entrance. At the door, she nods at the female guard before taking the stairs slowly to the third floor, avoiding the handrails.

The corridor is busy. Nurses push trolleys. Doctors, stethoscopes hanging around their necks, walk while reading files or talking quietly among themselves. The polished ugly-blue linoleum squeaks underfoot. Somewhere, machines beep steadily.

Inside a wide white room with a television mounted on the wall, a man is propped against the bed, reading through his glasses. The windows are wide open. A cold wind sweeps through the room, making it chilly. She walks over to close one.

“Don’t. I’m feeling hot.”

He doesn’t look up.

She lingers by the window and looks down at the strip of garden below, where a narrow path disappears between hospital blocks.

She walks back, places her phone on the bed beside his legs, then settles into the room’s only other seat, folding her legs like a Buddha. It’s a low green couch, worn smooth in the middle and along the arms. The veins on the back of his hands stand out like tributaries. She sits quietly and watches him read. She can hear him breathe, slow and deep, like an old mountain.

“Do you remember what you were doing when I was born?” she asks.

The man lowers his book but doesn’t look at her. Instead, he stares at a patch of white wall beneath the television.

She waits.

She’s used to these long interludes when he stares at nothing.

“There were no phones then,” he says, his voice thick with sleep, or as though he’d only just woken. “It had rained. Not for long, but it rained that night. I was at home. We didn’t have a phone, so there was no way of knowing. I heard about your birth the following day.”

“Heard from who?”

“Your mother sent word to my best friend. He had a phone at home. One of those loud house phones.” He waves a dismissive hand. “You wouldn’t know them.”

He looks at her.

“It had rained.”

“You said that.”

“It was very muddy. I had mud all over my shoes when I went to the hospital. They made me wash them at a tap behind the wards. I found a stick and scraped the mud off while holding the soles under the running water.” He pauses, as if seeing it again. “My shoes were still wet when I came back to the ward.”

He closes the book and sets it aside. He picks up her phone, studies it like a foreign object, then places it on top of the book.

He doesn’t say anything for a long time. The sounds of the hospital seep through the walls and under the door. A laugh drifts up from below the window, an odd sound in a hospital. Like someone eating sugarcane loudly in church.

“Did you ever see any of your children being born?”

He turns his bald head to look at her. His rheumy eyes are the colour of strong tea.

“See?”

“Were you ever in the room when any of them were born?”

He looks irritated.

“We didn’t do those things in those days.” He looks away. 

They sit in that rancid puddle of emotion. She studies her nails. As a child, she bit them until they looked like chewed ginger. She had always been timid, easily spooked by things. By life. Even now, she is often overwhelmed by the future and where she fits in it. As though someone promised her a role she never asked for. 

“When I left my village and went to college in the city, I was only a boy. I had asthma. I was very frail. I would fall sick all the time.” His voice softens. “The city was very big. Scary. All those tall buildings. Roads. So many people. Too loud. But going back to the village was scarier. There was nothing to go back to. No family to speak of. My stepmother was very cruel. I told you about her?”

“Yes. The witch, you called her.”

When he grins, his face folds like an old map. 

“I was determined never to go back. When my own father died, a fight broke out at the burial. My stepbrothers cut one of my brothers with a panga here.” He touches the side of his head. “We all ran into the bush. Me, my brothers, my sister. I never saw him lowered into the grave.”

“Yes, you told me about that.”

He starts coughing, a rough cough, as though someone is digging into his lungs with a blunt hoe.

“When you first saw me in hospital, what did you think?” she asks.

He groans. She can’t tell if it’s the cancer or the question.

He stares at the ceiling for a long time.

“You were small,” he says.

Nothing else.

“Where did you say your mother is now?”

“She’s in Mombasa.”

“Oh, yeah… yeah.” He mumbles something to himself. “What’s she doing there?”

“She got married there. She has been married there for many years”

He shakes his head.

“Yes, I remember.”

He doesn’t seem to remember.

“Mombasa,” he says, almost longingly. “The beach is nice. But the sand gets very hot during the day. You can’t walk on it barefoot. You have to wear shoes.”

A pause.

“I used to go to Mombasa a lot for work. I liked drinking beer there. Do you drink beer?”

“No.”

“Good.” He nods faintly. “Good girls shouldn’t drink beer.”

The feminist in her reaches for a burning torch, but the gentle hand of God rests on her shoulder and whispers, You are speaking to a mountain, child. Another round of coughing and aggressive wheezing. When it passes, he turns to the window and stares out for a long time.

She has learnt not to interrupt these spells, to let herself dissolve into them. His silences are stories too. She watches his side profile. An old head. A stranger with her blood.

“What was my mum like when you met her?”

She knows he doesn’t like talking about her.

He says nothing. Just when she’s convinced he won’t answer – which happens often, he simply ignores certain questions – he says,

“She was like you. Pretty. Small hands. Like yours.”

She watches the side of his face shift. He could be smiling at the memory. Or grimacing. Someone opens the door, pokes their head in, mouths sorry, then gently closes it again. He doesn’t turn.

She waits. 

“Your mother always wanted more.”

“More?” she asks, her voice suddenly sharp with hope.

“She wanted to go back to school.”

“She’d already finished her degree when you met.”

“She had. But she wanted to study again. Become a lawyer.” He trails off. “She liked the idea of courts.”

“Then she got pregnant.”

“Yes. But that didn’t stop her.”

He turns to look at her.

“When she took you away, I looked for you everywhere.”

“It couldn’t have been that hard to find me.”

He blinks, as though waking from a thought, then turns back to the wall.

He says nothing.

Finally, he asks for water.

She pours some from the pitcher into a glass and hands it to him. His hands tremble. The water trembles with them. He takes two careful sips and gives the glass back.

“I want to take a nap,” he says. “Please put this down for me.”

She reaches for the lever and lowers the bed until he is lying flat.

She finds a bench in the hospital garden and sits beside a weary-looking woman carefully studying what looks like a thick stack of hospital bills. You always have to study hospital bills. Every single line. Hospitals can be dens of thieves. More creative than fiction writers. They’ll slip in the strangest charges. Which is the worst kind of theft: stealing from the sick. Or worse, from the dead.

The sun is out, but the day is cold. Shadows drift slowly across the paving.

She could light a cigarette, but she’s trying to be disciplined. Instead, she unwraps a piece of chewing gum and begins to chew. She studies the ward windows imagining the sickness that lives in the people who lie behind them. Just bodies plagued by diseases. Some of who will heal and go back to their lives and some who will die, killing the diseases with them. Disease is like a kamikaze pilot. Sometimes the only way to kill it is to die with it. 

A woman passes holding the hands of a little boy who stares at her, the mother dragging him until they disappear through the two grey buildings on her left. 

She calls her best friend and they talk for an hour. Her friend asks how he is, whether she’s getting anywhere with the interviews. Interviews – that’s what her friend calls them. She doesn’t think of them as interviews. They’re conversations. Recorded. For posterity. For her children, if she ever changes her mind and has some. But also for the settling of ghosts.

“His myth is quite unremarkable,” she tells her. “He has always loomed so large in my life, but the more I speak to him, the smaller he becomes. Like an anecdote, not the main story.”

When she returns, a nurse is taking his blood pressure.

The nurse is younger than her. She has great Luhya legs. She slips the blood-pressure cuff around his biceps and waits for the reading. The nurse swabs his upper arm with cotton wool before giving him an injection. She looks away.

He asks where she’s from and, before she can finish answering, starts naming nearby villages. Then people. The nurse laughs.

“I don’t know them,” she says. “I didn’t grow up there.”

He seems brighter with her. Lighter. Almost playful.

When the nurse leaves, he turns to her. His voice is low and grave.

“All the answers you’re looking for aren’t with me, Lilian. I don’t have them. I lived my life, and now I’m dying… as you will, as everybody will.” He pauses. “You have to make your own story.”

“But I already have a story. Why should I make one up?”

“I didn’t say make one up.” He shakes his head. “I said make your story. Because that wasn’t your story to understand. It was mine. And your mother’s. Nothing beyond what I’ve already told you will change the course of your life. There isn’t some deeper meaning. It was just two people who met, had a baby, and then went their separate ways.”

“Only it wasn’t that simple,” she says, more sharply than she intended. “You abandoned me.”

“I didn’t abandon you. I broke up with your mother.”

“Yes. But not with me.”

He says nothing.

“Why didn’t you come looking for me? Was it because you had other children with other women and they mattered more? You can tell me.”

She expects him to retreat into silence.

Instead, he looks at her with the sorrow reserved for the newly bereaved. Or for someone who’s just buried a pet they’d had since childhood.

“Nothing you hear from me will make you feel better,” he says. “You’re asking an old dying man to remember your life.”

***

item.title: Nims Dai
item.description:
In 2016, I found myself sitting between the legs of a man called Yanick. He was Belgian. He was charming (but that’s not how I found myself between his legs) and to speak, he had to shout in my ear. I was scared. Because we were on a small propeller plane, gathering altitude over Diani trying to attain the height of 10,000 ft from which I could jump. Or we could jump. With Yanick. There were two girls in the plane who would do solo jumps. Pros. They grinned at me, at the discomfort of finding myself seated between a man’s legs. My fear amused them. I was the only one who was terrified. Terrified of the position I found myself in life – between a man’s legs, obviously – but also terrified of heights. Of sitting on the floor of a small plane with its doors open, seeing the clouds, looking down and seeing how suddenly everything was so small, the beach so wide, white and frothy and thinking God sure has a nice view.

Yanick – a skydiving instructor – was mad. At 6,000 feet – to distract me from my fear, for now my hands were shaking slightly – he shouted in my ear. “Do you feel that?” I felt a small prodding on my lower back and prayed that it was one of his many hooks.

I turned back and shouted, “Yeah, but barely.”

He laughed and said, “But it’s hard and nice, isn’t it?”

The ladies – used to his insanity – roared with laughter. The plane tilted upwards. I wanted to throw up with terror. It was a trip sponsored by Tembea Kenya and Chevrolet’s Trailblazers. I don’t know why I had volunteered to jump. No, I know, it was for a story I was writing. There were turtles involved. Najib Balala – the then CS for Tourism – had jumped moments before I did. If Najib Balala could jump off a plane, surely, so should I regardless of the fact that I am terrified of heights. I could never stand too close to the edge of a balcony of a very high building and look down. My heart races and my head swims. So going up the plane seemed like a romantic idea but now, heading up felt stupid.

Yanick made – shouted – small talk. He has had over 1000 jumps, had been jumping for 15 years. He was also a pilot by profession and a member of Kenya Sky Divers Association. He frequently jumped with his girlfriend, who was Rwandan. Over the roar of the bird, she squealed, “She figured a long-distance relationship would be exciting.” Then howled in laughter. “But I also jump with my mother, she is 60!”

“Do you also poke her in the back with your little friend back there?” I asked.

The plane chortled.

“Of course!” Yanick said. “Nobody gets special treatment here, buddy.” 

More laughter. 

At 9,000 ft, planet Earth looks like an abstract painting done by a kindergarten kid. The sea dominates to the left, and to the right land spreads out defiantly. A silver necklace of white beach separates the two, looking like an accessory. Yanick pulls and tugs and tightens and secures our suit as our little bird starts doing a small curve against the azure sky. “Girls are the best people to jump with!” he shouts as he double-checks our suits.

“Why? Because they scream your name?”

“No, they never scream my name. They are always screaming some other guy’s name! You might know this guy, he’s called God.” 

I laugh. “Yes, I think I might have heard of him.”

He then imitates a screaming girl, “Ooooh my GOOOOOOOD!”

I often think humour is the closest cousin fear has. One keeps the other company. Soldiers joke. Surgeons joke. Men climbing impossible mountains joke. Divers joke. People waiting outside operating theatres joke. We laugh because the alternative is to sit quietly with the terrifying possibility that this thing might actually happen.

At 10,000ft, we sit at the edge of the door, and he says, “Deep breaths now, Jackson. Deep breaths.” I’m shaking like a leaf. I’m telling him, “Hang on a second. Just wait a minute. Just one second.” He says. “We have had many seconds, Jackson, this is it. Remember the exit is key. Hold strap, elbows out, neck stretched back on his shoulder, and knees always bent between my legs. When we jump, I want you to relax, don’t fight it, just relax your body. When you feel me tap your shoulder, I want you to let go of your harness.” 

The ladies shout, “Good luck, boys!” 

Yanick taps me on the shoulder, and suddenly we are off the plane and plunging towards earth.

And my first thought, “I’m never doing this shit ever again.” 

Which, in hindsight, is a sentence I’ve said at least three memorable times in my life. Fear, I’ve discovered, has terrible memory. In the middle of an ordeal you swear blood oaths. Never again. You say it while bent over a mountain trail, while floating beneath the sea, after a brutal run, after heartbreak, after food poisoning. Then life wanders by with another ridiculous invitation, curiosity taps you on the shoulder, and before long you’re zipping up another jacket, signing another indemnity form, introducing yourself to another stranger with questionable hobbies. Fear leaves the body much faster than curiosity does.

Which was a lie because it was also the same thought that I had when I summited Point Lenana in Mt Kenya eight years earlier in 2008. I’m from the lake – I come from a long line of fishermen – I have no reason to climb mountains, but the allure of a good story is always a great temptress. We had trekked from Naro Moru route from Point Lenana, camped at the Met Station on night one (3050m), walked throughout a rainy and wet day, eating cold sandwiches and keeping our head low, until we set camp for the night at Mackinder’s camp (4200m), which was colder than a devil’s left nipple.

I remember very little conversation from that second day. Mountains have a way of commanding silence. Everybody retreats into themselves. You become aware of strange things: the rhythm of your own breathing, the weight of your backpack, the sound trekking poles make against rock, the annoying optimism of the guide who keeps saying, “one step at a time, focus on the one step,” as though slowly somehow makes gravity lighter. Your world shrinks to the pair of boots in front of you. You follow those boots because thinking too far ahead is exhausting. Thinking too far back is pointless. Mountains teach you to live in increments of the next twenty steps.

Then the following day at 3 am we set off in the night, torches on our forehead, towards a devilish, windy, and freezing darkness to find our way to the summit. I had a constant headache from altitude sickness. I felt nauseous. I was weak and tired and miserable. And I was sleepy. Very sleepy. I told the guide, please, let me rest my head upon this boulder for one second but he wouldn’t hear of it because I heard if you sleep you die.

I don’t know about you, but there is something deeply lonely about climbing in darkness. Your torch illuminates only a small patch of earth and the heels of the hiker in front of you. Beyond that there is nothing. No mountain. No horizon. No stars worth admiring; you are floating in a yawning chasm. Your head hurts. There is only darkness and breathing. Somebody coughs. Somebody lies and says, “I’m okay.” We were all pretending, each in our own way, that we belonged up there. We don’t. Nobody belongs up those mountains, except God. And the devil. 

When we summited, I had nothing left in me. The dominant emotion I had was deep misery. I flopped on the cold rock. God, it was cold! I looked up at the Kenyan flag and remember thinking, “The flag is made from metal! Metal!” Not even the flag was real. While people took photos and hugged and looked around saying things like, “this is so stunning! This is God’s work!” I remember thinking, “I will never come up this far again to see any of God’s work.”

People imagine summits are euphoric. They imagine triumphant music swelling in the background while eagles circle dramatically overhead. They imagine tears. Hugs. Revelation. That’s not what I remember. Your lips are cracked. Your head feels like somebody is tightening bolts inside your skull. Your fingers feel like sticks. You stand there because that’s what you’ve spent two days trying to do. Then, almost immediately, somebody says, “Okay, let’s descend.” And secretly, you’re relieved because descending sounds wonderfully like going home.

But then not long after, a few years later, I went scuba diving, and I remember how dark below the ocean was. How I wanted to cough and didn’t know I could cough in my regulator, and I panicked because I’m not a fish, I have no business being in a dark, cold ocean. Underwater is perhaps the closest thing to visiting another planet without ever leaving Earth. Sound behaves differently. Time behaves differently. Even your own breathing no longer belongs to you. You inhale. A loud hiss. You exhale. A stream of bubbles races past your face. It is impossible not to become aware of your own mortality. The deeper we went, the more the sea stopped pretending to like us. Colours disappeared one by one. Reds vanished first. Then oranges. Fish glided past us confidently, creatures who had evolved exactly for this place, barely acknowledging the awkward mammals invading their neighbourhood in rubber suits. 

I remember thinking that every environment has its rightful owners. Birds own the sky. Fish own the sea. The mountain belongs to itself. We merely rent these places for a few nervous hours. And you ask yourself what compels people to do such unnatural things. The easier answer is to “feel alive.” But then sometimes when I have eaten some good chapo and beans I really feel alive. But that is never enough. Perhaps “feeling alive” is too lazy an explanation. We all feel alive in ordinary ways. Watching your child sleep. Falling in love. Eating too many mandazis than you should. Those things make you feel gloriously alive too. Yet there exists a peculiar tribe of men and women who insist on borrowing danger to sharpen that feeling. They climb into the sky. They descend beneath oceans. They sleep on cliffs. They run across deserts. They run ultramarathons. [Nick/ Bhavesh] They push and push to feel something beyond pain.

Men will do wild things.

They will face nature. And nature is a force that disregards man.

Nature is wonderfully indifferent. It doesn’t hate us. Mountains don’t wake up plotting our demise. Oceans don’t hold grudges. Avalanches aren’t angry. They simply are. That, perhaps, is what makes them so frightening. You cannot negotiate with indifference.

Consider the sound of an avalanche, which I was Googling the other night. What does an avalanche sound like? Like the earth splitting in half. Like hell at your feet. I went on YouTube to listen to recorded sounds. I read accounts of people who survived avalanches. It led me to Reddit. And then to articles written by men and women who have gone up treacherous mountains, 8000m up, in deep snow and rock and death.

The internet has made voyeurs of all of us. You go looking for one thing and end up somewhere entirely different. You search for the sound of an avalanche and, forty minutes later, you’re reading up on hypothermia written decades ago. One link becomes another. Before long you’re lying in your warm bed long after midnight, reading about people freezing to death on mountains whose names you can’t pronounce, wondering what exactly it is you’re searching for. Information is a strange forest. You enter looking for berries and somehow find a naked woman holding an apple.

I stumbled on a brilliant article on Outside by Peter Stark on how it feels like to freeze to death. I learnt that there is no precise core temperature at which the human body perishes from cold. Somehow I found myself reading about the Holocaust at the Nazi death camps of Dachau (which I visited seven years ago because I like light but I’m seduced by darkness), where Nazi doctors, experimenting with cold-water immersion baths, calculated what temperatures hypothermia occurred.

I could have easily put away my phone and continued watching the white walkers on Game of Thrones but instead I read about a two year old in Saskatchewan (that can only be in Canada) who wandered out of her house into minus 40 degrees and was found near her doorstep the following morning, limbs frozen solid, her body temperature having dropped to 13.9 degrees.

She lived.

Nims didn’t.

And that’s the only reason I was reading this stuff. Because of Nirmal “Nims Dai” Purja. 

I was reading about this stuff because I had gone on Instagram and saw on my friend Martha’s status that she was praying for the safety of some ten mountaineers who had been swept away by an avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak. Nims was one of them, a celebrity Nepali mountaineer. I had never heard of him for the life of me, but I like such stories. So I started reading about him. Then I discovered his documentary on Netflix called 14 Peaks; Nothing is Impossible and thought, “this is bloody extraordinary.” It’s a bit like that story of the Tham Luang cave rescue in Thailand in 2018, when twelve boys entered the caves, left their bicycles outside and disappeared into the darkness, the monsoon rains having flooded the inner caves barring entrance. The whole world began looking for them from their living rooms, offices, airports and cafés. Nations tweeted and prayed. Hundreds of rescuers. Cave divers from around the world. Thai Navy SEALs. Engineers. Volunteers. Prayer warriors. They searched for these children they had never met. And we read about those caves and how extraordinary they are. They found the kids nine days later. 

The world hoped Nims Dai and his team would make it.

His Garmin device continued transmitting location updates. His battery was dying. He was dying. The weather was too rubbish to attempt a rescue without risking more lives.

His battery eventually died.

And Nims died too. 

It was tragic. 

Heartbreaking. 

But also strangely beautiful. 

Not because he died. 

Of course not because he died. 

But because he had spent his life pursuing something that demanded everything from him. There are men who measure a life by its length. Others like him measure it by its intensity. It’s a thing of beauty, a thing to be admired, sometimes from far. I did all those stupid things, even after repeatedly telling myself I wouldn’t again, not because of courage, or the danger, but because of the story that awaited on the other side of it. Maybe that’s the real addiction; the narrative. The hope that somewhere beyond discomfort, beyond fear, beyond common sense, there might be a story worth bringing home. 

RIP Nims Purja.
